MY SAXON BLONDE—A MADRIGAL They say the dark-eyed maids of Spain Are passionate and fond; But eyes of blue are tender and true: Give me my Saxon blonde! An arch coquette is the bright brunette; Blithe and merry and gay; ner love may last till the Summer LS past, • But my blonde's f)rever and aye! U bards of old the truth have told, The Sirens have raven hair; But o'er the earth, since art had birth, They paint the Angel fair. An, well ! may be, the truth to see, A lover is over fond; And I can't deny—nor will I try— My love is a golden blonde I dorm G. Sax.z.

Arrogance is the parent of infame.—Diogenes. A tourist who said to an idle Skyeman, "Why do you lie there all day with your your hands in your pocket's ?" must have been taken aback by the cool reply,'Cause she basna been far enough south to learn to put them in other people's." A • man about town" said to a young lady: No, I'm not exactly engaged, but I have the refusal of two or three girls." Be undoubtedly deserved the crushing rejoinder: "I suppose you mean you have asked them and they have said 'No." Friend (to young New York artist): "Why; Charley, I'm surprised to see you out to-day!" Yonne Artist: "Why so?" Friend: "I passed your boarding-house a little while ago, and I saw a shirt hanging on the line which I am quite sure belongs to you." Old Mr. Sharnley (leaning over the staircase in his nightgown): "Mabel !" Mabel (below): "Yes, papa." Old ker. Sharpley : "Just tell that Brooklyn riling gen- tleman in the parlour that if he's waiting for the morn- mg paper he can get it quicker down town." "It was a severe punishment," said the father, self- reproachfully, "but it answers the purpose. It kept Johnny from running on the streets." You didn't cripple the boy, did you ?" "No, I had his mother cut his hair for him. You ought to see the poor boy." At a certain chapel not 100 miles from Easington Lane. a local preacher was holding forth at considerable lengtb upon the sun, clouds, &c., when an old man, evidently considering such tonics more celestial than spiritual, called out:—" Coom back to the Scriptor. hinny; let's haeScriptor !"—Netreaatle Chronicle. Beware of making your moral staple consist of the negative virtues. It is good to abstain, and teach others to abstain, from all that is sinful or hurtful. But making a business of it leads to emaciation of character, unless one feeds largely also on the more nutritious diet of active sympathetic benevolence. A well-known umbrella maker was married the other day. and at the wedding breakfast, when the !usual bealtlis had been drunk, the best man rose and said, "There is one more toast which, for the sake of the future prospects of the happy couple now present, I call on you to drink, ladies and gentlemen, with all sincerity, the health of St. Swithin." In a church in Forfarshire, an old man, who was some- what famous for his eccentricities, had fallen asleep while the minister was preaching. He suddenly awoke in the middle of the sermon in a bewildered state, and, putting hi a hand up to his hend, and finding it bare, and thinking he was at home in his bed, he bawled nut, to the astonishment of the congregation, "Far's ma nicht- caip ?" A little dot of a. girl inquired of her mother the mean- ing of "transatlantic," and wee told "across the Atkin- tic." " Does ' trans' alyrays mean cross' mamma ?" she then asked. "Yes," replied her mother, "but don't bother me any more." - "Then I guess transparent' means a cross parent," was the conclusion the uncon- : acious little humorist came to as she relapsed into silence. "Is the editor-in-chief in?" asked a stranger, as he sauntered into the city reporter's mem at eight o'clock In the morning. "No, sir," replied the janitor kindly, •he does not come down so early. Is there anything I can do for you ?" "Perhaps so. Are you connected : with the poetical department of the paper?" "I am, sir." "Oh, what do you do?" "I empty the waste- baskets, sir." She had been treating him quite distantly. He didn't like it, and during a pause in the singing, he said—" Yon are such a stranee girl, Edith. I really don't know what to make of you." Then she smiled, and gave him, oh, such a look! as she demurely answered—"lf you don't know what to make of me, you ought. Charlie. Make a wife of me." Sodden transport of Charlie, and hint acted en at earliest opportunity. When Glengarry claimed the chieftainship of the Mac- donald clan, the generally tscknowlede,ed chief wrote to him as follows:—" My dear Glenearry,—As soon as you can prove yourself my chief, I shall be ready to acknow- ledge you. In the rneantime,l am gears. MACDONALD." This letter may have sueeested to Benjamin Franklin the note he wrote to a friend in England when the American colonies declared their independence, and which domed thus—" You and I were long friends. You are now my enemy, and I am yours.—B. FRANKLIN." She was rather an ancient maiden, and her companion was one of those nice young men who are always ready to sacrifice themselves on the altar of chivalry and de- vote their time to the wall-flowers who seem most in need of attention. The couple were sitting on an hotel verandah at Atlantic City, resting from the exertion of dancing in warm weather, and she had taken advantage of the leap-year privilege. An exeression of pain passed ever the nice young man's feeturee, but he was equal to the occasion. "It can not be," he said, sadly, but kindly—" it can not be, but—l will always be a son to you."

Aw buss Lerriree.—During the rebellion is 179f1. an Irish M.P. wrote the following letter to a friend in Lon- don :—My dear Sir,—!laving now a little peace and quietness, I sit down lo tell you of the bustle and con- fusion we are in from those bloodthirsty rebels, most of erhom are killed and dispersed. We are in a pretty mess can get nothing to eat or drink but whisky, and when we sit down to dinner we are obliged to keen both hands armed. While I write this. I hold a pistol in each hand and a sword in the other; I concluded in the beginning that this would be the end of it; and I see I was right, for it is not half ovsr yet. At present there are such goitres on tha• everything is at a standstill. I should have answered your letter a fortnight are, but I did not eeceive it till yesterday. Indeed, scarcely a mall arrives safe. No longer ago than the other day the coach with the mails from Dublin was robbed near this town. The bags had been judiciously left behind, for fear of accident, and luckily there was nobody in it but two out- side passengers who had nothing for the thieves to take. Last Thursday a notice was given that a gang of rebels was advancing here" under the French standard ; but they had no colours or drums except bagpipes. Imme- diately every man in the place, including women and thildrec, ran out to meet them. We soon found our force much too smell; and we were far too near to retreat. Death was in every face, but to it we went, and by the time half our little party was killed we all began to come to life again. Fortunately the rebels had no guns except pistols, pikes, and cutlasses; and, as we had plenty of guns and ammunition, we putlhem all to the sword. Not a soul escaped except some that were drowned in an adjacent bay; and in a short time nothing was heard but silence. Their uniform* were all dif- ferent colours, but mostly green. After the action we went to rummage a sort of camp, which they left behind them. All we found was a few pikes without heeds, a conple of empty bottles full of water, a bundle of French commissions filled with Irish names. Troops are now stationed all around the country, which exactly squares with my idea. I have only time to add that I am in great haste,—Yours truly,—. P.B.—lf you do not get this, of course it must have been miscarried; therefore I beg you will write and ISt me know. Fooressrus.—There is a soothing softrews In the found of the distinctive word in our title—Footpaths—apart altogether from what the term compasses in the way of suggesting endless glimpses of meadow, woodland, and shining stream. The hard, matter-of-fact highway, where the strong drive in their power with vaned results, and where the weak are trodden down in a strife in which chivalry and mercy have frequently a scant place, is, it Is true, one of the chief factors in our relationship; with toil and strife; but it is alike essential to our spiritual life that we turn aside from this dusty and travel-stained highway towards the soft, green, moss-fringed footpaths,. where we may hear the witching tnu&c of Nature's minstrelsies, or touch with reverent finger the hem of "the living garment of God." If we would have quiet enjoyment which will leave our souls wholesome and our tongues untainted, we can readily find it in those delectable regisns to which the humble grassy footpath leads. We can have there psalms from feathered throat, sung beneath aisles of green beeches moist and transparent in the first flush of summer sunshMe. 'Me melodious choristers, too, never break en- gagements; flattery turas not their dainty heads, and their songs are as much filled with the aweetnese of high-born praise as were ever the har- monies of the glowing seraphim. Apart altogether from the delightful nooks, trout-pools, shining shallows, and shady dells, to which our footpaths and country lanes lead, those green, meandering ways have a peculiar charm for the unconventional and open-hearted travel- ler. We experience an exultant sense of freedom the moment we leave the hard grit of the dusty highway, , and touch the soft, springy turf. We have, at once, that indefinable touch with Nature in sight, scent, and sound; and, before we are well aware of it, we discover ourselves audibly reassuring the startled squirrel as he skips from us—a living, nimble line in Nature's epic— into the midst of the screening branches of the umbra- geous elm. What a charming bird-medley, toe! All around call and answer are sent from bank to tree, irons dell to sky. Chatter, gossip. cawing (and this latter not without humour in leering askances and wonderful in- flection of notes), and thin metallic piping songs from tiny bird-dames, fall on our ears as we pass from nook to nook along our footpath; whilst from high overhead, in one rill of unbroken melody, descends the lark's song, 151 t ered through half a league of summer air.—. From Quival fir Sopeather. _

These sessions were held at the Borough Police Court on Monday morning, when a full bench of magistrates attended to consider the decision come to three weeks ago by the Licensing Committee. The Mayor (Alderman Sutton) presided,' and the other magistrates present were—Aldermen Pick- mere, Harrison, Davies, and Burgess, and Messrs. J. Pierpoint, R. W. Francomb, P. Monks J. Platt, Z. Armitage, E. .1. Guest, R Garnett, E. Milner, Dr. Gornall, and Major Litton. There AM a large atten- dance in court, and several clergymen andminieters were present.

Mr. Swift, barrister, Liverpool, asked the magistrates to grant confirmation of alicense which hadbeen granted by the Licensing Committee to John Sampson, for a new house proposed 'to be built on the westerly -side of Battersby-lane, between Scott-st. ancj Sharpe-a.. At the time, he said, when Mr. Sampson's applica- tion was laid before the Licensing Committee, it was stated that in the event of that application being granted, andsubsequently made final, the public-house called the Green Dragon, and the beerhou.se called the White Bear, would be discontinued, and at the same , time it was also mentioned with regard to another , application that if the second application was granted , the public-house called the Fox Inn, with two out-door licenses, would also be discontinued. John Sampson's application was granted upon the understanding that the Fox Inn and the White Bear would be given up. That was not quite what he offered. It was, perhaps, more than they intended to offer, but his clients did not wish in any way to dissent from the terms put upon them by the Licensing Committee. If the license. was confirmed that day the consequence would be that from the time that it became final the Fox and the White Bear would both be discontinued. Upon the former occasion he was very strenuously opposed by a member of the bar, who was instructed by Mr. Ridgway. The opposition, however, seemed to be very childish and weak. Out of five witnesses called two only appeared, and both were teeto- talers who themselves felt no necessity for publichouses . tie did not know whether Mr. Ridgway was going to offer any opposition to the confirmation of the license, but as a rule it was not the practice of benches to inquire again into what had been done before by the Licensing Committee. He was, however, quite prepared to go into the matter de nose, if the magistrates desired. What was done three weeks ago was done by a com- mittee of their own body. In the minty and in Liverpool city the practice was to adopt the action of the com- mittee, unless there was some especial reason for not doing so. With regard to the applicant, Mr. Sampson, there had not been, and he supposed.there would not be, any objection The plans showed that the propsed house would be a moderate size, and in all respects it would be a well-conducted house. There were in War- rington 70 shopkeepers holding off licenses. The total number of licenses, including those granted to shop- keepers, was 205, which left about 235 of a population to each house of every description. This was the only application that he had to make. The chairman a few weeks age expressed the opinion that the public-houses were very crowded in the town, and that was one of the reasons assigned by the Bench for granting the licence which ho now asked the magistrates to confirm.—Mr. Ridgway: 'I don't quite know whether my learned friend has finished his case, or if he is going to call evi- dence ?—Mr. Swift said he would do what the magis- trates thought right.—Mr Ridgway said that on behalf of the same gentlemen for whom Mr. Stewart appeared on the previous occasion he (Mr. Ridgway) now appeared to oppose the confirmation of both the licenses that had been granted by the Committee. If the magistrates were not going to have evidence called, he thought that it would not be necessary to say more than that he opoosed.—The Mayor : It is left to you gentlemen your- selves to bring evidence if you wish.—The Magistrate's Clerk : It is merely a question whether the action of the Licensing Committee is to be confirmed or sanctioned. —lt was decided not to take evidence.

Mr. Seger, barrister, Li4erpool, asked the magistrates to confirm a license granted to Elijah Lawton in respect ef premises known as the Grove Inn, Bewsey-road. Mr. Lawton had, he said, carried on business at the house in question for the last nine years, and had on one occasion been fined Is. for allowing drink to be consumed on the premises. That being so, the owner of the house, fear- ing that the Bench might think that that would militate against the application, had found a fresh tenant in the person of. David Crawford, who had been for eighteen years a publican. It was desired that the license should be transferred to his name after it had been granted to Lawton. With the exception of the time when Elijah Lawton was ffned Is., there had been no charge brought against the house, and there had been no complaints of any kind. Some three thousand people lived in the neighbourhood, and there were large works in the vicinity. For many years the house had had an off license, and the result had been that the roads about that neighbourhood had been made simply unbearable by the habit of the workmen of drink- ing beer in the street, instead of under the roof of a publichouse. They did not ask to be allowed to sell on Sundays.—Mr. Ridgway, in opposi- tion, raised an objection whioh, he said, was purely technical, but which was at the same time one that he was fully entitled to urge. The application was originally made for a full license for a particular house, and plans were put in showing considerable alterations. The application as granted by the Licensing Committee was that the license should be granted subject to the plans being carried out. As they had not been made, he submitted that the matter fell through. A provisional license should have been applied for.—The Mayor: The decision was subject to these plans being carried out, or something equivalent in the share of improvements.— Mr. Ridgway said that if the applicant wanted to alter his house he should have applied for a provisional licence. Applicant must be tied down to the plans that had beam submitted.

div.head: TB DECISION.
div.p: TB DECISION.
The magistrates then retired to consult on the matter, and on their return the Mayor said that he had to announce that the Bench had decided not to confirm either of the applications in question.
APPLICATION FOR AN OFF-LICINCE.

Mr. A. Browne applied on behalf of Henry Corney, a non-commissioned officer stationed at Orford Barraks, tor an off license for beer for premises 173 Orford-lane. Sergeant Cornoy, Mr. Browne said, had been 35 years in the infantry, and had an excellent character. He was desirous ot 'wring the sae-vice and taking the pre- mises in qumtion.—Thei naagiatrates refused to sanction the application. SPECIAL LICENSING SESSION. AN OFT-LICNNI3II °RANTED.

Yesterday morning, at an adjourned meeting of the Licensing Committee, Mr. Segar, barrister, Liverpool; appeared en behalf of Mr. John Clark, the landlord of the Old Coffee House, Horsemarket-et., to apply for an off-license for premises 148 Orford-lane. The Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alderman Harrison, and Councillor Francomb were the members of the Committee present. —Mr. Segar said that the matter was before the Licens- ing Committee some time ago, and, in consequence of a technioal difficulty arisiag, it was adjourned until that morning, in order that certain noticea might be served. He appeared to ask for a license to sell beer off the premises, quite apart from the question of a provisional grant. It was not neceeaary to ask for a license for premises to be built, because they were already built. This was practically an application to transfer a license from Dallain-lane to Orford-lane. Some 200 houses had been .zecently built in the neighbourhood of Orford-lane, and it would be no detriment to Dallarn-lane if the license was taken from that place. Mr. Clark was a gentleman of well known good character, and the premises in question were perfectly suitable for the purpose of carrying on this business. It was not like an a.pnlication for a new license, as it was simply a transfer from one place to another.—Alderman Harrison: I think applicant keeps a publio-house in Dallam-lane 7—The Magistrates' Clerk: He keeps the Old Coffee House, and has an off license in Dalla.m-lane.—Mr. S•sgar : He is going him- self to reside on these premises, and does not wish to remain where he is.—The Mayor: It is praetically, a removal of a license from one house to another, and not the granting of a fresh license.—The Magistrate's Clerk: It is only technically a new license.—The Mayor: I think that what should be shewn more than anything else is the wants of the neighbourhood.—applicant then gave evidence, and Mr. J. lA. Wright spoke of the suit- ability of the premises for the purpose of art off-licensed house.—Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of a property owner, and also on behalf of Sergeant Corney, who on Monday was refused an off-license for the same neighbourhood, opposed the application. If a license had been required in this neighbourhood, he thought that the Committee would have granted it when Mr. Corney made his appli- cation on Monday. If it was granted now, it would be making fish of one and flesh of another. It would be a perfect scandal if the license was now granted, after Mr. Corners application had been refused. The house would not be fit for habitation for some months, and he submitted that it was not actually in existence sufficiently to carry a license—Alderman Harrison said that the distinction between the two cases existed in the fact that the present applicant simply wished to re- move a license from one place to another.—Mr. Browne said that not the slightest opposition was offered to Corney's application.—Alderman Harrison: Ido not see myself why it was not granted.—The Mayor then inti- mated that he and his colleagues considered that there was a wide difference between the present application and the one made the other day. That was an applica- tion for a new license, but this one was for a removal. The application of Mr. Segar for an off-license would be granted.—Dr. Gornall, who occupied a seat on the Bench, said that he had had no voice in the matter, but he should like to ask the clerk whether the question would be submitted to the general body of magistrates ? —The Magistrates' Clerk: No; being an off-license it will not.

LmusTER, SATURDAY, SEN'EMBER 29 188, _ CALIFORNIA. SCHOOLS. BY LILRIMB M. WIIITEL!..SI. LNOTE.---The annexed racily-written and highly in- teresting letter is from the pen of one of Mr. Whit- hams daughters, aged fourteen. She is evidently a jolly English girl,with her father's gift of expression. and a spice of humour all her own. W. are sure our readers will echo the phrase when we say—" write again"—Er. Ex.] Dear Warringtonians,--I think it is my turn now to tell you a little about San Francisco ; Father has told you a good bit, but he does not care to go into schools and education. I think my former teachers, Mr. Twigs of the " PeAple's College " and Miss Slater of the Mount Middle Class school ,arid the school-girls, too, will like to hear something about the schools and scholars of this remote region, so to make it plain I will tell you my own experience as a-school girl. We had been adrised to try a school in , the city, -so ma took me there. - We were shown into the principal's office,Where•l had to undergo an exami- nation first. He asked me if Iliad been vaccinated. I told hienZl had not, so he said .he could do nothing for me until the ordeal had been gone through. So away I was marched 'to the doctor's. He seemed , quite confounded at the idea of my not having been '-vaccinated , before, for Americans are vaccinated once every seven years. He thought the English people were very careless, but he soon scratched my arm up ,and told me to come again the follow- in e Friday. Well, it had not been done two days -before my arm became outrageously bad, and when • I saw the doctor again, he said he felt certain that if -I 'hadn't been done , I should have been in the pest-house by now. • Isn't pest-house a horrid name for hospital? :It was three weeks before I was able, to • revisit school, ,and when I did so the principal commenced his examination. i First he pounced upon geography (their most loved of Studies.) • " Well "said Mr. D. .4SI guess youare aware that Philadelphia is the largest manufacturing town in. the world." I told him I thought Manchester was. "Oh," he answered." they have taught you your own country's worth." " Well," he continued, " how many pounds ,are there in a quarter ay. weight." " Twenty-eight " I answered. "Well you are wrong there," he returned, " there are only twenty- five; you must be very backward if you have not learned that yet.' " Well," I said, "it must be different in England, for I have worked sums with that table for two or three years, and English teachers neter teach us wrong." "Is that so!" he answered (that is their favour- it o expression of surprise.) "Well, then I suppose you still adhere to that silly old-fashioned rule of one hundred and twelve pounds making one cwt. We don't use that at all; understand now it is one hundred lbs. one cwt." And so herwent on for upwards of an hour praising Americas ways, and putting down the English until it came to my little sister Ruby's turn, she pleased him far better than I, because she never contradicted his cutting remarks about England ; but at ' last lie was "through," as an American would say, and condes- cended to remark that we had been well instructed somewhere. Ruby was sent to another school and I was put in the third grade, or fifth standard; but I have been removed since to the sixth standard. It is not the sweetest thing in the world to go into a room of fifty foreigners, to have to stand for a season before them, and at last to be marshalled to a seat in the. centre of them; then to have to sit still for an hour doing nothing, until I got tired and turned round to ask a girl for a book. She with the most solemn of feces placed her Anger on her lips and shook her head. I was made to under- stand afteithat none of the girls are allowed to speak during school-hours, and the teacher can tell very easily if they do, for each girl has a small desk all to herself and the nearest one to it is about two yards away; so if she feels inclined to whisper, she has to do it-loudly, and teachers seem to be made of eyes and ears. About half-past ten, a bell rang and all the children stood up and formed a line as if by clock- work, and marched downstairs into the play-ground for twenty minutes recess, or play-time, but they are not allowed to ru,n or skip, or play ball. They all stand together in groups and talk nonsense. Not one of them spoke to me or showed any signs of friendiiness ; indeed they behave to one another liketboys or bears ; but what is most horrid about them, they fight and quarrel just like boys or bears far more so than they do in England. Of course boys can be allowed to do it, I suppose,because they are nearer kin to the brutes; but girls have no relation at all to them so they ought to have mere sense. When the time was up, a bell rang, and the girls marched into their own lines like an army of soldiers, and stood still expecting a lecturo for their behaviour. They did not wait long for it, for Madame Cherbaux was looking, and at last she burst forth like a thunder-clap— " Yes 'kdith Bacigalupuvon " she began "its very fivany, very funny isn't it ?,you need laugh but I actually saw you with some others sit on the floor and play marbles." I think Edith must have had a laughing nature; for she went on smiling in a way that irritated a German girl for she suddenly began "Yeas yeas von need laugh, ven deine poor moorsha tin hardly appord to send von to school, por shame, ,por shame." At last we marehed into school again, but we had hardly beet in our seats ten minuted before a sharp whistle was heard. With perfect order the girls were up and running down the steps into the school- yard again. I did not know what to make of it, so I ventured to ask a girl--" Oh," she answered, " it's only a fire drill ; you know the wooden schools get on fire so easily, and if we were not drilled there'd be a panic if the school really got on fire." At exactly twelve we went home for lunch, but had to be back by one. About half-past one the principal came running in, greatly excited been itedto tell enustmdthaita aEzanmdetahnod that Professor d of fileat learning gt M sing h Mc Burney was °easing to teach as. I wondered whatever it could be, and was very much surprised 'when he began writing on the blackboard • • Doh, Ray, Me, Doh," the Tonic Sol Fah had never been taught here before. The principal asked me if I knew anythingabeut it ;I told him "yes "for it was taught is the schools all over England. The girls of course all turned round and had another good look at me. I suppose they thought I was " wondrous wise," so they asked the teacher if! might sing the scale for them, but I soon told them that I sang so well that Ma always said it made her head ache, and that it sounded like the squeaking ef a mouse ; so they were disappointed. It was a very miserable rainy afternoon, I remember, so we were allowed a whispering recess of five minutes; this time alittle Freneli girl came and spoke to me. She began talking about the Queen, and when I said that I had never seen her, she said she thought every- body had seen and spoken to each other in such a tinv place as England. Next she asked me if I didn't wish the nasty *ld woman was dead. I told her of course I didn't, and if she called inn MI old woman again she should repent it. That is the strangest part about us. In England we never cared very much how she was called, but here it's woe betide anyone that says a word against her. Pm not surprised: at this, fop I almost believe that Americans would draw a bit of patriotism out of the heart of a snail). I had noticed during the morning a cupboard filled with paper parcels, jars and other things, so I asked what they were for. "Oh," she said, "we have strikes here, don't you know? When the scholars don't like their teaches they join together and wont come to school, and if the teachers try to come near they throw stones at them ; 90 that they keep some provisions in school fear lest they can't got out, but at the end the didiked ones always have to leave." I don't believe all this, but tkere is mem to ho some truth in it. It is very bad, for the teachers must be wholly in the hands of the scholars. The girls are not allowed to be whipped in any of the schools, and they scarcely dare whip the boys, for they stand in danger of being shot if they do, for nearly any day the newspapers toll of some I parent shooting the teacher for beating his child. Con- sidering all this, I think the children are kept under very well, for if they are naughty they stand in danger ' of having a check—that is a bad-mark. These bad ' marks are counted at the end of a year, and if there are too many the pupil can't be promoted, for they have no government examinations like we have. But I've told you enough of this stuff; you must be ' sick of it by now; so I'll talk or write of something else. You cant think how lonely we are hero. If you had ever • felt the slightest bit of homesickness in a L foreign land and could sympathize with us, some of you would certainly write. At home somebody called ' to see us nearly every day, but here no one calls except ' an English lady Mrs. Crich (father used to know her ' husband in England) and a neighbour. ' Mrs. Hope and the children arrived here about a fort- night since,but I don't think she has much time for visit- ing. I am sure Mr. Hope must feel better now for he was getting very homesick I think, although maybe he would not own to it. I've not heard them say how they liked the place, but I think they are indifferent, and I'm not ' surprised for they had left comforts at home that they can never get here. We , don't see much of the other lady—Mrs. Page, but as much as I have seen I like her very well. Mr. Page is very poorly, but maybeit's the climate, for father has never been very well since he came. Indeed if he goes on as he is doing, he'll get positively ill, and so with all this and you not writ, ing as well, if you suddenly hear that the whole family of the Whitham's (there's eleven of them) have died of a broken heart, you'll know that you are partly our mur- derers, and if it happens, there are so many people in Warrington that Ishall pity the hangsman, and perhaps —but I don't know—beg him to spare a few; so beware and please write.

We en, holidays now—eight weeks of them. Isn't it a lot? And so I planned it all beforehand that I should go out and earn my own living for the time, because there is such a tribe at home. Ma told me I could please myself about it, so the first week in my holidays I found a place to mind a little baby, and away I marched to it thinking all the time how very grand and romantic it was; but I had not been there two minutes before that all vanished, and I found I had left a com- fortable home for a poor, poverty-stricken little shop in the city. But there,./ think I have gone beyond my spate now, so I'll leave the rest for another time, when I've said that let ten shillings a week now. But I hate it, and I'm going home to stay next Wednesday, for there's nothing grand and romantic in minding cats and brush- ing hair, ind fidgetty old maiden ladies; but I'll tell you more about it soon,for it really is amusing. And now Good-bye" is all I must say; for timeflies and the clock says that it's time for all good youngsters to be in bed.
13 Valparaiso-street North Beach, San Francisco. August, 1888.

DISESTABLISIIMENT. BY CABSTRIA.N. 'ln these days it cannot be necessary to define the heeding of this paper. The word has a definite historical association. It is an old battle cry. ,As a board in a political platform, it refers to one thing only, viz., the separation of Church and State, "the liberation of religion from State patronage and control." In England and Wales it applies to the Episcopal Church• solely; in Scotland to the Presbyterian Church solely. • Disestablishment pre-supposes establishment. But so far as the Episcopal Church in this country is concerned it is denied that it has, at any time, been "established." Indeed, it is not so long since a worthy Canon contended that the Church, K. far from having been established by the State. " was actually a formative element of the realm of England, and might be fairly said to have had an existence prior to the State.' A statement of that nature can be understood only in the light of the " continuity " theory which seems to be amazingly popular with "Church Defence" men, and the basis of which is as purely imaginary as the "Story of Blue Beard" or "Cinderella.' Accor- ding to the inventors of continuity, the Episcopal Church of England is identical in polity and creed with the ancient British Church which was planted by one of the Apostles (?) of Jesus Christ, or some a their early converts; and at the Reformation r (which not a few Churchmen of the " high " party regard as a most lamentable event), it was simply "purged from mediteval accretions, and emanci- pated from Papal tyranny." It is readily admitted that a Christian Church existed here prior to the union of the peoples of England under one king. History is unanimous ma that point. But we lack the testimony ot 1 history as to the existence of the Church prior to the State. What is meant by the "State" in this connection? Surely not a people possessing mani- Ifold and complex institutions, such as "King, , Lords, and Commons.' Laws may be rude, and rulers no less barbaroup than King Koffee of Coo- massie, but wherever a people exists with laws written, or unwritten, and a recognised ruler, be he I prince, king,or president, there a State exists. If we mistake not, we have read of British rulets who lived I at the time of the first Roman invasion, and, there- fore, prior to the planting of the Church in our midst. That being so, it is a mere quibble to say that the Church existed prior to the State. And it is only another quibble to assert that the Church has never been " established."

We have in this county such an institution as kingship. Can any one name the precise date when this office was purposely and deliberately estab- lished? Is it not of pre-historie origin? Then we have in this land an institution called the "Church," which is so closely connected with the State that its laws in respect of ritual and Articles of Faith, and -Creeds, are all settled by Act of Parliament; its chief ministers, and many minor ones, are appointed directly by the Crown; and its emoluments in the shape of tithes are secured by legal enactments, and not seldom enforced by policemen with drawn batons and soldiers with fixed bayonets. Is it known when this connection was first established? We do not know. Perhaps it was an act of usurpa- tion, conscious or unconscious. We have in our garden several young trees growing. We never planted them. The seeds dropped from somewhere. and took root without our consent. W e are forced now to recognise their existence, and as long as they serve a useful or ornamental purpose we will shield and support them. It might have been in a similar way that the connection between Church and State was first brought about. It grew quietly and imperceptibly. Then there came a time when rulers found it expedient to recognise it. It was useful. The clergy or missionaries had acquired great influence over the people. And so, even when the king was not himself a Christian, it VMS seen that it would be wise and politic to protect and patronise the Church. How the position thus gained was strengthened and consolidated at differ- ent periods is a matter of history too lengthy for us to go into now. But we know that according to the present constitution of the realm we must have a Church; the Sovereign must be a member of this Church. and in all State ceremonials her Clergy have a recognised *facial poeitian. It does seem to our simple and unsophisticated mind that the Church which has enjoyed these honours and privileges has not succeeded in every generation in preserving its identity. The fabrics may have been the same for two or three successive centuries, but certainly not that spiritual edifice which is commonly designated the Church. Was the Church of Elizabeth identical with that of King John Pot the Church of the Commonwealth identical with the Church of the Restoration? If it was, then it must have been very Chameleon-like in its nature. For Papists. Protestants, and Puritans have by turns had ascendency within its pale. But the objection to an Establishment is quite as strong whether the Church be Papal, Episcopal, or Puritan in its °reed or polity. We contend as .earnestl.y against the subsidies granted to Wesleyan Methodism in the West Indies as we do agaiest the tithes which support the Established Church in England and Wales. It is not because the Church is Episcopal that we advocate Disestablishment. We have no more liking for "established" Presby- terianism in Scotland Any Christian 'community which is subsidised or supported by the State is in a false. position. It dees not possess that freedom and independence which are necessary to the development of a true spiritual life. Moreover, not a little injury is done both to conscience and intel- lect by legal enactments which obstruot its progress in tke truth.

AN ANBCDOTH qv 1318MATICIL NY GRNIIIRAL SHERIDAN.— In the article entftled "Prom Gravelotte to Sedan," by General Philip H. Sheridan, which will appear in "Scribner's Magazine" for November, the following incident of a ride which Sheridan took with Bismarck, after the battle of Gravelotte, is related: " Our route led through the village of Gorze, and here we found the streets so obstructed with wagons that I feared it would take us the rest of the day to get through, for the teamsters would not pay the slightest hoed to the cries of our postilions. The Count was equal to the emer- gency, however, for taking a pistol from behind his cushion, and bidding me keep my seat, he jumped out aid quickly began to clear the street effectively, ordering the wagons to the right and left. Marching in front of the carriage and making way for us till we were well through the blockade, he then resumed is seat, remarking: This is not a very dignified business for the Chancellor of the German Confederation, but it's ' the only way to get through.'" "Going out on such a dismal day?' said Dr. Havarti to his protogee, when he met her one dull afternoon, thick-booted and waterproofed, in one of the lanes near St. Agatha's. "Oh, the weather is nothing to me—l can't pos. sibly stop at home: My nerves were positively set on edge from listening to the dropping of cinders iii the grate and the perpetual click of good old Wilson's knitting needles. Your Englancl is inimit- able for its amount of mist and ennui," Ursula said, with a little shiver. She was tired of her aspirations, weary of her seclusion. Even the dogs aid the birds had begun to pall upon her and her heart was beginning to throb with some new pulsations. "Where are you going to, my pretty maid?' asked the doctor, with curiosity. "To visit some of my poor people, to be sure," she answered. "You wouldet have me lead a lotus. eating existence; I leave that to Ray, who likes to have his lotuses served up on blue china." "There are few enough poor people here; don't let them impose upon you just because you are tired of your pretty things," he Said, as he looked at her In his fatherry way, wondering why she should be breathless and excited about nothing. "There's very little real poverty at St. Agatha's, though I confess I think there is a residuum of roguery." "I an tired of my prettythings—even Raymond is beginning to hate them—life is so uniform—so nu- varied in hue."

"Why doesn't Raymond continue his painting?" "He says he doesn't want to inundate people with common-place picture any more than I do. If he were certain of success, you know it would be different, but / shouldn't like him to make a bad third—no, we've done with all that now; as for me I never had more than a certain amount of technical aptitude; but it is different with Ray, he ought to have done well."

" To be sure he ought," her old friend said, more gravely than she had expected him to answer her. .And then, as if ho wanted her to understand how oddly her newly-acquired bits of English slang con- trasted with the pedantic words she still pronounced with a French accent, he added solemnly, "You ought not to let him take a back seat." , Back seat? what is that ? " "Don't let him be mock-nuidest. All young men should be ambitions--should, at least have something to occupy them. As you love your brother, do some- thing to make him exert himself." Why should he speak so earnestly? Ursula could not guess. Ray was not in ore idle than a lot of other golden youths who were always lounging about Abbeyford, amusing themselves at the expense of their country, and willing enough to serve her if they should be wanted. Ursula looked at her brother more critically when she returned with bright cheeks from her walk that afternoon. To be sure he spent most of his time in smoking, with his legs cocked up on a chair, whilst he amused himself with light literature from a lend- ing library. What's Hecuba to me, or I to Hecuba ?" he answered, laughingly, when she tried to lecture him, ani then quoted in his boyish fashion— ,
"%Leave us alone, what pleasure can we have To war with evil! Is there any peace In ever climbing up the climbing wave?'

Ursula noticed how sallow he was, with dark eircles beneath his eyes, and suddenly remembered ,tikow rarely he had an appetite for breakfast, and then thought with a pang how their present style of living suited him far less than the simple regime in Paris, when they had sometimes dined off bread and cheese, or been content with a few shell fish for their main nourishment.

She suddenly looked at him with the docter's eyes, and remembered how her "dear dried-up old mummy of a friend," as she called the doctor in her girlish irreverence, had said, "I am not going to lapse into cynicism, but when you enter the fifties you'll be more than ever convinced that the man who wears the longest is the man who has Wine keen interest in the atrairs of life; even we old fogies don't let our interests fall off, we should follow them very quickly if we did." "Oh, Ray, if you were only like you used to be, deteimmed to make yourself famous 1" she ex- Claimed. _ _

"Was I ever a noodle enough to think of distin- guishing myself? "he said, languidly removing the eager from his mouth and ' knocking off the ashes lowly against the mantel-piece. "Was I over fool enough to care about your little trumpery ambitions? The notoriety which you call success—no one achieves success now—everyone is always aiming at it." "Seek and ye shall .find" she said, not intending Ft flippantly; "there is plenty for you to stndsy, a trained eye like yours will find beauty everywhere, aid as to not achieving success, that is because we arc incomplete beings—we are sums not sAidetl trp," she added, looking CA, him a little anzioeely. It was evident let he was already hemming tor want some fresh stimulant for his jaded tastes ; that kis mind was no longer so able to receive such vivid impressions as when they both had to strive for the necessaries of existence. -

What danger had the doctor hinted at? She hardly knew, but, suddenly remembered the odd terms of the grandmother's will, and how she had to be father, mother, everything to Raymond. It passed through, her mind that she might do like the father of Corot, who sent his son from wateltin,g the shifting mists in the forests of Ville d'Avray, gave him two thousand francs a year, and told hies to 1.23 and amuse himself. Why not, but beee.itee, thongh sho fully believed Raymond had the talent, be waa too little in earnest to aim at prograie; and seoondly because he had already drank of the ex- citing ens, of pleasure given to the wealthy youth of the nineteenth century. She could not argue with him, but stood gazing at kint rather helplessly, till he burned the tables an herself. "Both of its are taking things pretty easily, and now the winter will soon be upon us." Than he rioted, or rather misquoted— ' Summer was a pleasant time, Flower, o' every colour; The water rin ower the heugh. And I longed for my true 10Tel."

"No, I didn't long for him at all," she meswer colouring and suddenly perceiving his moaning. Then presently she said, beginning with a sigh and ending with a laugh, "Oh Ray, how much nicer it would have been if we two had never grown up !" For the feeling of placid enjoyment which had contented her p,s a child wasnot sufficiently exciting now. The leafy shades, the translucent streams and tlio noontide heat of summer had only made her long for the old gipey-lika life in Pans. It was as if her eyes had been opened and she had eaten of the forbidden tree since she saw St. Agatha's in het childhood. She had not even told Ray bow often she had had to fight against the desire for greatin boldness, grandeur, and sublimity in this quiet home scenery. ''She had tried to take an interest in turnips or mangel-wurzel; in the shepherd who still wore his smockfrock, and, with Ins dog. carefully col. looted t.pdpatient sheep; in the poachers whom she encouraged in their poaching, but it had proved in vain. Instead of glimpses of the Briebor Channel, she wearied for the wilder Atlantis or the sapphire Mediterranean. A charming picture she knew the manor-house to be, but she was beginning to weary of all its details as we weary of pictures that we have sufficiently examined. The grey towelrs of the little church, the coombes on a small scale, the sheeny light, or the opalescent sky with the gleam- ing sun sometimes bursting through the clouds on these autumn days, were all effects of which she had begun to tire. And if Raymond had not tired of them, this dreamy, idle life was no doubt enervating his nature. The doctor had tried to warn Ursula,and her easily stirred anxieties were already on the alert. She looke4l at the lad as he reclined languidly on the easy chair, with some light claret on the table near to his hand, and a cloud of blue smoke curling up from his cigar. She had been so long accustomed, when travelling in France with her father, to have wine supplied gratis at two meals —breakfast and dinner—and to see her brother even in his childhood flushed and excited by it, that it had never occurred to her that he might some- times when he was thirsty be content with cold water. She began to see now with Dr. Havard's eyes, and to wonder if even the artistic luxury of the room might not serve still further to enervate Ray's mind. In the quasi-independent position which led the lad to ignore the fact of his real dependence on his sister, it was possible that he had Indulged the expensive fancies of his artistic temperament more extravagantly than he might have done had the money been his own. It was fashionable to lounge ,a little in the well- known Higlretreet if AbbqUi, and it was artistie

to wear one's hair long and to look as irone's was a trifle dislocated when reclining in certain f, tures either in the armchair or on a divan 4 striped Eastern coverings and soft plush cusil,_ which had lately been sent from London to Pi° his taste. hil During the hot weather Ursula had vexed little because she had refused to Wear limp 14 muslin, or to look contorted and strange,'l medimval saint. Just now he gazed at her wi7ll faction; for the sage-green, cloeely-fitting contrasted not only well with the colour of her Ptj but with the dark oak panelling, above which, „v irtd painted waving lilies, lanky stalks, an" ining fishes. • Her vitality was so much more healthy and tense than his that she felt a little irritated fell first time with her brother as ho surveyed her 13 long dreamy gaze, not taking the trouble to rouse self from his listless attitude. "Why don't you go out and take a walk or or—something? William tells me the mare ribly in want of exercise." et "Lab him exercise her himself. What do 3' grooms. for?" he answered nonchalantly leisurely fashion. "You look nice to-day.' b Under other circumstances she would haireo, very much amused by his patronising and To pined approval. But now she wished he c exert himself a little. She had never before t 4,ha

sideied, till the doctor had hinted it to her, complishrnents such as Rapnond's--;-poetry, painting—might have a tendency to make hin3 tr and unmanly. h "You used to spend a lot of time %ut Allstons. I don't generally like baronets, I'd Thomas makes much of you, and his estateh ours. And his son Hubert is not a sham." iy • "You offended the old fellow, when You fered with the keepers." "I think it is / who ought to be offeniPcl,:ie always abuses women, and talks about said Ursula,. with a flush. "But there are pIS others. Why not go and see old Mr. Sello,l;,e consult him about that new plan for heating " servatories ?" .

" Selford is all very well without 11,! pendag,es. The daughters are too much with their 'dearest mamma,'" drawled the iv/ was boo fond of drawing portraits, with Or ink, of the hunrdrum Abbeyford people, middle-class, conventional, Still and fashions, presented such an amusing contras' free and easy life at .Paris. An instinct, Ursula could scarcely have defined, made her ' to stop his cynical remarks, which would 10,t have been illustrated as usual by those terrio French axioms quoted so glibly by Leonard CI and familiar to them from childhood. Ursli
wished heartily, since she had known Pr. Pi that such people as La Rochefoncald or De had never existed.

"I wish you had a little mom entliusiasn'', she said, as she took his nerveless hand and t,r,iti gentle force to pull him up from the chair ; Ralph Melton always so ready to do thingsi l People ; only die other day I found him brisy''t sorts of commissions, and positively visiting $ of the cottages." " I hate anytodY to be full of entliusaial, so much trouble," he said, slowly raising hil,( " and as to poor people, Sir Thomas tells ,j we Should leave all that to the MendicitY °°a' 'Ursula winced. She had never been on go°, with Sir Thomas since a Certain night dismissed her keepers, and the poachers had to muck " amongst the partridges and pheasA,s„. Raymond had taken to the Allstons, and "'"'

any specimen of the model young man. It had always been one of her brother's resent the praise of others like a sidelong aimed at himself, and she could no longer I herself that since they had come iuto the good and the bad in his nati trembling in the balance. That little the grounds near the house had not been re( . . .
yet:For, as she declared there was the greY &Arch, already mentioned, about a mile cient for the needs of ,those of the bousell . _ . _ .

Ursula treated her own soul With about,i indifference as a naturalist treats an organ " lapsed into a rudimentary state. THY PRINCIZS OF WALES AND DAUGH- TERS.---ALARMING REPORT. A Sunday Tines Vienna telegram sayss—The Prince's of Wales and herdaughters have had a narrow escape from sudden death. It appears that the Princess was driving with her daughters in the aeighbourhood of Gmundea, whoa-the carriage approached a level cross- ing. It Joey be necessary ba explain that on litany of the Austrian railways the level erossings are pro- tected by drawbars, wlnch are dropped or raised to, close or open the passage. These bars are worked by wires from distant signal boxes, an electric bell being sounded at the crossing as a signal that „a train is approaching and that the bars are about fo fall. Tbe bed rang as the Princess's carriage reached the redacts'', but her Royal Riehness, net hearing, or not understanding the signal, did not check the pony. The carriage had barely passed the first bar when it I fell, knocking off the hat of the Princess Maud, and placing a barrier between the royal party and the equerries. Simultaneously, of course, the bar on the opposite side of the railway fell, and the occupants et` the carriage saw with alarm that they could neither ad- vance nor retreat. The next moment the %rain was seen approaching, and the destruction of the whole party ap- peared to be inevitable. Providentially, however, Col. Clarke, who was in attendance, took in the situation at a glance,'and in less time than it takes to toll had dis- mounted, ducked under the bar, and sesced the pony's head. With rreat presence of mind, he pulled the car- riage off the line and into the fence, just as the train, with brakes down and whistle blowing, rushed by within a few inches of the startled ladies. An eye witness says that the whole thing occurred so rapidly that their Royal Highnesses hardly realised the horror of the situa- tion until the danger was over and the barriers vore once more raised. Had Colonel Clarke been less proffipt, or had the pony proved obstinate or restive, all must have been killed. As it was, the Princess, although naturally much shaken, was able to drive her daughters back to the palace. Inquiry at Marlborough House on Sunday shortly be- fore nine p.m., elicited the fact that no official confir- mation had been received of the reported narrow escape of the Princess of Wales. Indeed no despatch referring to the matter had come to hand at all, and the officials in charge were only in possession of the facts as pub- lished by the Sunday papers. The Royal yacht Osborne arrived in Sheerness Har- bour, on Tuesday, from Flushing, having on board the Princess of Wales and her three daughters, returning from the Contineut. The flagship at the lore (11.M.S Duncan) fired a Royal salute* 21 guns, and their Royal Highnesses were received at Port Victoria by the prin- cipal officers of the port. A special train conveyed them to London. The Princess of Wales and her daughter reached Charing Cross at 12 15 pm. apparently in excellent health.
ANOTHER WOMAN MURDERED AND MUTILATED.-BRUTAL AND MYSTERIOUS MUR- DER.

A woman, named Jane Beatmoor. 28 years of are, was the victim of a horrible murder at Birtl7, near Gates- head, on Saturday night or Sunday &ming. It appears that the deceased, who was in delicate health, had been at the Gateshead Dispensary on \Saturday for medicine, and on returning home went out to purchase some sweets with which to take her medicine. She called at several farms while she was out, and at half-past seven at night left the house of an acquaintance, named Mrs. Newell, evidently with the intention of returning hoine. She had not arrived at 11 o'clock, and her mother and stepfather went to look for her, hilt without suceess, and concluded that she must have spent the night with some neighbours. Early in the morning a miher, named John Fish, going to work, found the body of the deceased at the bottom of a railway embankment in a horribly mutilated condition. The county police were comnv,ni- cated with, and Sergeant Harrison awl Sergeant Hutchin- son, of Birtley, were soon on the spot. The body was conveyed to Birtley and a doctor sent for. The doctor expressed the opinion that the body had been mutilated with a knife. The affair has caused quite a panic in the district

The greatest excitement continues to prevail in Birtley and the surrounding district concerning the terrible out- rage on Jane Beatmoor, which was enacted there on Saturday evening. The local police cast their suspicions upon a man named William Weddell, an ironworker at Birtley, whe for some time past has been endeavouring to force his attentions upon the deceased. He has absconded, and the police have been furnished with his description. He is about sft. 9in. in height, with a sal- low complexion, high cheek bones, and generally sharp features. He has a slouching, stooping gait, and a furtive expression. The inquest wasopeued on Monday morning and adjeurned for a fortnight. The injairies sustained by the deceased are shocking. On the right side of the face there is a deep cut about an inch wide, whloh has hid the lower jaw open to the bone. On the left side of the neck below the ear there is a gash about two inches in length ad extending right down to the tep of the spine. This wound alone, in the opinion of the medical men would have mused instant death. The third ind most severe of the cuts received. by the poor woman is in the abdomen, from the wound in which the entrails protruded. It is aPsumod,that the unfortunate woman was killed by the blow on her neck, and that subsequently her murderer endeavoured to hack the body to pieces. Dr. Phillips, who made the post-mortem examination of the victim of the last Whitecha,pek murder, has been sent to Durham, with a view to ascertaimine whether the I injuries inflicted on her resemble those inflicted on the Whitechanel With reference to the murder and mutilation near Gateshead, Dr. Phillips, divisional police surgeon, states that it is evidently not done by the same hand as the Whitechapel murder, that at Gateshead being simply a clumsy piece of butchery. The young woman was buried on Wednesday, at Birtley, in presence of an enormous crowd.

div.head: WHITECHAPEL MURDERS.
div.p: THE WHITECHAPEL MURDERS.

The-inquest on Mary Ann Nicholls, who was murdered in Buck's-row on Sept. Ist, was resumed in Whitechapel on Saturday, and ooncluded.—Robt. Ede, who had stated previously that he bad seen a man with a knife in the neighbourhood, new said that lie had since seen this man, who had a wooden leg and arm, and was de- clared by the police to be entirely innocent of the crime. The Coroner summed up, and laid stress on the similarity of the four recent murders in the district, especially in regard to abdominal mutilations. The taking away of some organs from the body of the latest victim suggeeted that as the cause of death, and he suggested that Nicholls might have been murdered with the same object, but tho perpetrator was disturbed before accomplishing his object. The only way in which he could account for the mur- derer failing to attract aKention in consequence of blood on his person, was that a great number of men worked in slaughter-houses in the district.—The jury retired to consider their decision, and alter Sim absence of twenty minutes, returned a verdict of a Wiliol murder against some person or persons unknown " •

INQUEST ON ANNIE CHAPMAN. Mr. Wynn Baxter, on Wednesday, resumed the inquest at Whitechapel on the body of Annie Chapman, who was murdered on the Bth inst. in the backyard of 29, Han- bury-street, Whitechapel, London. The coroner at once proceeded to sum up the evidence. He recalled the important facts of the case, which have already been fully detailed. The coroner then proceeded to observe—there are two things missing. Her rings had been wrenched from her fingers and have not been found, and an internal organ has been taken away. The body has not been dissected, but the injuries have been made by some one who has considerable anatomical knowledge and skill. There are no meaningless cuts. The organ has been taken away by one who knew where to find it, what difficulties he would have to contend against, and how he should use his knife so as to abstract the organ without injury to it. No unskilled person could have known where to find it, or have recognised it when it was found. For instance, no' mere slaughterer of animals could have carried out these operations ; it must have been some one accustomed to the post-mortem rooms. The conclusion that the desire was to possess the missing organ seems overwhelming. It is clear that there is a market for the missing organ. Within a few hours of the issue of the morning papers, containing the report of the medical evidence given at the last sitting of this court, I received a communication from an officer of one of our great medical schools. I attended at the first opportunity, and was informed, by the sub-curator of the Pathological Museum, that. some months ago an American had called on him, and asked him to procure a number of specimens of the organ that was missing in deceased. He stated his willingness to give £2O for each specimen, and said his object was to issue an actual specimen with each copy of a publication on which he was then engaged. He was told that his request was impossible to be complied with, but he still urged it. He wished them preserved; not in spirits of wine, the usual medium, but in glycerine, in order to preserve them in a flaccid condition, and he wished them sent to America direct. It is known that this request was repeated to another institution of a similar char- acter. Now, is it not possible that knowledge of this demand incited some abandoned wretch to possess him- self of a specimen? We are confronted with a murder of no ordinary character, committed, not for jealousy, revenge, or robbery, but from motives less adequate than the many which still disgrace our civilisation, mar our progress, and blot the pages of our Christianity. The jury immediately returned a vedict of wilful murder against some person or persons unknown.

ANOTHER TRAGEDY II? LONDON.—A. case of fratricide occurred on Wednesday at a public house known as the Round House, Hall-street, Goswell-road, London. Two brothers had a quarrel at dinner time, and subsequently drew knives on one another. One received injuries of a fatal character, and on removal 'to St. Bartholomew's Hospital was found to be dead. On the police going to arrest the other brother he endeavoured to commit suicide by stabbing himself, and was removed to the same hospital in which his brother's body was lying. He is in a very serious condition. THROWING A MAN OPT OF A RAILWAY CApRRIAGE.— A man named Heaton is in custody at Ashton-under- Lyne on a charge of having thrown a mulatto, whose name is unknown, from a train on the London and North-Western Railway on Monday night. THE BX-TOWN CLERK OF BALFORD,—A meeting of the creditors ot Mr. John Graves, late Town Clerk of Salford, was held in Manchester, on Monday. Proofs were lodged of liabilities amounting to £3,805. The Assistant Offioial Receiver said nothing had been heard of the bankrupt since the announcement to the court that he had absconded. A request had been made that the Official Receiver should apply for a summary order to deal with the estate, but as the assets were likely to exceed £3OO. inasmuch as they will probably come up to £4OO, and possibly to £5OO, this course could not be adopted. It I was likely that further liabilities would be discovered, but, on the other hand, there was evidence of consider- ably heavy debts owing to the bankrupt. Mr. T. W. Handley was appointed trustee, and a committee of inspection will be appointed atla future meeting. HORRIBLE Snooriwo Casr.—On Saturday night, at the raining village of Mexborough, near Sheffield, a boy named William Barras, aged seven years, son of the cap. I tain of the barge Lily, of Thorne, was shot by Patrick I M'llamara, a mate on the barge Nero. The captain was away, and the injured lad strayed into the cabin. The mate is said to have then picked up a revolver loaded in six chambers, and, pointing it at the bead of Barras, said "I will show you how they kill pigs." He at once de- liberately fired at the boy. The shot entered the fore- head, and penetrated to the back of the left eye The poor little fellow rushed out of the cabin, blood stream- ing from his face. He was seen and carried to a doctor, who extracted the bullet. The child lies in a very criti- cal condition. The mate absconded, and has not since been seen. It is supposed he did not know the revolver was loaded. On one occasion, when principal of Lampeter College in Wales, he was walking in Cardiff, where he saw a crowd in the street looking at, but not offering to interfere with a big, burly sailor, who, in a half-drunken frenzy, was roughly as- saulting a woman. Mr. Jayne made his way through the crowd, and remonstrated with the man, who forth- with, letting Rothe woman, turned upon Mr. Jayne and dealt him a tremendous blow, which left an ugly bruise on his face. Thereupon Mr. Jayne closed with the mast pinned both his arms behind his back as if he had been a child, and quietly held him there till a policemar came up, to whose custody he handed him, with the quiet reprimand," You should not strike a woman, my -man."

div.head: MR. DILLON AND THE GOVERNMENT,
div.p: MR. DILLON AND THE GOVERNMENT,

Mr. John Dillon, M.P., speaking on Tuesday, at the fort- nightly meeting of the, National League, over which he presided, said that since he last spoke at the League meetings he had suffered three months' imprisonment, but it had not brought repentance for his deeds. If it was s crime to endeavour to win for the people of Ireland the privilege of freedom, to devise a policy by which they could de- fend their homes until the time they could live peaceably, and make their own laws; and to attempt te withdraw the r,eopie from the dark WRVS of secret com- bination, murder, ar.d outrage, and lead them into paths of honourable evenbination and noble action—then he would continue that crime. Be could not share the im- patient remarks that had fallen from sonic of his friends in reference to the action of the English people. No doubt it was herd to beer the present tvigime : but they should be patient The English people were no.sv their friends. There was a time when he hated the name and power of England and Englishmen, but the present noble action of the English people had banished that feeling, and now he could not find any trace of it left in him. He denied that he was imprisoned for a breach of the law, but for defying the f.%overnment. He was found guilty most scandalously, on evidence no Crown prose- cutor would place before even a packed jury. The English were being converted at a wonderful rate. Looking along the line since his release, he gladly saw the people holdhig the mitrenchineet, save in a law in- significant cases. The winter was coming, and he chal- lenged hie critics of the Plan of Campaign to place before the country a better, and he would gladly give it his support. He could not, however, advocate a retiarr. to the Itibbms. Lodge and Secret Society. Lord Salis- bury had declared against a reduction of judicial rents, ‘.nit by the Plan of Campaign the tenants had the advantage of a quarter of a. !Militia a year, or since the adoption of the Plan of 188 d, about £750,000, besides preventing numbers of evictions. He I was setieked that if the Government suceeeded in

breaking down the men fighting in the forward line, the crowbar and eviction lie.,gatie would sweep over Ireland like a devastating tompeet. He claimed that the Ettityilu of the evictors' hands was due to two causes alone— fear caueed by the Plan of Campairn, and the boyoottinr evicted farms. (Applause,) It was said, "Let sensible men meet and settle the question." He wished sensible men woukl, but he would not go int. conference, having laid down his arms. The whits ttag resulted in failure and disaster, and ex- perienee taught that those who wished peace must be prepared for war. When the Government wooki dis- arm the Irish oonstabulary, and break up the Land Cor- poration and the Property Defence Association, then he would consider the propriety of laying down his arms. (Applause.) But the idea that the people should kneel and be mercy from those who never showed any tilt fear drove them tot it, was as foolish as could be. (Ap- plause-) So long as he found any body of Irish temente willing to fight us the forward line for the home that sheltered their w, yes and little ones, he should net cease

to raise his voice to encourage them, and appeal to the aNI t te,,rfel Irwin-03er' of the Irish race bn rally round thete. (Applause.) Mr. T. M. HEALY said the Irish race should be self-re- Bent, and not depend too much on England or any other country. The tenants should give the landlords as much legal annoyance as possible, and when their homes were levelled by bailiffs ho did not see why they should not apply for compensation. He believed Judge Oglagan to be one of the greatest cursea ever inflicted on the c..ountry, but he had tatt Sc learn whether that judge would pass ever iajaations done to; men like Lord ChM- ricarcie in levelling the tonnes of his tenants.
TUE 'WELSH CH ORM ANT) WEII-11. DISSENT.-EXTRAORDINARY CORRESPONDENCE.

Canon Byte, son of the Bishop of Liverpool, late Prin- cipal of Lampeter College andlseart Professor of Divinity at Caurbrielge. was invited to preal the in- augural sermon at the St. Asaph Diocesan Conferenee, at rorwen, on the 15th September. The Vicar ef Brymbo, DenbiYhshire, wrote to Canon Ilyle directing attention to eivisages in his sermos wherein he gratefully ac- knowledged the work of those who fought for light against the powers of darkness when the oondle of the historic Church burned low, and recognising the efforts of all those who are working in the spirit of Christ, not as rivals, but as comrades. " I take it for granted," adds the Vicar of Brymbo, " that you refer here to the work of Dissenters. Dissent is schism, and schism is sin." In the course of a lengthy reply, Canon Ryle says:—At a time when in Wales many Churchmen are tempted to see in Nonconformists only political opponents, it is not unreasonable 'to remind them of the service rendered by Nonconformist brethren towards the evang,elisatinn of neglected districts. For their act of schism God shall judge them, not I. It is not for me to bring an accusation against those whose holiness and walk with God put my own life to shame. God alone knows the tempations they endured, the pro- vocations they received, the lack of privilege, oppor- tunity, the instruction in which they were reared—how much of that Nonconformity has not resulted from the unsympathetic and even hostile attitude of the Church towards the untutored zeal of comparatively uneducated men. The repulse of emotions far more than the diver- Elity cif theological views has occasioned the Noncon- formity to which I allude. Let him that is without the inint of controversial bitterness throw the first stone at them. Mr. Osborne Morgan, M.P., 'presiding on Monday aieit at a meeting of Calvinistic Methodists at llrymbO, referred to the above correspondence. The hon. mem- ber said that in making the assertion that "Dissent is schism, and schism is sin" the Vicar must have forgotten the Reformation, which was "the greatest schism that ever rent the religious world in twain." It was, he added, the survival of a spirit of narrow exclusiveness which made it difficult for tolerant and fair-minded men to remain members of the Church of England. s

div.head: CLEVER FEMALE COINER.
div.p: A CLEVER FEMALE COINER.

At the Liverpool Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. Raffles, a young man, named Charles Bourke, and Susan Bourke, his wife, were charged with being in possession of base coin and implements for manufacturing the same. According to the evidence of P.C. Williams there was found on the male prisoner a bag containing six base half-crowns and four shilling pieces. In the pri- soner's house were found implements for manufacturing coin. The female prisoner said when she came out of prison after serving nine months for a similar offence to that with which she is now charged her husband told her that she would have to go at the same game again, and that he would work no more. She replied that if she commenced again and was taken for the crime he must be taken with her. She then commenced to make base coin for a living and she used to sell them to people who passed them, and she received 6s. and Bs. for the pound's worth of bad money. her husband used to sell the coin for her to people who passed them, but the last lot he sold he drank the money and came home drunk. It was stated that the whole family of the female pri- soner were base coiners, and her father had just recently been committed for trial at the assizes. The prisoners were remanded for seven days.

Mr. Poland and Mr. Mead prosecuted, and Mr. Tickle defended the prisoner. The trial will probably occupy the whole of the day. SANKEY BRIDGE V. RAVENREAD.—These teams met On Saturday, when the former won by 1 goal and 1 try to nil. WARIUNGTON JUNIORS V. FRODSHAM "A" TM.—The first pine of the Halton football season was played on Saturday, at Halton, when the home team were opposed by the A team of Frodsham, who they defeated by 1 goal, 8 minors, to nil.
