HECEMONDWINR.—On Saturday Widnes journeyed into Yorkshire with a weak team, Plumpton and Farrell being absent, and were also placed at a disadvantage through lack of practice. Another disad- vantage was that Hughes, one of the best forwards of the VVidness team, had his right knee sprained at half- time, and had to retire for the rest of the game. Before the game had been on a minute Widnes compelled the home team to save. Heckmondwike added several minors (nearly all dead balls, from long kicks), and Duffy succeeded in getting a try near the goal. The place was an easy one, but Sutcliffe failed to add the major point. A couple more minors were scored by the home men, and then Gill ran in near the touch line, Sutcliffe again failing a to improve. In the second half Heckmondwike added six minors, the Widnesians, not. withstanding the manner in which they were handi- capped, playing up well. Finalscore :—Heckmondwike, two tries and eleven minors; Widnes, one minor. FRODSHAM V. WIDNES TRUE BLUES.—This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday in splendid weather, and in the presence of upwards of 500 spectators. Fred- sham were without the services of Rogers, Darlington, Ashworth, and Dimelow, and played four second team men. For a quarter of an hour the game was very evenly contested, when Brooks got over the line for Frodsham, for which Goodall kicked a goal. No further score was made up to half-time, but most of the play was in the True Blues quarter. Score at half-time— Frodsham, one disputed goal ; True Blues, nil. On change of ends, after some open play, Thomas obtained a try for Frodsham from a very neat dribble made by Brooks and F. Darlington, no more being made from it. Shortly after Tudor made a nice run from the centre of the field, and placed the ball between the posts. After a very fast-played game Frodsham won by three tries and two minors to nil. The two second team men,F. Dar- lington and Helsby, played verb' fast forward, and are likely to be tried in the next match. Disputed goal in first half decided against Frodsham. .

RrNCORN "A " tE.&3I V. ST. ANNE'S GYMNASIUM.— Whilst the first team were busily engaged at Bradford, the Runcorn second string were engaged at the Irwell- lane ground, meeting the St. Anne's Gymnasium, a team in connection with the St. Anne's Church, Birken- head. St. Anne's having choice of ends, Gatley started the ball facing a strong sun, and Cartwright failing to send the ball back, play located in the visitors half. Cartvitight by a lucky fly kick saved a bit of smart passing by Cawley to Woods, the latter to Lunt, t Woods following up e effort by a drop at goal; Cartwright kicking dead. Minors quickly followed owing to the fast play among the forwards. New and then some passing was done, but with a little more judgment the home forwards would have scored freely. When the interval came Runcorn had 5 minors to their credit, St. Anne's nothing. After change of ends, John- son started. Forward efforts by Rigby and Hailwood got play near the St. Anne's line where from a scrim- mage Evans threw out to Woods, who very coolly dropped a goal. Hailwood did some smart collaring, being in this department closely followed by Rigby; and again the visitors were pressed back on their lines. Though Gardiner, Nott, and Platt worked hard to relieve the pressure, they could not prevent Abrams getting in at the corner after a spirited run. No goal resulted. Shortly afterwards Whinyates sprinted, scoring a good try, the „oxial kick failing. The attack was still kept up by the Runcorn lads, S. Abrams again scoring by a determined effort The next to score was Cawley, from a pretty pass by Woods. Still no gaol was obtained, Woods only missing by the merest shade, the ball this time striking the post. The home team still had the best of the play, which was chiefly confined to the St. Anne's half, until Woods ran in easily from a pass by Abrams, and a very pleasant and spirited game resulted in a decided victory for the home players by one goal, five tries, eight minors, to nothing. The -St. Anne's team, though over-matched forward, played with great deter- mination. Fairbrother, Johnson, and Cartwright were the most prominent. Behind thpre was little to choose. In the winning team Woods played a capital centre I game. S. Abrams was very smart at half back. Rigby, Hailwood. Shaw, and Bowyer shone in the forward division. The teams were :—Runcorn " :" S. Booth, back; E. Lunt, T. Woods, and W. H. Cawley, three- quarter backs; W. Evans, and S. Abrams, half backs; J. Gatley, J. J. Bcwyer, T. Cox, W. Shaw, R. Hailwood, T. Abrams, W. Rigby, J. Ford, and T. Whinyates, for- wards. St. Anne's Gymnasium: J. Mitchell, back; J. W. Fairbrother, D. Cartwright, and C. Kelly, three- quarter backs; J. Johnson (captain) and W. Gouldson, half backs; J. Gardiner, 8: Platt, J. Nott, H. Rogerson, A. Salter, T. Salter, H. Bravey, A. Davies, and F. Holy- oake, forwards. WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE HORNETS, " A " TEAMS.— The Warrington "A " teim journeyed to Rochdale on Saturday to play their old opponents the Rochdale Hornets"B "team, and the fixture being looked for- ward to with considerable interest a large number of spectators witnessed the match. The home team won the toss, and Bate kicked off for Warrington at 3.15 p.m., -Smith returning into touch. It was soon appar- ent that the combination of the Warrington team was far superior to that' of the Hornets, especially in the forward division. The ball was worked into the home half, the visitors scoring a dead ball after a grand dis- play of passing on the part of Lawless, Appleton, and Bibby. Bamford dropped out. Appleton returning to Smith, who obtained a free kick, and sent the ball into touch. Bate got nicely away and passed to Lawless; who kicked and followed up, another dead ball being registered for the visitors. Soon after the drop out Warrington' by good forward play, again forced the home team back on their line. the ball was eventually passed to Bamford, who scored a dead ball for the home side by a long kick. Appleton dropped out, Hawks- worth returning to centre. Appleton was next to the front with a good run and kick, and Adamson prevent- ing any return, Warrington penned their opponents near the goal line, their efforts being rewarded by Nevins gaining a try, which J. Bate converted into a goal. On call of half time the score was—Warrington 1 goal and 2 minor points, Rochdale Hornets 1 minor point. On change of ends Holman re-started for the home team, Nevins returning to the former player, who obtained a free kick in front of goal, but the ball was charged down by Adamson. The home team had the best of the game for a time, scoring two minor points; one from a long kick and the other from a dribble on the part of Nuttall and Rhode. Smith next tried to get away, but Boscow returned well, and the Warrington forwards, by short stages, took play to the Hornet's territory, Nevins crossing the line but the point was disallowed, and Holman and Schofield broke away with a dribble to centre, Appleton saving. A strong rush of the War: I rington forwards, foremost among whom were Adamson, Lloyd, Holmes, and Bate, again placed the ' home line in danger, and Lawless charging down a kick by Smith, gained a splendid try, J. Bate this time failing at goal. On call of time the score stood :—War- rington. 1 goal, 1 try, and 4 minor points; Rochdale Hornets, 5 minor points. The special feature of the game was the splendid combination on the part of the Warrington forwards, they playing with great dash and exercising good judgment, completely outplaying their opponents. The backs also played well, their passing eliciting the applause of the spectators. Warrington team :—Full back, Boscow ; three-quarter backs, Daniels, Appleton, and Bibby half backs, J. Bate and Lawless ; forwards, Adamson Molvneux, Eyes, F. Bate, Holmes, Jones, Nevins, Lloyd, and Beard. WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE HORNETS.

Previous to Saturday Warrington and Rochdale Hornets had met on five occasions and in every instance the game had resulted in a draw. On Saturday, however, the monotony of this record was broken, the home team managing to gain a victory by two goals to one. There was again a large attendance on the Wilderspool ground and a game of a very exciting nature was witnessed. Warrington losing the toss the ball was started by Frank Turner in face of a bright sun. Evans was the first to become prominent with a neat kick,' but the opposing forwards, headed by Groves, neutralized the effort. Antrobus essayed to get away from the pack, but Barnton checked his career. The latter player put in a tricky run, and after Barnes and Speakman had indulged in some quick transfers, the visitors' centre placed the game well in the Warrington quarters. Still closer the home team were pressed on their line, and although Barnes, Speakman and Massey raised the hopes of their admirers, the relief was only momentary. Evans now made headway, and passed judiciously to Ashton, but wild play gave the Hornets a chance, and quick and clean passing finally ended in Barton gaining a meritorious try, Pennington placing a goal. Massey, soon after restarting, showed up with some grand work, and after Speakman had placed the Hornets on the defensive, Groves put in a well-timed dribble, which

placed the game at midfield. Give and take play was now the order, until Groves and Sugden almost got in. Littlewood spoiled Pennington, from replying to a kick of Barnes, and after each side had indulged in smart work, the whistle sounded for half time, the Hornets being a goal to the good. It was thought that the home 'team would soon equalize matters, but the hopes enter- tained were not realized for a considerable time. After Groves had charged Barnes' reply to the kick off, Fair Turner came through a pack and collared Barton before he could part with the oval. Massey and Barnes gained ground by well-timed punts, and after Bandies and Povey had dribbled in neat style, the game was found to be at the "Insects "quarter flag. Smith made a spirited run and almost got in, unfortunately going in touch a few yards from the line. By the aid of Evans the oval was worked away, but not much headway could , be made against the splendid play of Pennington, the visiting full back. E. Dillon held T. Smith at midfield, and both Pennington and Massey were loudly cheered for individual efforts. The visitors now showed signs of distress, whilst extra exertions were put forth by the Warringtonians. Ashton baulked Barton in his passing, and after Bandies had put in a neat kick, quick passing by Antrobus, Evans and Massey ended in the first- named scoring. All eyes were now rivetted on Fair Turner, who was taking the place, and loud cheers announced the fact that the scores were equal. Re- suming hostilities, the home team went away with a dash, Barnes putting in a spirited run on the popular side, which finally ended in Antrobus again grounding, Barnes placing a goal. The visitors were now beaten, and Mr. Vickers' whistle for "no side" only prevented the Warringtonians from inflicting a severe defeat. Taken on the whole the game may be described as even. In the first half the visitors displayed the more con- sistent play, their passing at time:being really fine. The home team on the other hand did not seem to pull well together, though individual players nowaand then show- ed brilliant form. During the latter part of the second half, however, the Warringtonians gradually gained the upper hand and managed to snatch a victory even after many had concluded they were finally beaten. At full back Sanson made only an indifferent display, but the three-quarters were all in good form. The half-backs as usual played with energy, but did not gd in so much forprompt passing as is desirable. The forwards were in good condition, and it was a treat to witness the fashion in which they wore down their opponents towards the finish. Of the Hornets Barton and Pennington at back and Groves and Millidew forwards deserve mention.

The following were the teams :—Warrington: Sanson, back; Massey, Barnes, and Evans, three-quarters; Antrobus and Speakman, half-backs; Dillon (captain), Fair Turner, Frank Turner, Ashton, Povey, Littlewood, E. Dillion, Cragan, and Randles, forwards. Rochdale: Pennington, back; T. Smith, Barton and Lord, three- quarters; Smith and Tattersall, half-backs; Groves (captain), Holt, Sugden, Mellidew, Parkinson Ashworth Griffiths, Row and Warburton, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. W. Vickers, Salford F. C. RUNCORN V. BRADFORD. This important match was played at the Park Avenue ground, Bradford, on Saturday, before about 6,000 spectators, and in brilliant weather. The Run- corn team arrived at Bradford at 2.30, after a tedious journey of four hours, and were somewhat jaded They were also minus the services of W. H. Broady, who got his leg injured in the match against Salford the previous week. The match was a splendidly contested one, the teams being very evenly matched. The Bradford players were, however, the heavier team but this was counterbalanced by the smart tackling of the Runcorn team. Hawcridge was in grand form, his running, tackling, and kicking could hardly be surpassed. He was extremely difficult to stop, and even then he would manage to part with the ball. He never seemed to make a mistake, and picked up cleanly. On the Run- corn side Wainwright had the longest sprint, and was instrumental in getting the try for Runcorn, though owing to a misunderstanding amongst the reporters this credit has been given to Gayter. W. Hughes and Faulkner bow the brunt of the scrimmaging, and of the backs, H. Hughes and Brazendale had a lot of work, the former preventing Hawcridge getting a try just on the posts. Brazendale delighted the Bradford players and spectators, and Hawcridge expressed himself in loud terms of his abilities. Details of the play are found below. Hickson kicked off and Davies returned. W. Riley also gave relief, but Hawcridge securing made tracks for the Runcorn goal. W. Riley checked his career, though Hawcridge recovered himself and punted to Brazendale, who nullified the advantage. H. Hughes then passed to Crompton, who in turn gave it to Davies, play being brought to the centre. Hickson and Wilkinson dribbled well into the Runcorn 25, but Hancock got the ball away, and W. Hughes continuing the movement, play was transferred into the Bradford quarters. Bonsor then passed to P. Robertshaw, Crompton collaring him, and several short scrimmages were fought in the centre, where Ritchie got a free kick. but without advantage. Wainwright then showed up with a grand run, and H. Hughes picking up, transferred the ball to Crompton, who dropped at the Bradford goal, a touch-down giving the first score to Runcorn. Severe scrimmaging gave the Bradford' forwards the advantage, but to the joy of the Run- corn partizans, Brazendale sent the ball into neural ground. Potter and Grey dribbled back, and W. Hughes secured a free kick, which being well followed, up by Gayter and Stubbs, Runcorn were placed in a favourable position. Hickson dribbled back grandly, only to see Brazendale take the ball from his toss, and to punt lof ily to the centre flag. Bonsor gave the ball, under extra difficulty to Hawcridge, who dodged beauti- fully and passed several of thq Runcorn players, and was just about te score when H. Hughes pushed him well into touch. Half-time was shortly al+ erwards called the game standing, Runcorn,one minor; Bradford, one minor. W. Hughes re-star ed the game, and a moderate re urn by P. Robertshaw lodged play into the Runcorn half. P. Robertshaw also rar in a good punt, which Brazendale returned with interest added. The Bradford

forwards worked the ball well into the Runcorn twenty- five, and. Critchley ge,ting hold, gave it to Po:ter, who passed to Ritchie, and the latter player just got behind the line. The kick at goal by Willman failed. The Runcorn forwards then in turn attacked the Bradford goal, W. Hughes, Faulkner, Wainwright, and Hancock in turn dribbling. Bonsor, however, put in a fine run, and H. Hughes screwed to Hawcridge, who had a free kick. From a line out Bonsor passed to P. Rober shaw, who struggled over the line, the kick at goal again being at fault. Runcorn now made strenuous efforts to score W. Riley, Davies, and Hollingwortla, by short runs, transferring play to centre. Gayter, S übbs, and P. Riley also pressed forward, and in the midst of a com- bined movement Wainwright got a try. Brazendale, however, failed to gain the major point. Final score— Runcorn, one try, two minors; Bradford, two tries, two minors. Bradford: Willman,taback ; F. T. Ritchie, J. G. Hawcridge, P. Robertshaw, three-quarter backs; F. Rouser, S. CH( chley, half backs; L. Hickson, E. Wilkin- son, M. Bonsor, W. Grey, W. Fisher, C. Higgins, J. Potter, W. Jowett, and Ne tleton, forwards. Runcorn: IJ. Brazendale, back; T. H. Davies, W. A. Riley, J. 11. Cromp on, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes, J. lolling- wor h, half backs; W. Hughes, W. Faulkner, G. Wain- wright, F. Hancock, W. Dolan, J. Gayter, W. Scubbs, P. Riley, and Hampson, forwards. WARRLNGTON V. WIDNES.

-- After an interval of two years, the above organiza- tions met at Widnes on Thursday evening, when a large attendance witnessed the match. The visiting team were weakly represented, but nevertheless a pleasant game resulted. Warrington won the toss, taking ad- vantage of the wind. The 'lig, ing forwards were quick on the lea, her, spoiling Plumpton returning. Warrington missed a grand chance of scoring, and from a pack near the line Farrell ran back and saved, Lit lewood clinging to him. The drop-out found play at the 25 flag, Bate saving a dangerous rush. Clarke endeavoured to get away, but the smart tackling of Lawless was too much for him, and from the succeeding pack Unsworth gained a try. Barnes essayed the kick at goal with success: The Widnes team from the re-starting at centre went away with a dash, but Farrell loss a good opportunity. By well-timed kicks, Widnes took play to the Warrington ' quart er flag, Clarke putting in a good kick to the line. Russell here headed a dribble, and relieved to half-way. II Massey stopped the Widnes team in an endeavour to in- vade the Warrington quarters, and W. Dillon smartly tackled Plumpton with the oval in his possession. Plumpton was ins rumental in relieving hislines, and the same player made his mark from a return of Barnes, but it availed his side little. Smith headed the Widnes team to the visiting quar,er flag, and after Bate had tackled Bingham on his own line, Parkinson took the game to centre field with a pretty run, after receiving a neat pass from Farrell. Widnes now had to kick dead, and the drop out found play at half way. Useful kicks by Pennington took the game to the line, but a tall kick by Clarke was well taken up by the Widnes forwards, a minor accruing. Bandies dropped out, Plumpton re- plying. Unsworth and Bate came in for some applause at this point of the game, each iif turn helping to trans- fer the game to the Widnes quarters. Give and take play followed, until Bate missed an opening through passing forward when scoring seemed a certainty. Half time was then called, with the score Warrington one goal two minors to a minor. With a goal to the bad, Plumpton started the second half, and for the first few minutes play rested in the Warrington quarters. Off- side tackling allowed Bingham a free kick, and Barnes replied in good style. Plumpton made his mark in a , good position, but Farrell failed at the place. Evans tried to relieve his lines, but only made little headway. Barnes put in a huge kick in reply to a mark of Farrell's. Both teams were working with renewed vigour, and neither side could claim aeadvantage. Kiddie and Gordon made an extra , effort, and a mistake let in Pennington, no goal resulting from the place. Widnes were now having the best of matters, until Povey transferred play from the quarter flag to half way. The playing was only destined to stay here for a few minu- tes, until a good kick by Evans removed play to centre. However, fortune favoured the home team directly after, for good forward play enabled Clark to cross the Warrington line, no goal again resulting. Daniels inter- cepted some passing of the home team soon after ' restarting, but a free kick removed hostilities to the Warrington quarter-flag. Massey came to the rescue of , his side, and after Evans had spoiled Plumpton, the t visitors rushed the leather over the line, a minor t resulting. Widnes eventually forced a minor, and

time was called, Warrington gaining a victoty by one goal three minors to Widnes two tries and two minors. It is pleasing to note that rough play was conspicuous by its absence, and scarcely has a more pleasant game been witnessed on the Widnes ground. On behalf of the winning team, all the forwards are worthy of recogni- tion, whilst in the back division Bate, Lawless, and Barnes were the pick. In the-Widnes ranks, Parkinson, Farrel, Smith, and Gordon were the choice. Teams : Warrington : T. Barnes, full back ; three-quarterbacks, W. Daniels, .1. W. Evans, and J. T. Massey; halfbacks, J. Bate and J. Lawless; forwards, W. Dillon (captain) H. Ashton, W. Povey, W. Handles, R. Littlewood, T. Creaghan, Russell, C. Unsworth, and J. Holmes. Widnes: J. Bingham, full back ; three-quarter backs, F. Plump- ten, Parkinson, and Clarke; half backs, Farrell and Wilkinson; forwards, J. Smith, Kiddie, Gandy, WI- Hams, Gordon, Wright, Barber, Holt, Pennington Referee, Mr. Roger Wilcock, West Lancashire Union.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

In his descriptive account in the 'Athletic News" of the match Warrington v. Rochdale Hornets, on last Saturday, , "Philistine" says :- 1 "They have some beautiful specimens of the genus speetatoribus (early English—very) at Warrington. There is the common penny plain shouter, pure and simple (exceedingly), who only opens his " walloper " and agitates his lolliker " when the home team do anything conspicuous. Then there is that bane of life—the candid critic (?)—who always puts his best clothes on to go to the matches, poses as a superior:person, and all the time the game is in progress keeps up a running commentary on the faults only of the players. A pass is never gives right in his omnipotent judgment; a run is never made but it should have been further and faster; and a try is never got but there is something about it which this cynical sneerer objects to, and when a place kick is having its momentous preliminaries arranged, he knows for a ertainty that the chosen kickist will make a miss or a mess of it. This individual is usually very much in evidence behind the press stand, but some of these dark days a long suffering fraternity will lure that genius to the murky banks of the muddy Mersey, and there will be a Warrington mystery and the football field will see that man no more. The referee and umpire insulter is also present in sufficient numbers to make gentlemen officiating in those capacities immediately qualify for martyrdom, but as this particular imbecile species is,quite harmless, a lapsing into a semi deaf and dumb state is most becoming, and is as efficacious as the hide of the hippopotamus. All these disagreeable lumps of spleenish supporters are, however, delightfulty leavened by the presence of the impartial class of both sexes. The ladies especially have been attacked by the epidemic most severely, ad the gushing maid and the comely meter flock there to see the play and admire the players." .

The Hornets from Rochdale will, we should think, very feelingly acquiesce in the saying that "there's many a slip between the cup and the lip." Up till within a very measurable distance from the end of the game against Warrington, on the Wilderspool ground on Saturday, they were a good substantial goal to the good, and it was gen- erally conceded by those who witnessed the game that the visitors were in for a win. The staying powers of the Warrington team, however, again did them a good ser- vice, and, puffin.' themselves together towards the finish, they completely 'beat down the defence of their oppon- ents and notched two goals in quick succession. It is worth noting about this game that no minors were scored on either side; nothing less than goals would serve. At times there was some very fine passing on both sides, and it was instructive to note how effective this class of play is. Last year both Rochdale Hornets and Warrington " A " teams had some claims to be regarded as the char- pion "A" team of the county, but last Saturday the wire-pullers gave the quietus to any pretensions ot that sort for this season on the part of the " incts." The meeting took place on the Rochdale groulW, but front beginning to end the visitors showed greatly superior play and ran out easlwinners by one goal, one try, and four minors to five minors. After this it may surely be said that Warrington's second string begin the season ait the premier " A " team of the county. A Maori football team arrived in England on Wednes- day, having engagements to the extent of sixty matchei with the best English clubs, They play the Rugby Union game, and the expenses of the trip are being defrayed by a syndicate of colonial gentlemen.

div.head: REV. P. MACKENZIE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE REV. P. MACKENZIE AT WARRINGTON.

On Tuesday afternoon the Rev. Peter Mackenzie preached in Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, and in the evening he lectured in the adjoining schoolroem. At the afternoon service there was a large atten- dance, and the rev. gentleman took as his text Zachariah xiv, 6 and 7., "And it shall come to pass that at eventime it shall be light." In the course of his sermon the preacher applied the words of the text to the condition of the church and the country at the present day. The outlook, he said, was not dark, for though there was a great deal of indifference and worldliness amongst people, the gospel was penetrating into France, and. Spain and China. Poor China; The Americans were prevent- ing the Chinese from going there, and the Austra- lians wished to do the mine with regard to their country, but if America would not have the pig- tails, Jesus Christ would, and if the Australians would not let them into Australia, Christ would let them into the gospel. lie was at Newport some time ago and a well-known merchant told him how , one of his ships,when far from land, met with a storm which battered her almost to pieces, and nearly disabled her, but her captain stuck to the vessel and through days of toil and danger brought her safe into port. He thought there was a lesson for his hearers there; they might meet with rough weather on the ocean of life, but if they stuck by their ship, they would reach the harbour safely and in the evening time there would be for them light. In the evening, he Rev. P. Mackenzie gave a lecture in the Bold-st. Wesleyan Schools, on " Queen Esther." There was a very large attendance ; Mr. T: Morris pre- sided, and there were also on the platform the Revs. G. E. Young, W. Brooks, E. H. Jackson, and Mr. W. siicock.

The CHAIRMAN said that, a few nights ago many of them heard described in most forcible language from that platform the character of President Garfield. That evening they were to listen to Mr. Mackenzie, between whom and President Garfield there were, he believed, similarities. Mr. Mackenzie at one time worked in a. coal mine, and Garfield drove mules along the towing- path. Whilst listening to the Rev. A. Mursell, the other night, he could not,help thinking of those grand. old lines of Longfellow'' : Lives of great men all remind us We can make our lives sublime, And, departing, leave behind us Footprints on the sands of tim• , (Hear, hear.) For his own part, he would ten times rather hear the history of Mr. Mackenzie's own life than the life of Queen 'Esther. (Applause.) However, he was told that it would be a real treat, and that those who, like himself, had never heard Mr. Mackenzie. lecture, would go home and hardly sleep that night for thinking of what he had said. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It was not only what he said, but the way in which he said it. (Laughter and applause.) The Rev. PETER MACKENZIE who was very cordially received, said he did not know of any lecture that he would sooner give than that on Queen Esther. She was a diamond without a Raw, a rose without a thorn, an evergreen without a sere leaf, and a luminary without so I much as a spot upon her disc. She was of Jewish ex- traction, the daughter of Abihail, and of the honoured tribe of Benjamin. Saul belonged to that tribe; and the three hundred left-handed men were of the same tribe; r the man who travelled more miles and built more. Churches for Christ and His cause than anybody who had ever lived—Paul, was always pleased and proud of belonging to the honoured tribe of Benjamin; and last, but not least, Esther was of the same stock. Esther was born in captivity. She lost her father and mother when only a child, and her father's nephew, Mordecai, adopted and brought her up in the faith and fear of th:i God of her fathers; and God's providence richly remu- nerated him for the goodness he had shown to the orphan child of his dead relative. Having narrated the circumstances which led to the raising of Esther to be queen, the lecturer said that when she got promoted she did not forget Mordecai, her guardian, who had watched over and cared for her. He became an attendant at the gate: that was, a member of Parliament. (Laughter.) Some people thought that Mordecai was only a porter; but no, the House of Commons in those days was at the gate, the House of Lords was at the gate, and all the business was transacted at the gate. ,(Laughter.) The downfall Of Haman and the elevation of Mordecai were next described with dramatic vigour, the lecture threughout being very heartily appreciated by the audience. At . the conclusion, a. hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Mackenzie was moved by Mr. J. Gandy, seconded by Dr. Starkie Smith, and supported by Mr. R. Garnett,and warmly accorded. A similar vote to the Chairman was adopted on the proposal of the lecturer, seconded by Mr. Silcock. The singing of the Dogology brought the meeting to a close. • INTEMPERANCE CURED.—A wealthy Almeriam Lady whose only son was for years a slave to intemperance, after seeking in vain tor a cure, and trying all known remedies, at last found a simple means that cured and save him from a drun- kard's grave. Anyone suffering or desiring to help others in this worthy cause, by sending a self-addressed stamped en- velope to Mr. James Holland, 25, Hart-st., High Holborn, London, will receive this information free of charge. Men- tion this paper.—Advt. At Worksop, Wm. Cauldwell was committed for trial on a charge of attempting to murder Mark Hollely, of Sheffield, by shooting him on the 16th Inst. while he was leaving the Wesleyan Chapel with his two brothers. Mr. John Redmond, M.P., was sentenced at Wexford on Wednesday to five weeks' imprisonment on a charge of intimidation arising out of a speech made by the hon. member on the occasion of the eviction of a tenant by Captain Walker.

Mr. Jou:Ahem:or proclaimed at the Dublin meet- ing of the National League, on Tuesday, that he is still a hardened sinner. "If it were a crime, "he said, "to wish to see the people of Ireland prosperous ittla happy,if it were a crime to help them to defend their homes against rack-renters untilbetter times, and if it wen.: a crime to try and withdraw the People' from crime and murder—if these acts were slime, it was a sin for which there was no remedy. The sin was engrafted in his heart." It will be gathered from this that Mr. BALFOUR'S process of Information by means of prison discipline is an litter failure so far as Mr. DmioN is concerned. And who is there that loves truth, and justice, and high-mindedness that would have it other; 'Wise? Whom does the world respect •at this raoment ? The MINISTER who in the name of the QuNEN administers a brutal system in a brutal 4.faalline ; or the man who, just free from felon's treatment, sets Coercion at defiance, and declares that he is hardened in his sin ? We shall never settle the Irish question by putting men in gaol who are beloved by the people because they ,fight the people's battle, and whose honesty unquestioned even by their bitterest lents. It would be a disgrace to Irish- if they were to settle down under such _ ,ion—just RS it continues a disgrace to ~,,...nglishmen so long as such oppressjen is inflicted, we say Englishmen advisedly, for it is a fact which needs to be driven home that majorities le Ireland, Scotland, and Wales have shown at the polling booths that they have no part or lot ill a policy of coercion. It is England which krges the chains by which Ireland is bound; and 1... t is to English Liberals that we must look to set •Lreland free. Mr. Dimore was good enough to 'lay, on Tuesday, that he does not share the impa- tience of some of his friends; but he admits that he impatience is natural; and it is for the people of this country to remember that they who permit aPPression share the crime. Cynical FirLYOURS, distrustful CHAMBERLAINS, and cold-blooded IEARTINGTONS affect to believe that Irish Profession of, better feeling towards the flglish people as a whole is a Imre pre- tence for a special purpose. Granted that, in anine cases, there may have been reason to doubt the sincerity of certain utterances; the tleubt, admittedly, does not apply to such a Straightforward and unflinching Nationalist as Mr. John Dillon. And what does he tell us? "The flglish race," he says, "were being converted at a Wonderful iate. He, for his part, could hardly tiotice the difference in the reception which he Would receive in English and Scotch towns as com- Pared with the reception he would meet with in Cork or Dublin. When he considered these and other matters he failed to see any reason for iinipatience. Coming though he did from prison, an could not find in his heart any feelings of bitterness towards the English people., He tecollected the time when the name and power of ligland were hateful to him." Language such 1 se this is transparent in its candour, and what a revelation it is! Mr. Dillon speaks the simple !Nth when he tells us of the change which has °e'en wrought in his own case by the pursuit of a Policy of Conciliation as contrasted with that of Coercion; and we may be sure that what is true . him is true of hundreds of thousands of Irish- 'fltql. It is this touch of nature which is making 4,the two peoples kin. It is a grand thing for Mr. 'ladstone to have achieved in so short a time, it gives promise of a grander future. We ,40uour Mr. Dillon for speaking out so frankly and !oldiy. Let Englishmen show that they know t'alv to appreciate such nobility of character; and ;sake it plain before the next election that they ,eel the stain of having recognised Irish patriots 153' Putting them in prison.

COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN THE RHONNILL VALLEY.—An alarming colliery explosion occurred on Tuesday. at Tynybedw Colliery, Rhondda Vafley, 'South Wales, whereby three- men—named William Davies, married, three children; Thomas Evans, married, four children; and Edwards, a single man—received severe burns about the face and body. The pit, 'which is owned by Messrs. Cory Brothers, of Cardiff, had been idle for some time (owing to a dispute respecting the royalties) and was now being restarted. It is believed the explosion was due to an accumulation of gas reach- ing the fire at the flue, and thus igniting. The utmost commotion prevailed throughout the district.

Storm Warning; At the meeting, on Tuesday next, of the Warrington Town Council a proposal will be submitted for the dismissal of Mr. Din- Widdie. Wind expected to be exceedingly high.

The sparrow controVersy waxes warm. Miss Ormerod is amongst those who believe that the bird is very destructive, while others contend that it does more good than harm. Meanwhile Master Sparrow looks on and takes care of himself. He will have his crop full of one thing or another.

Mr. Balfour has been releasing another M.P. on account of the state of his health. This time it is Mr. Blane who is set at liberty. Are there no other criminals in the country suffering from ill- ness? Mr. Balfour never makes any d'stinction between political and other prisoners ; and he is sa modsl Of consistency.

John Livesey, of St. Helens, doesn't fistlre very well in having to be sued by the Corporation for the maintenance of his wife and daughter in the Infectiou.s Diseases Hospital—particularly when it is known that the charge made is only one third the cost. But he had to pay ;he deserved to be made pay, for he was able to pay.

Whether Stanley be alive or notis as yet an open question ; but there seems to be no doubt as to the death of Major Barttelot and Mr. Jameson. It is suggested that they were cruel to the natives; but that is unlikely,for they needed help from them. Be that as it may, there can be no question that the natives have been cruel to them.

As the Scotch have just now a fit of statue- raising upon them, would it not be as well to direct their attention to the completion of the National Monument on Calton Hill? Or, if they will have something new, and as they always have an eye to everything relating to "the bawbee," how would it be if they were to raise a monument to the National Debt?

It is not everywhere that there will be heart- burning over the arrangements for new County Councils. The Urban Sanitary Authorities of Haydock and Newton have agreed to amalgamate for county government purposes. How pleatiant it is to see neighbours thus living together in harmony. Newton-le-Willows will be the name of the new division.

"Leather Apron" is in luck. He was libelled in connection with the latest Whitechapel murder, and is turning his misfortune to account. He is suing newspaper proprietors who have abused his good name, and is making a nice little thing out of cases of compromise. If he can only discover, say, that a score of• provincial papers have been down on him, it will be "the making of him."

Miss Amelia B. Edwards has been giving some account of the finding of a live frog in a bed of clay, which was deposited, it is coolly assumed, some 420,000 or 30,000 years ago. A matter of 10,000 years is, to be sure, of little moment when you come across a frog of the olden time. Miss Edwards' it should be mentioned, is a writer of fiction. Can it be that she has been telling mother " story " ?

Mr. John Pierpoint, J.P., seems to be "catch- ing it." It is rumoured that, though he could not, as an interested person, vote on the Battersby- lane license, he intimated that he intended to rote against the full license for the Grove, in which, of course, he was not interested. As the trade" love looked on Mr. Pierpoint as their own peculiar friend, some of them are making remarks more forcible than polite. His virtue in the mat- is altogether beyond them. --- Canon Ryle, son of the Bishop of Liverpool, shows good sense and good f:eling in giving Non- conformists credit for the good work they have done. The Vicar of Brymbo displays neither when he rounds on the Canon and spitefully remarks that "Dissent is schism, and schism is sin." He might just as well blurt it out in the old, blunt fashion and say—" Dissent is of the devil." That is the sort of man ke is. He should have lived when George the Third was king.

The publication of extracts from theiliary of the late Emperor Frederick is making a stir. There is an official attempt to discredit what has appeared; but with little success. It is altogether new and most likely altogether true that Napoleon, after being beaten at Sedan, tried to get Germany to enter into a hostile alliance with him against England. It was like Napoleon the Little to do such a thing; he was a compound of dis- honour and corruption. '

Honour to the memory of Anthony Thompson, who has died this week at the Leeds Infirmary. He was an engine driver, and the other day, as he was running between Bradford and Leeds, a back draught flashed upon him and his stokes% They were enveloped in flames' but they stuck to the post of duty, and ran the train safely into Leeds. The stoker (Robert Hicks) is still laid up ; but Thompson has perished of his injuries. Honour therefore to his memory. Such bravery as his "Proclaims the hero and the man complete."

The Rev. Morley Stevenson is ma' ing himself exceedingly useful as a member of the Warrington Association for the Promotion of Technical In- struction. A few weeks ago he gave a lucid exposition of the Government Bill on the subject, and on Tuesday evening he delivered an address on Recreative Evening Classes. It was a valuable 'contribution to an important subject; and we commend the facts which he sets forth, and the observations he makes to the attention of our readers. It is to be hoped some good will come of the new move which is being made.

Mr. Robert Yerburgh, M.P. for Chester,is a for- tunate fellow. He is an illustration of the adage that it is better to be born lucky than rich. It is doubtful whether he would have been in Parliament if there had not been a Duke of Westminister to pay his election expenses in 1885. A few months since he was married to the only daughter of Mr. Daniel Thwaites, the wealthiest man in Black- born. He has just lost his father-in-law, however, but it is believed it will be some consolation to him to know that by his fathel.-in-law's death his wife will become possessed of between two and three millions of money. That is something to be going on with. The members of the Runcorn Board of Guardians discussed, on Tuesday, the advisability of paying a salary of £lO to a Roman Catholic priest to attend upon the Catholic inmates at the Work- house. Some of them seem to have been in a pettifogging humour, and,made a question of the amount, notwithstanding the fact that the Church parson is to be made "passing rich on forty pounds 3 year." But why. if they thought £lO too much, did they not grant £.5? It would at least have paid the priest's cab fares. By failing to vote anything, they are guilty of an injustice.

The Welsh Wesleyans, at W,idnes have got a new chapel, and their old chapel is being put to a use which is shocking to them. It has been con- verted by. a Wigan man named Grierson into a dancing saloon. "To such base uses must we come at last, Horatio." It seems that Grierson has not yet completed his purchase of the old building, and meantime the county court judge has granted an injunction to stop his little game for the present. Dancing, with herb-beer for refreshment, may not be the wildest form of dissipation ; but it is hardly the thing in an ex-Wesleyan chapel.

have nothing to complain of. The law provides for the course which has been taken; and it is always satisfactory, when a false step has been made, to find that there is an opportunity of re- tracing it. Unfortunately for the repute of the Licensing Committee, there is no evidence that they did their work, in the first instance, in a workman-like manner., They do not seem to have taken into account either the wishes of the inhabi- tants in the localities to be affected by the new licenses, or the startling fact , revealed by the Chief Constable's annual report that there was an increase in the number of convictions for drunken- ness, amongst 'males, of not less than 30 per cent. It was a ease of an inexperienced Committee giv- ing proof of its inexperience—to say nothing worse and it is a relief to the public to know that I bat ety has again been found in the "multitude of counsellors" that attended,the Licensing Court on Monday morning. With regard to the magis- trates present, it was a surprise to many people to see Mr. John Pierpoint take a seat on the Bench; for it was known that he was inte- rested in one of the licenses,having given evidence at the previous Court as architect of the proposed new public house. Mr. Pierpoint did not, we believe, intend to vote on the particular license in which he was concerned; but it was "not the thing" to take any part in the business, and it is very ques- tionable whether it was legal. As it happily hap- pened, he was not in a position to affect the Majority, which was decidedly against his view of the situation. Another point which excited a good deal of comment arose out of the proposal to turn Mr. Elijah Lawton out of the Grove Inn, and put in another tenant in case the granting of a full license was confirmed. It is Mr. Lawton who has for ten or eleven years aPplied as tenant for an extension of license ; it is Mr. Lawton to whom the license was being granted; but the owners of the premises, fearful from the fact that Mr. Lawton had once been fined one shilling, were about to substitute as tenant an entire stranger— that is as soon as the new license had got nicely to work. The brewer has of course a right to pro- tect his own interests. As the law stands, he can set up whom he will and knock down whom he will; but this being so what is the worth of all the talk one has heard of compensation to public- axis? Row was Mr. Elijah Lawton to be com- pensated on his marching orders being given him—when another man was called in to reap where he had sown P A case such as this, laid bare in open court, shows unmistakeably how drink-hollers become the catspaw of brewers. It is farcical to talk of compensation to OM publibans ; it is the brewer who will take the lion's share if ever compensation is granted. But we are turning aside from our main purpose, and that is to thank the magistrates as a body for having so resolutely done their duty, an d congratulate the town upon having in this instance been delivered from the , tender mercies of the drink interest.

Ma. TKonus Baer, M.P..has been taken to task for supporting the prayer of a memorial in favour of working-men being appointed justices of the peace. He repudiates,however,the statement that he has ever either said or thought that a working- man, simply because he happens to be a working- man, should sit in judgment upon his fellows. He might have added that the converse of this is too often true, namely, that the working-man is denied a fair share in the control and administration of the business of the country simply because he is a working-man. We do not deny that Magistrates, Town 'Councillors, and members of Local Boards, perform the duties which devolve upon them in a creditable manner. But surely it will not be con- tended that there are no representatives of the labouring classes who are fit to occupy such pos- itions. And if there are such men, is it not a singular thing that they are conspicuous by their absence ? We have a strong opinion that our governing bodies would be all the better if they were more in touch with the people by having men of the people amongst them; and, holding this view of the matter, we are glad to sec that the Warrington Trades Council have determined to take some steps to secure direct representation in the Warrington Town Council. The issue is one which rests mainly with themselves. I If they act with promptness, unity, and determination there is nothing to prevent them achieving their object. They must not expect those who are a step above them to go out of theirgay to lend a helping hand. God helps those who help themselves. The classes, it must be remembered, have their own , interests to serve; they are not likely to trouble themselves about' the masses—except in so far as they can make use of them. If this be kept in mind, in Warrington and elsewhere, there will be a larger hope of labour representation becoming a reality. It is aiming higher, of eourse, to try to reach the magistracy ; but already several promin- ent men who have been identified with labour move- ments have been appointed justices of the peace; and there is no good reason why the number should not be increased. Mr. BURT is right in saying that "the best thing would, no doubt, be to have only thoroughly trained men selected to administer justice." But meantime, whilst we are slowly travelling in the direction of stipendiary magistrates, it would do no harm, and perhaps quicken the pace, if the magisterial body were leavened with a few more of those who may be justly styled the direct representatives of working-men.

div.head: RUNCORN REVISION COURT,
div.p: RUNCORN REVISION COURT,

The annual revision of the voters' lists a the Runcorn Polling District which comprised Run- corn, north and south, Halton, Clifton, Weston, Stockham, and Norton, took place yesterday. Mr. , Clement Elphinstone Lloyd was th.• revising barris- ter. Mr. W. Handley represented the Liberals and Mr. C. J. Hughes, assisted by Mr. A. Lightburn, was for the Conservatives. The Liberals had made 14 owners' claims, 35 occupiers' claims, 43 old lodger. and 20 new lodger claims. They had also. served 5 objections on the owners' claim list, and 2 to old owners' register. and also two on the occupiers, list and 4 old lodgers' The Conservatives had Made 9 ownership claims, 5 occupiers, 33 old lodger claims, 13 new lodger claims, and had served 3 objeetions to ownership claim list. The lists showed that there were 313 women entitled to vote feu* members of the County Council to be formed undpr the Local Government Act. MR. WIGG'S GARDENER. .

Thomas Moores claimed as an occupier of a house at Halton. Mr. Hughes said the man paid the rent and rates and the house was partly furnished by him.—Mr. Hanley said Moores parents were poor, and he found them a house for which he paid £8 a year. He paid the rates as well, bu,,t in no case was he the occupier.—The Revising Barrister Does he appear on the rate book ? —Mr. Handley replied that he did but a man could not occupy a house by reason of his family. It would make no difference to Moore if he were struck of the list as he was gardener to Mr. C. Wigg, near Chester. and had a qualification there.—The Revising Barrister : I have no alternative but to take him off -,- if he does not occupy the house, he has no right to be on.

SIR RICHARD BROOKE. In reading over the Halton occupiers' list of voters for members of the County Council, Mr. Handley said the name of Sir Richard Brooke should be struck off; he was dead. Mr.. Hughes contended that this was the name of the present baronet, but Mr. Handley pointed out that his name was Sir Richard Marcus Brooke.—The assistant overseer said the present baronet was intended.—The Barrister: If I strike out the name I am taking off a dead mm and a living man as well. (Laughter.) The

vote was allowed.—Mr. Handley: All right sir. I am told Sir Richard is a Liberal. (Laughter.) Mr. Hughes: lam quite satisfied sir. He sent me £5 for registration expenses the other day. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Handley: He must be a Unionist then. WARNING TO LODGERS. In consequence of some lodger claims being suspici- ously signed and attested, the Revising Barrister announced that in future in any glaring case he should not only summon the claimant to another Court but also. the person who had actested the claim.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

JURY LISTS AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the jury lists for the various townships in the district were Submitted and approved. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—Yesterday Rachael Rawlin- son and Alice Johnson, were each fined 10s. and costs for tising obscene language in Lord-st. on the previous evening. ELLESMERE-STREET IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—RUNCORN.— About 35 members spent a pleasant afternoon in Chester on Saturday, this mode cif opening the session meeting with much favour. _ _

ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Hugh Jones, labourer of Beaumortt-st was walking across the kitchen of his house when he fell down and fractured his left leg just above the ankle. Dr. Hutchinson attended to tOse injury. FARNWORTH WESLEYAN CHAPEL ANNIVERSARY.—On Sunday, the chapel anniversary services were celebrated in the above place of worship. Two sermons were preached, one in the morning by the Rev: T. Law, and one in the evening by the Rev. J. Bryant. Collections were made at the close of each service in aid of the trust fund. There was a good attendance. WIDNES SALVATION ARMY-.On Sunday special memorial , services yvere held in the Widnes Drill Hall in connection with the death of Captain Mrs. Ihrrereaves, of America, late Miss Eleanor Leyton, of Widnes, who died on September 11th. During the day a recognition meeting was held to welcome Captain Mrs. Leymour, who has taken a position in the Widnes Corps. IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE, WIDNES.—At a meeting of the members of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League on Sunday Mr. B. Fox, headmaster of St. Patrick's schools, delivered a lecture on "Mr. Parnell ; his life and times; from 1846 to the present time." The lecturer treated his subject with marked ability, and he Jr,p cordially thanked at the,close. STUBBS' FURNITURE CREAM.—For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany- and French polished furniture with half the usual labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottles, Id., 2d., and 3d.—lsaac Stubbs, Lowlancls-rcxul. Run: curn.—.4 d,d. POACHING AT Cnowros.—Richard Wright, of Cronton, an old offender, was summoned before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday charged with trespassing in pursuit of game.—Henry Andrews. gamekeeper to , Mr. Young, of Mossley Hill, said that gentleman had the right of shooting over the property of the late Colonel Park. On the 16th September he sawthe defendant in a field on the property ; he was beating with a stick and hunting. with a dog —The defendant, who denied that he was in search of game, was fined 30s and costs 12s, or in default a month's hard labour. A CHILD RUN OVER.—On Tuesday, a child, a year null 1 nine months old, named John Woods. son of James Woods, 10, Irwell-street, was playing in Davies-street, West Bank, when it was knocked down by a horse andi trap belonging to Messrs Sexton Bros., grocers, Water- loo-ro ,d, and one of the wheels of the trap passed over its neck. The man in charge of the trap picked the child up and it was carried home by Mr. Gerrard. Mr.l Richards, assistant to Dr. McDonnell, was called in and he found the child in a very serious condition. He is now progressing towards recovery. PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN CURATEI—The members of the Runcorn parish choir on Monday evening pre- sented the Rev. G. A. Tindell, formerly a curate under the Vicar, now Rector of Heage, with a richly engraved silver Docket communion service as a memento of the regard' in which he was held. The pres•ttation was made by Master Hampson and speeches appropriate to tile occasion were made by Mr. Jordon, (who presided). Mr. Johnsen, Mr. Janice Littler, Mr. Gaites. Mr. Tindall cordially acknowledged the gift, and spoke of the pleasure he had experienced in co-operating with the choir during his stay in Runcorn. ST. AMBROSE IMPROVEMENT SOCIETy, WIDNES.—The members of the St. Ambrose Church Mutual Improve- ment Society inaugurated the Winter Session On Thurs- day evening by a tea party and concert. About 100 members and friends were present at tea, and at the concert, the room was crowded to exceSs. The vicar, as president, occupied the chair, and gave a brief address en the advantages of such societies. A capital progranmae was'eonetkrough and was much appreciated by a crowded audience. Glees were rendered by the Allerton Glee party, and songs were ably given by Miss Leatherbarrow, and Miss Williams (Liverpool); ilessrt Smith (Liver- pool), Platt, And Perks. A fine performance on the fairy bells was given by Mr. Guy, (Liverpool) and Mr. Le Bert (Liverpool) recited " Eugene Arain's dream.". The duties of accompanist were ably fulfilled by Mr. E. M. Harrison, the organist at the church. THE RENOWNED RUNCORN RELISH is prepared from the choicest herbs, roots, and apices, which retuier it of most valuable assistance in the digestion ef food.--Prepared and sold wholesale by Isaac Stubbs, Lowlands-road. Beacom.— Ade. RIVAL WATCHMAKERS AT WIDNES.—A, Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday Thomas Sharp, a watchmaker, was summoned to answer a charge of threatening to assault James W. Prescot. Mr. J. o.Swift,of St. Helens, , represented the complainant. It appeared that the ' defendant had been employed as manager of the shop No. 10, Waterloo-road, by Mr. Pownall watchmaker,of Prescot, but on Monday he was summarily dismissed, and the complainant was put in his place. On Tuesday ' and Wednesday mornings the defendant went into the shop and acted in a most violent tnannnr, and threatened to break the complainant's neck. The complainant was afraid to leave the shop for a whole day.—For the defence it was alleged that the complainant had threatened to shoot the defendant, and had done all he ' possibly could to annoy him. The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for two months, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each. PROPERTY SALE AT RUNCORN. —At Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, on Thursday evening, AlrAuke Holmes con- ducted a successful sale of leasehold property. The first lot comprised two dwelling.lmuses in Regent-st., num- bered 19 and 21,1 and were held of a term of 1000 years, subject to an apportioned ground rent of £3 55. 4d. The competition was very keen, and eventually the pro- perty was knocked down to Mr. Blinston for £7OO. Lot 2, two dwelling houses, 19 and 21, Brunswick-street, held for a term of 1000 years, subject to an apportioned yearly ground rent of £4 10s, was sold to Mr. Howard for £2lO. The sum of £230 was paid by Mr. Poole for the third lot, which comprised the Iwo dwelling houses, 23 and 25, Brunswick-st., held for a tersn'of 1000 Years, subject I o an apportioned yearly ground rent of £5 6s ed. The purchaser of the last lot was Mr. J. Douglas, who paid £247 for the two dwelling houses, 4 and 6, Shaw- street held for a term of 900 years at a yearly ground rent of £ll9s 2d. Mr. F. A. Lake was the solicitor in the mat er. CAMDEN IMPRovsmENT CLASS, RUNCORN.—Last even- ing week, the Camden improvement class held their opening meeting in Camden school. The room was tastefully laid out in drawing-room style, the walls being adorned with oil paintings. The chair was occupied by the President of the class, Mr. A. Harrigon. The quar- tett party, Messrs. T. Fox, J. Pennington, R. Edwards, and H. Pilgrim, rendered two quartetts in excellent style. The programme was one of judicious selection, Mr. Hampsori, Miss E. Ainsworth. Mr. Williams, Mr. C. le Couteur. Mr. T. Fox, Miss C. Taylor, Messrs. W. J. Millington, J. Birkett, Jessop, Rev. R. U. Hughes, Miss Eden, Mrs. Kay. and Messrs. Kay and Siinkin taking part therein. Miss Simister played the accompaniments and the entertainment was of a highly creditable nature throughout. The Committee for the ensuing season is composed as follows :—Misses Tyrie, Cook, Simkin, Spearing Crosby, Forster, Littler, and Messrs. F. Eden and G. A. Hayes (secretaries), Moulton, Patin, Millington. and Molyneaux. IMPUDENT ROBBERY AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, Catherine Matthews, a middle aged woman, of no fixed abode, was charged with stealing a basket, and several other articles, Valued at Sa.. the property of Mrs. Jameson, pawnbroker of Ann-street. It appeared that at noon on Tuesday the prisoner entered Mrs. Jameson's shop, where there were a number of women waiting until the pledge office was open. She asked the women ' why they were waiting. when Neil's place was opened on the other side of the street. The women thereupon trooped across to Neil, but finding that they had been falsely informed, returned and met the prisoner coming from the shop with a basket. The prisoner went into Mr. Neil's shop to pledge the articles but seeing Mrs. Jameson she ran away, and was afterwards apprehended by P.C. Ratcliffe. Wh6n charged she replied "Glory Hallelujah lam going to join the Salvation Army." As this was the prisoners 46th appearance, she was coin- nutted to the Quarter Sessions for trial. A COOK'S CLADS. —IMPORTANT TO SERVANTS. —At the St. Helens County Court on Wednesday before Judge Collier, Mary Davies sought to recover damages from the Aev. B. A. W. Norrie, of Huyton, for board and lodgings. Mr. Swift, who defended, said the plaintiff was formerly cook in Mr. Norrie's service and the day for the payment of her wages was the Ist of each month. On the 14th July he gave the plaintiff a month's notice to leave, and on the 4th August he paid her off entirely. She now cliiimed ten days board and lodging from the 4th ,to the 14th A ugust.—ln reply to His Honour plaintiff said she received a full month's wages.— . llis Honour said the plqintiff had no claim. The law was that an employer might dis•nias his ser- vant any time on paying a month's wages or giving a month's notice. IiAYDOCK PARK COURSING MEETING.—The Lan- cashire coursing season opened most auspiciously at llaydock l'ark on Wednesday IA tine weather, excellent sport and stout-running hares being en- joyed by a representative body of coursing- men. Cases ware frequent during the day of the faster greyhound being beaten. ''.Fullerton fairly carried off the honours of the day by two good displays, and in a stiff course in the second round he showed that he inherited his sire's pluck. Greentick. like nearly all the Greentick and Governess litter. showed plenty of pace, but an absence of the other essential attributes. Hamner, Meols Marquis, and learns all deserve special mention for their clever running, and Churchtown displayed both good pace and a resolute if not a quick style. In the Oaks several of the bitches ran very smartly. The judg- ing and slipping were both satistactory, and the excellent management left nothing to be desired.

JUVENILE GOOD TEMPLET.—The autumnal ses- sion of the South-West Lancashire District Council of Juvenile Good Templars was held in the Tempe- rance Hall, Southport, on Saturday, under the presi- dency of the district superintendent (Bro. A. Awell, Liverpool) representatives being present from various parts of the district. The report of the D.S.J.T. dealt with the position and work of every temple in the district and showed that re- markable progress had taken place during the past half year. gaily of the Setnples had doubled their membership, whilst all had done a good work in training the children in the principles of the order —viz., total abstinence from intoxicating drinks, smoking. gambling, and profane language. New temples bad been instituted, old ones re-opened,and the membership increased at the rate of 62 per cent. during the half year. The DC. Seerehry (Bro. W. 11. Dodson, Bootle) reported the work done the executive; and the D.C. Treasurer (Bro. D. Reid. Toxteth) reported a balanee, on the right side. The vhrions temple superintendents then gave ex- cellent reports of the work done by their respective temples; after which several business matters were considered. St. Helens was selected as the next place of meeting. Bro. D. Gavin, P.D.S.J.T. (South- East Lancashire) was introduced and addressed the Council. At the close of the session, ant-excellent tea was partaken • .f, for which the Southport friends were awarded the hest thanks of the council.

Advt THE thrums' Wanus QuEsrrolc.—Considerable interest is centred in the movement among the colliers of South West Lincashire for obtaining an advance of 10 per cent. ie their wages. It is stated that at some of the collieries deputations have waited on the employers urging reasons why the advance should be granted, and replies have been received that it would be given if it became general. A conference of the delegates of the col- liers of the north of England who are free from the sliding scale of wages has been held on several days during the present week. The conference was con- tinued in the Co-operative Hall, Manchester, on Wednesday, Mr. S. Woods presiding. The confe- rence was called to determine the best means of securing alO per cent. advance of wages. In addi- tion to the delegates who at tended on Tuesday there were delegates from North Wales and Staffordshire, representing 10,000 men. The whole of the morn- ing was devoted to the reading of reports from dis- tricts and counties. These showed that pit-head conferences and mass meetings had been held in every place represented at the conference, and that in each cape resolutions had been unanimously passed pressing for an advance of 10 per cent. in wages. In the afternoon discussion took place, and the following resolution was passed unanimously: —"That each district represented at this conference pledges itself that its men will give in notices to secure an advance of 10 per cent. on all underground men's wages, and further pledges itself that when the notices are so given in the same shall not be withdrawn unless and except the advance be con- ceded." The conference_to‘en adjourned. Balm() FLOWER STANDS. rland, Ironmonger, Warring ton.--Advt.

THE REPRESENTATION ON THE COUNTY COUNCIL.

The Chairman said he had to report formally, that the Committee appointed at the last meeting to confer with the magistrates of tlin division within -Runcorn Union and the Runcorn Board of Improvement Commissioners had held a meeting at Warrington to consider the repre- sentation of the Union on the County Council. After ' some discussion the meeting came to the conclusion that they ought to put forward a scheme to divide the Rune.;orn Union into four electoral divisions. One divi- ' sion was to comprise the townships on the southern side of the Weaver, aid be named the Frodsham Division. The Daresbury Division was to com- prise Acton Grange, Aston by Sutton, Aston Grange, Bartington' Clifton, Daresbury, Sutton, Halton, Keckwick, Moore, Newton-by-Daresbury, Nor- ton, Stoekham, Sutton, and Weston. The Appleton division, comprising the townships of Antrobus, Appleton, Great Budworth, Crowley, Hatton, Seven Oaks, Stretton, Walton Superior, Walton Inferior, Whitley Superior, Whitley Inferior, Grappenhall, Latch- ford, Thelwall. Runcorn with a population at the last census of 15,126, and an estimated population, of 18,482 formed a division of itself and was allotted two members. The other divisions had been allotted a member each. The Daresbury division had a population at the last census of 6,167, estimated Population 7,173; Froclsham division, population at last census 7,297, estimated population 7,916; Appleton division, population at last census 7,040, estimated population 7,523. This scheme was sanctioned by a meeting of magistrates and it was submitted to a meeting of county magistrates at Knuts- ford on Saturday last. It had yet to .come before the Quarter Sessions for confirmation.—Mr. Aaron: You have done very well. MEDICAL OFFIcER'S REPORT.. . . .

The Medical Officer (Dr. Adams) reported that in con- sequence of acomplaint received he visited IlelstV on the 20th inst. On the farm premises, occupied by Mrs. Sarah W. Davies, a pool of stagnant sewage existed, which in its present condition constituted a nuisance. He would suggest that the pool be deepened, the level of its upper surface lowered, and that ir be provided with an efficient outlet. An inspection of the village revealed the fact that there were several road inlets which discharged into sewage drains, and, being all untrapped, gave off very offensive effluvia, the number of these is from 12 to 15. These.should all be properly trapped in accordance with the requirements of each case. He had also furnished a (;eitificate to the inspector, condemning after due inspection, as unfit for .human habitation, a , cottage at Weston Point, occupied by J. Andrews. Pro- ceedings would be- instituted: It , was decided. ta serve notice to abe be the nuisance upon Mrs. Davies.

div.head: TIM PROPOSED CATHOLIC CHAPLAIN.
div.p: TIM PROPOSED CATHOLIC CHAPLAIN.

Mr. P. Speakman said what he was about to propose might be considered by some of the Guardians as anew departure. The Committee hat had under considera,ion the resignation of the late chaplain and the appointment of his successor, Mr. Bennett, had fulfilled its duties. Some of the Committee thought that the salary should be reduced from £4O /to £3O, and that £lO should be given to a Roman Catholic priest to attend to the spiritual wants of the inmates of the house. The Com- mittee decided that it would be a fair and reasonable thing tcr give a priest £lO a year for service rendered to the Board—that he should visit the house once a month and as often as he might be required. Hitherto, one of the priests at Warrington had been at the beck and call of the master; and rain or snow or whatever kind of weather it was he had always come and given spiritual advice or consolation. This was not a question of pounds shillings or pence, but what was right and just. At Prescot the Catholic chaplain received not £lO a year but £75 mysar. No doubt there was a greater number of Catholic inmates in that Workhouse than there were at Runcorn ; but he contended that this was a question of religious equality, and he hoped that the gentlemen round that Board would accord his resolution their support, not on account of expense but on account of the righteousness of the cause. If a priest cam. ' regularly to the Workhouse, there were a great many people in the surrounding neighbourhood who would avail themselves of the opportunity to worship in the manner they had been brought up to. He moved that the Rev. Dr. Ga,staidi of Runcorn be appointed Roman Catholic chaplain at a salary of £lO a year.—Mr. Once seconded the proposition. He thought every member of the Board, and every member of the com- munity, would perceive that it was only an act of justice to a large number of their fellow rate- payers who were members of the Catholic faith; and that it was also an act of mercy to the Catholic inmates of the House that they should have the benefit of the ministrations 'of a clergyman of their own faith. Surely their Protestant fellow ratepayers would have no objection to pay their share of the £lO required, as the Catholic ratepayers had to pay their share towards a Protestant chaplain.—Mr. Whitlow: How many Catholics are there in the House at present ? Mr. Speak- man 17.—Mr. Whitlow : What number of other denom- inations ?—Mr. Speakman: 150 Church of England and Dissenters.—Mr. Whitlow thought , £lO was much too high a figure for 17 in comparison to 150. Moreover, they had no bussiness to increase the expenses of that establishment in any shape or form. • A great deal of rates came from the land, and he did not know when the farmers had worse prospects than they had this year. He was quite willing that the Catholics should have the same facilities as the re- mainder of the House, but he wanted the expenses kept down. It was the expense he objected to.—Mr. Speak- man: lam thankful that you do not object to the principle.—Mr. Whitlow : If we did our duty to the ratepayers we should ask for a reduction of the salary of every official connected with the Union, so that they should be made to meet the costs along with the people who had to work for the money. -(Laughter.)—Mr. Mclntyre objected not only on account of the money, but on principle. In that House were 42 Dissenters, and if there was-any right or justice, as claimed by Mr. Speakman, these inmates ought to have the same amount voted for their, religious instruction. But not a single penny was to go to them, although three times the number of the Catholics.—Mr. Speakman: The law does not allow it.—Mr. Mclntyre: Then if the State does not allow it in one case it ought not to allow it in the other. He had not much faith in paid prayers for anyone. (Laughter.) If they did not come voluntarily he was afraid they were not of much value. As to the expenses, this proposal was simply the thin edge of the wedge, which would only want driving hotee. He should. be no party to keeping the ratepayers pockets open to allow anybody to dip into, to an illimitable extent.—Mr. Brandreth said he believed that the Roman Catho- lics or any other persuasion ought to have their expenses paid. He thought about £5 would be enough for the Catholic priest, hut Mr. Mclntyre's remarks about the thin end of the wedge had almost converted him to the other side. Mr. Stokes pointed out that the Local Government Board did not recognize any ministers on behalf of the Dissenters. —Mr. (Bice: If we had power to appoint a ministerial gentleman to attend upon every denomination, I should think that would be the best course, or abolish the chap- laincy altogether, We have no power to appoint any- body to attend Dissenters—nobody but Catholics or Church of England.—Mr. Smith said there had been
t 5

great complaints of the expenditure in thp union and the ratepayers could scarcely pay the calls. He thought the proposed payment to a priest was extravagent. At a visit once a month it would be .£1 a journey.—Mx. Aaron said he represented almost the second largest ratepaying township in the Union, and there was not a single Catholic out of that township in the House nor were the ratepayers paying a single farthing to a Catholic pauper in that township. As one third of the ratepayers were Catholics and paid their rates was it right or was it wrong that the Catholics in that Hotise Should be denied the privilege of having the regular ministratiens of their priest because of a paltry £lO a year. He hall never been in a Catholic chapel in his life and he hoped he never should go in, but he said pay no minister or pay all. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Knowles: Pay none then.—Mr. Grice : We are obliged to have a Chaplain, are we not P—The Clerk :Yes.—Mr. Speakman said he was simply asking the Board to do what other Unions did all over the country and if they refused the act of justice the burden lay with those who voted against the resolution.—The motion was put to the meet- ing and was lost by 10 votes to 9. Those who voted for, were the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Speakman, Grice, Taylor, Aaron, Lewis, Stokes, Jones and Hey- wood.
