RUNCORN ADJOURNED LICEMING SESSIONS.

The adjourned Licensing Session of the Runcorn Police Division was held on Monday. Mr. John Brundrit occupied the chair, and there were also on the Bench Dr. Steele, Mr. 11. Reynolds, Mr. James Handley, and Mr. G. L. Wigg.

THE THEATRE ROYAL. Mr. Wynne Humphreys appeared on behalf of the pro- prietor and lessee of this theatre to support an applica- tion for the renewal of the license. A month ago the Bench adjourned the application in order that the County Surveyor (Mr. Stanhope Bull) might inspect the building. The Surveyor submitted his report; and sug- gested that several alterations and repairs be done for the safety of the public using the theatre. The owner of the theatre was represented by his solicitor and Mr. _ White, builder, during the inspection.—Mr. Humphreys said that the report showed that steps had been taken to make the theatre as safe as possible from fire, and if a fire should by any accident arise, the Surveyor stated that the exits were ample. The theatre was capable of holding 1,500 people and the place could be easily emptied in three minutes, but the ordinary attendance could be got rid of in a minute Mr. Humphreys expressed the willingness of his clients to carry out the whole of the alterations, if such was the wish of,the Bench, but he submitted that some of the suggested alterations were not necessary.—Superinten- dent Hollingworth pointed out that according to the rules of the license smoking is not prohibited, and it was evident that the county surveyor desired to have the floor close boarded, in order to prevent people throwing lighted matches amongst the debri.4.—Mr. Humphreys said that although personally a non-smoker, still he was afraid that the class of people who frequented the theatre would practically desert it if they were not al- lowed to solace_ themselves with a pipe of tobacco.

There was no refreshment bar, and having taken away the poor man's beer, to take away the luxury of a uipe would be a little too bad.—Mr. Brundrit : Have any of these alterations been made P—Mr. Humphreys replied that they had not. He thought it best to see what the, exact requirements of the Bench were.—Mr. Brundrit said the Bench could not grant a license for twelve months, as the alterations had not been made.—The Bench ultimately decided to grant a provisional license for a mouth. BY that time hey hoped that the altera- tions would be made, with the exception of the stone passage, which could be repaired in the manner sug- gas ed by Mr. Humphreys.

div.head: RENEWAL OF LICENSES._
div.p: RENEWAL OF LICENSES._

At the last Licensing Sessions a month ago Superin- tendent Hollingworth objected to the renewal of the licenses held by the following parsons because convic- tions had been recorded against them during the past twelve months :—William Fitton, Waterman's Arms, Weston Point • John Coxhill, Greenway Hotel; Henry , Kelly, Holyhead Harbour, High-street ; Thomas Philips, Friendship Tavern, ' Fryer-street; Joseph Grundy, Masonic Hotel, Devonshire Square ; Sinclair Armstrong, Bull's Head, Halton-road; and John Done, Royal Oak Inn, St. John-street.—The Superintendent now made no further -objection, and Mr. Brundrit remarked that these convictions were not creditable, and advised the applicants to be more careful in future.

THE MAN AT THE WHEEL. Mr. James T. Thompson, of Birkenhead, applied for a renewal of the license of the "Man at the Wheel," Church-street, now occupied by Alfred Ellison.—Mr. Brundrit : Why has the name of the house been changed ?—Mr. Johnson: The name was changed and no notipe was given of it.—Mr. Brundrit : I think it is very strange.—Superintendent Hollingworth said, he had no objection to raise, as the house had been better since. —The licenSV was granted.
THE LICENSE OF THE GOLDEN LION ABOLISHED.

• Mr. Cooper, barrister, instructed by l'ifess;7l-Niarsh, son, and Calvert, solicitors, of Leigh, applied for the renewal of the license ()Rho Gclden Lion, Fryer-st., to David Snell.—Superintendent HollingsVorth opposed the license on throe grounds. First, that the applicant had been fined £4 and costs for harbouring prostitutes. Secondly, that the house was the habitual resort of reputeel prostitutes, and had been for many years. He should put in a register to show that the house had been. generally badly conducted for twelve years, and that convictions had taken place time after time. In two instances the license had been endorsed. As soon ap one tenant was convicted, he was got rid of and another put in his place. Thirdly, that the license was not required in the neighbourhood. Fryer-st. was very narrow, and " was not much used by any persons, except those who resided in it and by sailors, to whom this house held out an attraction by harbouring prostitutes. Within a radius of 400 yards there were 19 public houses and 23 beerhouses, BO that there could be no necessity for a house of this description in Fryer-st. In answer to the . advocate Superintendent Honing- worth said Snell took possession of the house in March 1887, and there was only one conviction against him. The •nearest beerhouse was the Friendship Tavern, 35 yards away : and the nearest fully licensed house was the Fleetwood Arms, 95 yards away.—lnspec- tor O'Donnell said he had visited the Golden Lion fre- quently during the four months he had been in Runcorn. On only one occasion had he visited the house and not found a prostitute there. There was no necessity -for this license.—P.C. Thompson deposed that he had known the house for six years. It had always been a "har- bouring place" for prostitutes.—P.S. Woolley statedthat he had frequently seen prostitutes in the house during the past 18 months, and on the 10th March a man com- plained of being ribbed in the house. He had never seen any respectable people in the house.— Mr. Cooper: These women will have drink, I sup- poso.—Sergeant Wooley'r There is no doubt about that.—Superintendent Hollingworth asked that the clerk should put in the register of the house.— Mr. Cooper suggested that this was a personal matter. Snell had only been convicted once, and the offence was so trivial that the license was not endorsed. The license was granted last year in face of that register.—Mr. Brundrit : He was a good tenant then.—Mr. Cooper: He has to labour under exceptional difficulties. He con tended that these women were entitled to reasonable refreshments, and Snell could not pfevent them entering , his house. He did not allow them to stop more than ten minutes, and did not serve them twice on the same occasion. • S,uch evidence as that given by the Inspec- tor he never heard in his life, and he asked the Bench were they going to take away a license on the evidence af a man like that, who seemed to have a very treacher- ous memory. He then called William Bradshaw'," cabinet maker, High-street, who said that since Snell had taken the business the house had been better con- ducted than it had been for the past 20 years. By Superintendent Holling,worth : He had seen Snell put people out two or three times a week. They annoyed him (witness) in the street. They stood at the corner a considerable time, and then went back.—Mr. Cooper :—Where do you say these people will have to go if the Golden Lion is closed P—Witness To the devil, I suppose. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. Cooper: I don't think he has got a license. (Laughter.)—By Mr. Brundrit : They were principally women and sailors that he had seen Snell putting Croley, shoemaker, High-st., also gave Snell a good character.—Mr. Brundrit : Who are the owners of this honse P—Superintendent Honing- worth :—Bedford Leigh Brewery and Malting Company. —Snell gave evidence confirming his advocate's state- ment, and then the Bench retired to consider their decision. After a considerable absence they returned,. and Mr. Brundrit said the magistrates had very carefully considered the case in all its bearings. They had come to the conclusion that the house was the habitual resort of prostitutes, and that it was not necessary. The license would, therefore, be refused.—Mr. Cooper gave notice of appeal.
THE CHANGE OF NAMES. 16. Brundrit said it was very desirable that notice should be given to the police when the name of a house was changed. He hoped publicans would observe this.

THE VALUE OF ADVERTISING. From the /featerie, Oborver. Sometimes, when we have been dilating upon the value of advertising to tradesmen, we have cited —the examples which they have every week before their eyes in the various patent medicines adver- tised in this journal. We have often said that we know, from unsolicited testimony, that it pays to advertise with us; and we have further said that when a reader buys anything through this rstedium we should be pleased if that fact were notified by the vendor. In return, it is equally incumbent upon us, if business is done satisfactorily, to say so. * * * * * * * *

One day we met a young man whom we have known for several years, Mr. Herbert Ball, of Albert-street, Kettering, a bricklayer by trade, and he informed us that he had met with an accident, and was on the sick list. A brick or some heavy substance had fallen on his right foot, injuring it rather badly. It was at one time feared that lockjaw would ensue. Happily, it did not; but the shock to the system was so great that it caused extreme nervous debility. We saw Mr. Ball in a reading room when he could not hold a newspaper for five minutestogether, and his whole system appeared to be completely unhinged. He looked like one who was fast becoming a physical wreck. The next time we met with him—about a fortnight afterwards—a great change had been wrought in his health and appearance. "What do you think?" said he. "I had seen and read se much in your paper about Warner's Saps Cure, that I thought I would try it. So I purchased a bottle and a box of pills, at Mr. Moore's, the chemist, in Gold-st. The first dose took effect, and in three days I was like a new man. I had been under the doctors three weeks, and was not getting any better. My appetite had failed, and I was fast losing flesh; but now it's all right again. As a proof of that, I've just been eating a plate- ful of pickled onions. I'm all right now. I can eat almost anything. People laughed when I said I'd try the Sara Cure, but I am thankful I did try it. If my testimony is worth anything, you can publish it, and at the same time express my gratitude to the discoverers of such wonderful medicine." That is, as nearly as we can recollect it,the pith of the statement made to us by Mr. Ball, and as he is one of our townsmen, we thought we would publish this, because it serves to show—first, that advertising pays; second, that patent medicines are of real value in some eases ; and, third, that testimonials are not always mere concoctions of untruths, as some persons suppose.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATIIRDAT.—Before Alderman Burgess. A DESERTEI2.—John Duffy, last from Liverpool, was charged with being a deserter from Her Majesty's Ist Battalion 100th Leinster Regiment, stationed at Calcutta, and was remanded to await an escort. MONDAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton) Coun- cillors Monks and Mr. Robert Garnett. DRUNKENNESS.—The following cases were disposed of: Ellen Smith, in Irlam-street, on Sunday morning, dis- charged with a caution • George Tomlin, in the Market Place, on Saturday night, discharged on payment of costs; John Mulgrove, in Winwick-street, on the 18th Inst., fined ss. including costs; Catherine McDonough, in Crossley-street, on the 18th inst., discharged on pay- ment of costs; Frederick Clarke, in Knutsford-road, on the 17th inst., remanded in custody until the following day; Selina Oultram, in yore-street, on the 17th inst., discharged with a caution. BERACHiS OF THE PFACE.—Thomas Garrity, charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Howley-lane, in April last, was ordered to keep the peace far six months in his own recognizances of £5, and one surety for the same amount, or to go to prison for • month.—Thomas Griffin, for creating a disturbance by assaulting Walter Moseley, was similarly dealt with. —James Kelly and Patrick Cale, who admitted having fought in Dial-st., were ordered to enter into their ewn recngnizances to keep the peace for six months.— Michael McDonelfigh and Thomas MCDonough, who pleaded guilty to a charge of having fought in Buckley-st. on the 17th inst., were ordered to find a surety for their good behaviour for a similar period.—Thomas Burke, and Patrick McCrow, who were charged with fighting on Pinner's-brow, on the 17th inst., were similarly dealt with. _

FEMALE Ptromsrs.—Two women named Kate Pole and Maria Alcock were charged with fighting in Winwick- st., on the 18th inst., and were each bound over in one surety of 20s. to keep the peace for six months. DISORDERLY Coiamcv.—Mary Quinn, Bridget Moriarty, Patrick Salmon, and Mary Salmon were summoned for disorderly conduct in the Old-road, Latchford, on the 16th lust, and were each ordered to find a surety for their good behaviour during the next six months.—John Butlerand Thomas Shields, summoned for a similar offence in Platt-st., were discharged with a caution. SvoNE-rwnowrieg.—Martin McQuire (12), was fined 3s. 6d. for having thrown stones, to thedanger of passen- gers, in Tanners-lane, on the 16th inst. Joseph Warbur- ton (Mill-st.), aged 12, and Joseph Warburton (Richard- son's-row) aged 14, were alsofin,ed 3s. 6d. for committing similar offences in Mill-lane, on the 16th inst. BAD LANGDAGE.—For having made useof badlanguage in Mersey-et., on the 17th inst, MichaelMelia,a labourer, was fined 10s. and costs. STEALINOrTIIRNIPS AT LATCTITORD.—George Minshull, Michael Makin, Herbert Appleton, William Edgar, and Thomas Ashton, boys aged from 10 to 14 years, were summoned for haring damaged certain turnips in a field at Wash-lane Latchford, the property of James Ashley, fanner, to the amount of 20s. It appeared that the boys were seen by the farmer in the field, pulling up the turnips and tramping the young plants down. The Bench, considering that the practice of turnip stealing should be put down, fined the defendants 3s. 6d., with the exception of Makin, who was discharged. UNREGISTERED LODGING Wells VMS summoned for keeping lodgers without haying her house registered, and was fined 20s. including costs, Mr. Norman, Nuisance Inspector, stating that he had refused to register the house as he did not consider it fit to be a lodging house. Smoot. ATTENDANCE CASES.—The following persons were summoned for not sending their children 'regularly to school, Mr, T. J. Garnett, School Attendance Officer, prosecuting :—Richard Hodson, farmer, Moss Side, Rixton, fined ss. including costs; William Sumner, labourer, Rixton, case dismissed on production of a medical certificate ; Robert Bond, farmer, Rixton, fined Sc. including costs. BYE-LAW OFFENCES.—For having allowed the chimneys of their dwelling houses to be on fire Thomas Hibbert, and Annie Salmon were each fined Is. Trmsoar.—Before Messrs. E. J. Guest and R. W. Francomb. SEVERE SENTENCE UPON A DRUNKARD.—Frederick Clarke, labourer, Latchford, was brought up on remand charged with having been drunk in Knutsford-road, on the 17th inst., and alsowith a similaroffence in the police- court on the previous morning.—The prisoner was sum- moned on Monday for the first offence. When his name was called, he did not appear, but soon afterwards he came into the court in a ,drunken, state, and was ordered by the magistrates to be sent down to the cells until he was sober.—The Bench ordered him to go to prison for a month without the option of a fine. DRI:TNIC AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence a man named William Hodgekinson was tined ss. including costs, with the alternative of seven days imprisonment, with hard labour. TRIIRSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster.

DRIJNICEZTS9S.—John ko-u—gii-s-dge was fined ss. and Costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Mersey- 'street, on the evening before.—For having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, on the evening previous, two young men named James Welsh and John Fell were each sent to prison for a month FElDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Aker- man Harrison, Councillors J. Pierpoint and Francomb, and Dr. Gornall. BECIGING.—John Cunningham Was sent to prison for a month for having asked alms in Mill-street. DISTURBING THE PRAM—Winifred Conway and Char- lotte Daley, girls, were summoned for having disturbed the peace, by fighting in Buttermarket-street, on the 21st inst. They were bound over to be of good behaviour for I six months, and were also ordered to pay costs. CHARGE OF WIFE Dam-mos.—Edwin Gaunt was sum- ' moned by his wife Deborah, who alleged that he had I deserted her. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence, and submitted that the case did not come within the jurisdiction of the magistrates, as the alleged desertion did not take place in Warrington. After a little con- I versation on the matter the parties came to an amicable understanding. QUARRELS.—Mary Rabbitt, an old woman, was sum- moned for assaulting another old woman named Catherine McDonough. The case was dismissed.-Baml. Jackson, who was summoned for having assaulted Margaret Forber, Was also dismissed.—Ann ''Corbett was bound over to beef goo i behaviour for havhig assaulted Elizabeth Stretford. MiscetiAirsocs —Francis Riley, for window breaking, was ordered to repair the damage and pay a fine of los and costs.—Thomas Frannon, a lad, who lives at New- ton.-was tined 2s 6d, including costs, for writing an objectionable word on a wall in Bank Park.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. Tinsnay.—Before Messrs. E.Greenall, J. C. Parr. W. Long, and R. Pierpoint. JURE Liars—The jury lists of the various townships in the division were presented to the bench and signed. ADULTERATED COFFNE.—Thomas R. Carter, of Grappenhall, grocer, was summoned for having, on the 16th August, unlawfully sold a quantity of coffee which was adulterated with chicory, and not of the quality and substance/ demanded. Superintendent Hollingworth said the coffee was only adulterated with five per cent of chicory. Defendant was ordered to pay costs. ASLEEP IN CART.—J. Pilling, of Tarvm, was ordered to pay costs for having been asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Antrobus on the 14th Sept. ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF A Pio.--Christooher Bowers, Warrington, was charged with having, on the 11th Sept. caused a pig to be removed through an infected area, and was fined ss. and costs.—J. Clark was charged with

having rernoTed the pig ix que,stion, but the charge against him was withdrawn. DRIIIMINNB69.—Edward Ratcliffe was charged with having, on the 19th Sept., been drunk and disorderly at Stockton Heath, and was fined as. ed. and costs.

ROBBING ORCHARDS.—WiIIiam Smith. a lad, living at 72, Lord Nelson-st., Warrington, was charged with stealing a quantity of pears growing in an orchard at Appleten on the 23rd September, the property of James Warburton; and William Fudge, a boy, living at 40, Bowcock-st., Warrington, was charged with committing a trespass on land belonging to Mr. Warburton, on the same day.—From the evidence it appeared that Smith was caught in the orchard with a bag of fruit in his hand, and Fudge had with him a basket.—The lads pleaded guilty and the case not being pressed were dis- charged on payment of costs. EATING, RAW Fuosn.—Patrick Colman, a labourer, was brought up in custody charged with stealing, at Dutton, on the 27th August, a turkey, the property of John Campkin.—The prisoner was found on tke afternoon of the date named lying asleep in one of Mr. Campkin's fields with the remains of a turkey by his side. The bird had been killed and partly plucked, and a portion of it eaten raw.—Prosecutor said that the theft was not induced by want, as the prisoner was in good work at the time. He had been on the spree from the Saturday until the Monday.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and slid he was drunk at the time, and remembered nothinz about it.—The Chairman said he found that the accused had been in gaol a month already; that being so, the Bench had decided to commit him for only seven days.— Prisoner was then charged on a warrant with drunken- ness at Sutton in February, 1886. He pleaded guilty, and was ordered to undergo seven days' imprisonment; both sentences to run concurrently. DRUNK AND DANOB Dors.—James Smith labourer,

Moore, was charged with stealing three caps, value is. 6d. at Daresbury on the sth September.—Whilst the children were at school at Daresbury the prisoner went into the cap-room and abstracted three of the boys' caps. When apprehended and charged he replied "I do not know what I was doing to take them. I went and got drunk."—Superintendent Hollingworth remarked that to show the mood the prisoner was in on the day in question he might mention that he threw a boy into the canal, and it was with difficulty he was saved from drowning. Serious complaints had been made concern- ing his eonoluct.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for six weeks with hard labour. ALLTIOND ASSAULT.—WiIIiam Webster, labourer, Stock- ton Heath. was summoned for assaulting Elizabeth Cooper, at Appleton, on the 4th September.—The com- plainant stated that after some words had passed between them defendant struck her three times in the face and neck.—Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, for the defence, called evidence to show that the complainant was a quarrelsome woman. She had, it was illeged, been annoying the defendant's father-in-law, and that was the origin of the disturbance. Complainant thrust her fist in defendant's face, and dared him to strike her. He then pushed her away, using possibly a certain amount of force, which caused complainant's nose to bleed.—The case was dismissed. _

Scnoor. CAS3B.—The following cases were brought under the Education Act by Mr. W. R. do Prez, school attendance officer :—Noah Hart, labourer, Seven Oaks, fined ss. ; George Gibbons, labourer, Great Budworth, fined ss. ; John Miller, labourer, Appleton, fined ss. ; Charles Deiooze, labourer, Walton Inferior, fined ss.

div.p: FRODSHAM POLICE NEW.

At Eddisbury Petty Sessions on Monday, the follow- ing cases of interest to Frodsham were heard : CHAnon AGAINST A KEBPER.—A case against Richard Tweedall, keeper, of damaging a fence belonging to Martha Edwards, complainant in the last case, at Helsby, on the 4th September was also dismissed.—The only material evidence was that of Gleave, who said from a distance of about 200 yards he saw defendant undo the forme and leave it open.—Defendant emphati- tically denied this. He said it was to his interest to keep it shut, being keeper to Mr. Arrowsmith. A SHIP CANAL NAVVY' ON THS Spa.—Edward Jones, a Ship Canal navvy, was charged with having been drunk and incapable at Frodsham, on Saturcley after- noon last, and was fined is. and costs (125.) DAMAGING BLACKBERRY BUSHES AT HELSBY.—Martha Edwards summoned a boy, named Albert H. Tweedall, for unlawfully damaging certain blackberry bushes, to the value of is., her property, at Helsby, on the 12th September. Complainant said that on the day in ques- tion she went to pick the berries on her Id, and saw two of Richard Tiveedall's children there. She sent them off, but their mother sent them back, and another with them.—P.C. Boyle said there was no hedge marking the boundary, and children had gathered blackberries there for yeifts. This was the first time they had ever been stopped.—Complainant said thete was a: hedge.—A man, named Bailey, corroborated komplainant's evi- dence.—The case was dismissed.

OFFENCE ACIAINST THE POALTIING PREVENTION Aar.— ' Hannah Foster was charged with having, on the 29th August, at Frodsham, come from land where she was suspected of having unlawfully been in pursuit of game, or with aiding and abetting those who had been unlaw- fully in pursuit of game.—Sergeant Whalley stated that on the 29th ult., about a quarter past eleven o'clock in the forenoon, he saw the defendant coming down Main- at., in Frodsham, carrying a basket which appeared to be rather heavy. He had suspected her before of being in league with poachers, so he searched her, and found ten rabbits in the basket. He asked how she accounted for them, and she said they were "landed in the house" of a man who kept her and her son, near Frodsham Bridge, some time that morning. He knew the two men were poachers, and accordingly took possession of the rabbits.—P.C. Pearson corroborated.—Defendant, who did not appear, was fined 20s. and costs. ASSAULTING A SISTER-IN•LAW. —AN EXEMPLARY SENTENCE.—George Briscoe was charged on remand from Frodsham, with having on the 27th August, at Frodsham Lordship, assaulted Mary Ann Briscoe, his sister-in-law. —Mr. W. H. Churton appeared for the defendant.— Complainant alleged that she was having some words ' with the defendant on the day named, because he had been pulling her boy about, who is aged nine, when defendant ran her in the house, and struck her twice. She said if there was a drop of warm water she "would shift him," and shethen ran into the pantry. Defendant followed her there, and struck her again. He then tried to carry her out of door, and when he found he could not be threw her on the floor, knelt on her, and beat her shamefully. She was bruised all over. Defendant had had drink. It was not the first time he had assaulted her.—Sergeant Whalley stated that on the 29th ult. he saw the complainant. Her face was one mass of dark flesh. Her breasts were black, and her eyes were "knocked up." He had never seen a worse case of assault in his life.—Mr. Churton said the assault had risen out of complainant's boy interfering with defend- ant's fence. He was continually doing this. The com- plainant had not the best of tempers, and when she saw that defendant was dhastising her boy a little, she ran into the house for a poker. Defendant followed to prevent her, when she got hold of the kettle, and threw it at him, but it did not do him any harm, as he avoided it. He did not deny that he then struck the defendant, but as they ,were now living quietly near to each other, and now that the temper was over, he would ask their Worships to deal leniently with the case.—Defendant was fined 50s. and costs, or two.months.in default.

-- ASSAULT AT HELSBY.—Edwin Cobbe Was summoned for assaulting Richard Tweedale, at Ileb3bv, oa the 24th August.—Complainant alleged that as he was going along the road at night with a man named Moss, he met the defendant, who was in drink. Defendant used abusive language to him, and afterwards pulled his coat off and hit him first on one side the head and then on the other, his injuries being so severe that he could hardly eat anything for three or four days.—A police constable said he saw prosecutor after the assault and his face was bruised.--Defendant said he only struck prosecutor once on the side of the cheek, and that was because when he asked him if he was going to shoot him again (referring to the accident which took place about a week ago when complainant nearly shot him) he said he would.—The man Moss was called as NI witness for defendant, and said he did not see any blows struck. He was in a stable near to at the time.— The case was considered proved, and the defendant was fined ss. and costs.

Davies. Dagnianornss. John Sweeney, Thomas Powell, Phillip Antrobus, James Shaw, and Fred Duckett, were each fined ss.and costs for being drunk and disorderly; John Crogan was fined lOs. and COBt.S. THEFT OF Paans.—Samuel Worthington and James Ormes, youths,were charged with haying on Sunday the 23rd. inst. stolen 30 lbs. of pears,belonging to Sir Richard Brooke, of Norton Priory. On Sunday afternoon, P.C. 252 saw the prisoners walking along the canal bank at Bate's Bridge. Noticing that their pockets were unusually bulky, he stopped them, and found they had the pears (produced) in their possession. He afterwards ascertained that they had been stolen from the garden of Sir Richard Brooke at Norton.—The prisoners pleaded guilty and were each ordered to pay 10s. 10d., or go to goal for seven days.

THIIIMMAT.—Before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, ana Mr. H. Gaskell, jun. DRUNICHNINESS.—For this uffence James Ilynaa, of Nelson-street, was fined 7s. ed. and costs; John Burns. Waring-street, 10s, and costa ; Martin lhoom, Elizabeth- street, 7s. 6d. and costs ; Patrick Tardy, 16 Grove- street. 56. and cots; .Tarned Tobin (10th appearance) 76. ed. and costa.

Brock and Sullivan, was charged with being a rogue and vagabond and with having on the previous day improperly.exposed himself .—The prisoner, who said he was in the "horrors of drink," was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

HARVEST FESTIVALS IN WARRINGTON. BOLD STREET (WESLEYAN) CHAPEL. lhanksgiving services for the safe gathering in of the ' harvest were held in the 80ld-street Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday ._The chapel was beautifully decorated wi,h plants, cut flowers, vegetables and fruit. The pulpit was an especial feature in the decorations. The top was fringed with tiny bunches of oats, which in the dis'ance presented a feathery appearance, while from the corners drooped exquisite clusters of grapes. The corners were filled with begonias and other hothouse plants, and the sides were c6vered with snowberries, ferns and flowers,. the panels being marked by Mats of oats,theeffect being crowned by a mirror which covered the centre panel. Inside the communion rails there was a fine collec ion of fruit and vegetables, and the sables were occupied by a number of caoice plants. The rest of the sacred edifice WU adorned with sunflowers, dahlias, bulrushes, wheat, , oats and fruit, which looked exquisite against a background of green fern, the front of the organ being extremely admired. The following ladies carried out the work of decoration :—.Mesdames Starkey Smith, J. R. Young, W. Silcock, R. Silcock, G. E. Young, Goma% and Misses Crornall, Stelfox, and Black- burst. Material for the decorations was also sent by Miss Dutton (Moore), Mrs. Bilsborough (Latch- ford), Mrs. R. Silcock, Mrs. Starkey Smith, Mrs. Gandy, Miss Stelfox, Miss Blaekhurst, Mr. John Cros- field (-Walton Lee), Mr. Whit field, &c. In the morning the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. John Codd, of Leeds, who took as his text the words, "And it was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them," (John vi. 17), upon which he delivered an address both pointed and interesting. .In the afternoon the Rev. Wm. Brookes, whom it was feared would not be able to preach, much to the gratification of his hearers, preached an excellent sermon upon the subject of "What shall the harvest be ?" in tne course pt which he said many people had , wondered whether there would be any harvest at all this year, and some had fancied that if there were a har- vest they would not have suitable weather to get it in. Instead of grumbling it seemed to him they would have boon doing their duty had they given thanks to the Giver of all good for the weather he had sent them. they had had a summer this year like the one they had last year, where would they have been to-day? They would have had a water famine; and that was worse than scarcity of bread. It would not only have been a great inconvenience to them—that they were all ready to admit--but fever germs, cholera germs and pestilence would have been prevalent in the large towns and cities. One could excuse the farmer for doing a little grumb- ling ; they said it was natural to the farmer to grumble. It might be a libel upon him, and he did not know why other people should have grumbled as they had been doing. They had not had as, much sunshine for their holidays as they would have liked, but for his own part, he did not remember ever having experienced ten days of sunshine such as had prevailed during this month of September, and the weather of the past fortnight was the very best kind for the maturing and gathering of the grain. God was good, awl though they sometimes grumbled about the way things were managed above, if they only managed affairs down here as they were managed up there things would, be very much better. Collections were made during the day in aid of the cir- cuit funds, the total amount realized being £l3. In the evening, the choir under the leadership of Mr. C. EL rigot, rehdered the anthem "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy," Mr. Harrison presiding at the organ. ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.

Tho annual harvest thanksgiving was held in this church on Wdnesday night. There was an extremely large congregation, every part of the church being filled. The sacred edifice was beautifully decorated by the ladies of the congregation, Rowers and fruit for that purpose being sent Irina far and neat. The pulpit was draped with long rows of oats which were varied with bunches of grapes, and beautiful scarlet gladioli. In the centre was a beautiful cross of yellow dahlias, which in the distance looked like gold. The communion rails were wrapped with evergreens and fern, dotted at intervals with asters, while around the base was a collection of flowers, fruit and vegetables. A noticeable , feature in this portion of the decorations was a " Cob " of bread, about two feet in diameter,,,which weighed nearly twenty pounds. The front cif the choir stalls was decorated in harmony with the rest of the church, two branches of black plums which were completely hidden in fruit, together with some fine apples and pears, representing the product of the orchard. All the stan- dards were draped with green, dotted at intervals with flowers, adding immensely to the affect., The window ledges were covered with green moss, upon which were laid dahlias, asters, lilies, and beautiful bunches of pur- ple violets. All the available corners and spaces were tilled with evergreens and hothouse plants, which pre- sented in the gaslight a beautiful appearance. The ser- vice, which was fully choral, opened with the proces- sional hymn, "Come, ye thankful people, come." The clergy present were the Rev. Canon Lefroy (Arch- deacon of Warrington), and the Revs. F. W. Willis (rector of Warrington), S. Wilkinson (vicar of St. Paul's), G. D. Wray. (St. Peter's), Rebt. Phillips (curate of St. Paul's), H. G. Smith, J. J. Langham, and Thomas Fellowes. The anthem, " O'God, my soul thirsteth for thee," was sung by the choir, the solo being taken by Mr. Parr. The sermon was preached by the Venerable Archdeacon Lefroy, who took as his text the words, "What mean ye by this service ?" In the course of an interesting and eloquent address he mentioned that the late harvest was less than usual by five million quarters of grain, and some people might wit unreasonably look upon this as a punishment for the wickedness of the people. He commented upon the growing desecration of the Sabbath, remarking that it was now a common thing for their ears to be assailed with the names of sporting papers shouted in the street as they passed to and from the house of God. This undoubtedly conduced to the spread of betting, and to the ruin which this pernicious practice brought upon hundreds of young men at the present day.

div.head: ST. PETER'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. PETER'S CHURCH.

The annual harvest thanksgiving in connection with this church was held on Thursday evening. The school- room was decorated with flowers, fruit, etc. by the ladies of the congregation. There was a large congregation. The Rev. S. Wilkinson occupied the pulpit, and preached

an interesting *WINO'. Thserrioe was hilly choral, and the anthem " Yearnot, 0 Land," (Symper) was sung by the choir in a most creditable manner. A eollsotion amounting, to 18s., was taken in aid of the day school. 9T. BARNABAS 'CHURCH.

A service of thanksgiving ft,r the harvest was held at this church en Thursday evening. The Bev. . Mayo, of Liverpool, was the preacher ; the prayers wore intoned by the vicar, the Rev. G. The sacred edifice was beautifully decorated, some of the designs being very handsome and chaste. At the oast end there was a large cress, in height six feet, which was oovered with golden sunflowers given by Mr. Potter; it had been decorated by Mrs. Potter and Mrs. Warburton. The Vicar had charge of the einbeLlishinent within the altar rails. Upon the steps were plants lent by Mr. J. Piorpoiut and Mr. W. Unlined. The follow- ing ladies and gentlemen had charge of the other decorations :—Altar rails, Miss Short ; screen, Mr. A. Ct. Allton and Mr. Potter ; pulpit, Miss G. Gifts of various kinds had been supplied by the following :—The Vicar and family, Mesdames Morris, Warburton, Potter, Platt, Roscoe, Lewis, Parsonage, Lomax, Jones, Smith, Britton, Parr, Evans, Davies, Dutton, and Flelsby ; the Misses Short, Parsons, Praeger, Connibear and Aston ; and Messrs. div.head: SANKE'Y SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: SANKE'Y SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the members of this Board was held at the schools, Great Sankey, on Thursday, when there were present Messrs. J. C. Ridgway, (chairman), J. Halton, W. P. Skelton, and S. Sutton (clerk ).—The clerk stated that there was a balance of £53 18s. 24. in favour of the Board, and cheques to the amount of £4O were signed.—The Chairman announced that Captain Royse, Her Majestys Inspeotor, had mentioned that the children had passed well in drawing. The head master (Mr. Clarke) presented his monthly report.—. The Clerk said he had prepared an estimate of the receipts and expenditure for the year ending 29th September, 1889. There was at present a balance in hand in favour of the Board of £53 18s. 2d.; the esti- mated grant from Government for the ensuing year was £180; school fees, £l4O ; sale of books and material £5; total estimated receipts £378 18s. 2d. The esti- mated expenditure wolld be :—eutstanding which the cheques of the day would discharge, £4l 53. id.; salaries of officers £3O; salaries of teachers £275; books apparatus and stationery £2O; fuel, light, an , d cleaning £3O; replacement of furniture and repairs, £10; ratee,taxes, and insurance £3; principal and interest on loan £125 ;general station- ery, printing and advertistg £lO ' • clerk's petty dis- bursements, (postage etc.) £2; miscellaneous expendi- ture £lO ; total expenditure £556 ss. id., less receipts £378 183. 2d., leaving a deficiency to be provided for of £177 es. 11d.—The clerk intimated that this would be met by a rate of ed. in the pound, which would raise £lB3, and would be levied 3d. per half-year. He asked the Board to sign a precept for £9l 10s., (half the sum required) at that meeting. The precept was accordingly signed.—This was all the business.

div.head: ALLEGED ;CHILD MURDER AT HA YDOCK.
div.p: ALLEGED ;CHILD MURDER AT HA YDOCK.

A REMARKABLE .TALE. A single woman named Hannah Harrison, who lives at Clipsley-row, Haydock, was on Tuesday morning brought before a county magistrate at War- rington, and charged with having, or the -Sunday previous, murdered her child, who was three years qf age, and was named George Albert Harrison, From a statement made by P.C. Brien, who is stationed at Haydock, it appears that on Sunday that officer, in consequence of a rumour that be heard, went to the house of the prisoner, who lives with her mother and stepfather. When he got there, he saw the dead body of a child of about three years of age on the sofa. , It was dressed and its clothes wore wet. He saw the I prisoner, and her clothes were also wet. He took her ' clown to the Police Station at about eleven o'clock at night ; she there made a statement to him which he (witness) took down in writing. She said she left her brother's house at Ashton at eight o'clock with her child, and walked by the boundary wall into Kenyon's-lane- lane. Than she went down Kenyon's-lane till she got to the footpath, where she met two men. They asked her where she lived, and she said (pointing) "Down here." She asked the men where they lived, and they said at Bolton. They also asked her if she had any money, and she replied that she had not. She walked down the footpath in the direction of Queen Pit. The two men , followed closely behind her till she came to the stile near the Queen Pit Colliery. They came up to her there, when one of the men caught hogof the child and took it out of her arms, while the other seized hold of prisoner, both mother and child being thrown into the E Queen Pit dam. When the men caught hold of her she screamed out twice "Oh, my child; oh, my child." I Prisoner, in her statement, further said she grappled in the dam for her child, which was found, and she took it home in her arms. The prisoner was seen close to her own house about' eleven o7clock at night by a man named Harrison who took the child from her, but found it was dead. The officer said he asked the prisoner what time she was in the water, and she replied that it would be about a quartewast nine o'clock. She could not state how long she had been in the water, nor could she give any explanation where she was from a quarter- past nine till eleven o'clock.—Mr. Stubs: So you arrested her ?—P.O Brien: She was arrested last night. —Sergeant Bage, of Haydock, said the report of the alleged murder was sent to the Coroner on Monday night, and the inquest would be probably held on Wednesday.—Mr. Stubs: And you want a remand till Saturday 2—Sergeant Bage : Yes, sir.—When asked what she had to say why she should not be remanded, prisoner said "You are charging me with something I am not guilty of."—She was then remanded to the Newton Petty Sessions, which will be held on this (Saturday) morning. INQUEST. Mr. S. Brighouse. county coroner, opened an inquest on the body of the deceased at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, on Wednesday forenoon. The mother was present in the custody of the police, who were represented by Superintendent Heywood. The Coroner said that on the night of the 23rd inst. the deceased was brought home dead by his mother, and she was in custody on a charge of having caused the death of the child. Addressing the mother, he said that if she thought the inquiry ought to be adjourned to enable her to have the services of a solicitor, he would adjourn it for that purpose. He thought it would be far better for her to be represented by a solicitor, if she or her friends could obtain one.—The mother said her friends had said nothing to her about it, and she had no means to pay for one.—The prisoner's mother, Mrs. Cross, was then called, and she said they would have had a solicitor, but someone told them that a solicitor wouldw not be allowed to attend at the inquest. —The Coroner said that was not so; a solicitor could attend on behalf of the prisoner. He would therefore take only formal evidence and then adjourn the inquiry. —Mary Cross, wife of John Cross, collier, Clipsley-row, said Hannah Harrison was her daughter by her former husband, and the deceased was her daughter's illegiti- mate son. Both the daughter and grandson had lived at her house. The inquest was then adjourned until Mon- day morning, Superintendent Heywood, in reply to the coroner, stating that the prisoner would be brought up on remand at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday.

div.head: WARRINGTON. MI7SICIL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON. MI7SICIL SOCIETY.

The members of this Society held their annual meeting izr Cairo-st. schoolroom on Monday even- ing, when the chair. was occupied by pr. C. WLite, in the absence of the President, Mr. John Ryland. There was only a moderate atten-

TEI ANNUAL UNPORT. The annual report, which was road by the honorary secretary,Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins,stated that the first concert id the season, given on the 16th December last, com- prised the dramatic cantata Ariadne,' by John More filmieton, a selection of choruses from Handel's oratorio • Solomon,' and from Cowen's cantata Ruth,' the solo vocalists being Mrs Lane, Mimi Monks, Miss Rose Gun- ton, and Mr. W. H. Wallington. It would be remem- bered how seriously they were threatened to be ham- pered in the production of these works by the resignation of the hon. organist, through ill-heallh, just before the concert, and how Mr. Dnffield so generously gave his valuable services, at no small amount of inconvenience to himself. To that gentleman they were under great obligations. The concert was a /MCCAW from a musical point of view. The second concert took place on the 16th March last, when Handel' oratorio ' Samson' was rendered, the principals being Miss Thudichum, Miss Monks, Mr. Henry Piercy, and Mr. Cleaver, and Mr. Driffield again presided at the organ, the work being given with as full an orchestral accompaniment as the I resources of the society would allow, the players being gentlemen selected from Mr. Charles Hall' s Band. Mr. Jenkins added that after the Committee met on Thurs- day last, he communicated with Dr. Hiles, giving him as fully as ho could in a letter the position of the society, and asking it he had any suggestion to make with re- gard to the work of the present session. He had received the following reply from Dr. Hiles :—" Dear sir,—l am sorry to hear that the Musical Society is in difficulties, but, having no particulars, I can form but little idea of the situation. The only suggestion I can make is that we might either attempt three concerts, or reduce the number of practices. If we go back to Tuesday even- ings (as I should advise), the reduced number of prac- tices could be arranged so as not to interfere with the monthly lectures of the Literary and Philosophical Society. I believe that a little canvassing would set the financial condition straight ; and if not, insist upon subscriptions being paid in advance, as for all other societies. I should deprecate the spending of any money on the organ, so long as it is in its present position, and until the existence of the society is thoroughly secure. I shall be engaged at the Atheneum on Monday evening, and, indeed, could I attend, it would probably only lead to waste of time in discussing that work ought to be done, instead of absorbing the attention of the meeting upon the really important question."—The report was adopted.

FINANCIAL STATEMENT. Mr. L. W. RayNotas (hon. treasurer) made a statement with reference to the accounts, from which it appears that the subscriptions kr 1887-8 realized £122 75. 6d., the sale of tickets for the first concert £5 is., and for the second £l6 13s. ed., the sale of programmes £5 15s. 10d., while 10s, had been received for the use *f the society's stare at the Public Hall. The total expenditure was £163 Os. 3d. That, he was sorry to say, left the society a deficiency of £l2 6s. sd. on the season 1887-8. The deficiency on previous accounts was £ll 14s. id., making a total deficiency of £24 Os. 6d. Mr. Reynolds compared the present accounts with those of several previous years to show there had been a falling off in the amounts received, and observed that tho Committee had done their best to keep the expenditure within the income.— The accounts were adopted on the motion of Mr. P. C. Price, seconded by Mr. John Reynolds.

ELECTION OF OFFICERS. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Richard Fairclough, it was unanimously decided to re-elect Mr. John Rylands as President of the Society for the ensuing year. In making the proposition the Chairman said that Mr. 'Wands not only possessed a knowledge of music, but he had a love for the society, of which, he believed, he was one of the founders.—Mr. John Reynolds proposed that the following gentlemen be appointed vice-presidents :—Messrs. James Marson, W. Beamont, John White,Charles White, F. Monks, P. Pearse, and L. W. Reynolds. In seconding the motion, Mr. H. Roberts suggested that increasing the number of vice-pre- sidents might have theeffectof drawing in more subscrip- tions. The president and vice-presidents, if approached, might wipe off the existing debt amongst them. (Hear, hear,) The proposition was then carried, the names of Dr. Gornall and Mr. David Garnett being added to the list.—Mr. Jenkins was re-elected honorary secretary of the society, and Mr. L. W. Reynolds was arain asked to serve the society as honorary treasurer. Mr. William Scotson was re-appointed honorary assistant secretary, and the following gentlemen were elected a committee ; Messrs. R. Fairclough, T. Dinwiddie, J. Newcombe, P. C. Price, J. Reynolds, and H. Roberts,

THE POSITION OF THE SOCIETY. The CHAIRMAN remarked that ten years ago the society had a subscription list of £IBO, but now it was little more than £lOO. The Musical Society did not seem to find favour with those who considered them- selves the elite of society. ,There would always be a num- ber of the lulu who would support them, but they must endeavour to get that support which had not been extended to them during the past two or three years. In a town of 47,000 inhabitants, was it not possible to keep going such a society as this without appealing to the ereniede la er'enle, who looked down upon their concerts, and said they could have better music in Liverpool or Manchester with a very short railway ride But it seemed to him that they ought to be true to them- selves, and instead of looking to the rich for support they should look to those who were not so rich, but who were still able to do something in the way of annual subscriptions. He was rather astonished to find that the members of the choir generally only paid 2s. 6d. a year, though some did pay more. He contended that the members who received so many valuable lessons from Dr. Hiles ought to pay more than half a crown a year. Not only did they only pay 2s. 6d. a year, but they had a right to two tickets, one for each concert. He believed the cost of the tickets would be 18d. each, so that they were doubly benefited. He hoped they would decide that night that the annual subscription should be a minimum of 55. There was anothrr practice adopted which was not altogether legal, namely, that people who sub3cribed for the dress circle and did not attend them- selves gave their tickets to their friends or others who did not like to appear in the dress circle, but demanded tickets for other parts of the house. He thought they. ought to empower Mr. Pearse, Mr. Jenkins, and the treasurer,to say that no such exchange of tickets would be permitted.—Mr. JENKINS said tho transfer of the tickets had been a nuisance, and had given a deal of trouble. —The CHAIRMAN said they need not feel appalled by the debt, because he thought he might guarantee that with the help of vice-presidents and others it would be wiped off. Ile suggested that the ladies form a Committee of their own, and he believed that, if they all exerted themselves, the society would prosper more in the future than it had done in the past.—Mr. H. Roberts said that there were many members who would no doubt feel it their duty to increase their subscriptions, but he thought it would be a mistake to alter the sum. The members got quite sufficient in the way of tuition, without being entitled in adJition to a free ticket for each concert to give away. He did not like the system of receiving free tickets, which seemed to have rather a pauperising effect.—Mr. W. IL Wallington said that the members gave their services to the society. Personally, he did not consider that they received any tuition from Dr. Hiles. They simply met at rehearsal, and not to receive a lesson. He did not think that they got more than they gave for the 2s. 6d. It wasultimatelv decided, on the motion of Mr. H. Roberts, seconded by, Mr. Silcock, that in future the minimum subscription should on{y entitle members of the choir to tuition and personal attendance at the concerts. After a short discussion had taken place with regard to the music to be given at the forthcoming concert, the proceedings terminated by the passing of a vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Dr. Gornall; and seconded by Mr. Tauranac.

div.head: 1,200 MILES ON A TRICYCLE.
div.p: 1,200 MILES ON A TRICYCLE.

Mr. J. C. Copland, member of Surrey Bicycle Club, England; and of the Sydney Bicycle Club, Execu- tive. New South Wales Cyclist Union, writes ;—" I feel convinced I should never have been able to , have successfully completed my tricycle journey of nearly twelve hundred miles, from Sydney to Mel- bourne and back without St Jacobs Oil, and it gives me great pleasure to express my thankfulness for the wonderful benefit I received from it. At the ' end of each day's journey I anointed myself all over with this restoring balm, and felt completely re- strengthened and refreshed. I ate my food with renewed appetite, slept healthfully and as sound as a child. Once my ankle weakened and gave way, but one application of this sovereign care set it right, and it did not again trouble me. The Sydney, N.S.W., Australia Herald, publishes the following editorial comment :—" Not only have Eng- land, India, Canada, Spain, France, New Zealand, Australia, and nearly every other civilised power under the sun recorded their grateful appreciation of the merits of St Jacobs Oil, but we have besides received within the last few months spontaneous words of praise from the champion 'cyclist of England and Australia, the champion youth walker of Australia, a sculler who has held the championship of the world, the champion sprinter, a crieketer of universal reputation, and a host of other less distinguishedi athletes, all of whom attri- bute their success n a great measure to St Jacobs Oil. Unanimity of praise is as decided among athletes as among nations." The Bicycling News, London, says that St Jacobs Oil is without doubt one of the most useful articles a wheelman can have in case of a sprain or bruise.

THE NEW WIMBLEDON.—Another site has been offered to the National Rifle Association for the annual shooting meeting. It consists of two farms, aggregating about seven hundred acres, and is situated four miles from Windsor Castle. It is said to afford many natural ad- vantages, and to have been favourably spoken of by Lord Wautage and other competent judges.

TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION IN WAR- Ring a WAR- RINGTON., even On Monday • general meeting of the Warrington Association for the promotion of Technical Instruction was held at the Museum. Mr. J. C. Parr presided, and amongst others present were the Rev. Morley Stevenson, Rev. Gibson Smith, Messrs. F. Monks, W. Long, W. Owen, T. Morris, L. Greening F. W. Monks, R. Pierpoint, C. J. Holmes, C. Twigs, T. Flood, J. R. Yount/. MAD/MET, (hon. secretary), said he had two or three letters of apology for noa-attendance, from Lord Wimmarleigh, and Mr. W. 11. Blackly, and there was also one from the Rector of Warrington.— The CHAIRMAN mentioned that, since he attended a meeting in that room, he had been to the great meeting in London for the promotion of technical education, and he gave a report as to what took place at that meeting.—Mr. MADBLEY next read the report of the Committee of the Association as to the extent to which technical instruction is already given in Warrington. This report was given in our columns last week.—Tke Rey. MORLET STEVENSON , then gave an address upon " DOREATIVB 11111071N0 cLasses." To maks plain what he meant by recreative evening classes he must trouble them to carry back their memory-for sorneyears to the old-fashioned night-school. He supposed that 20 or 30 years ago the night-school was a very flourishing institution in many parishes in England, and an institution which he believed in many cases did a great deal of good. In proof of the good which these schools did he perhaps need go no further than to say that Mr. ailundella himself owed his early education to the 'clergyman in a village night-school. How was it then that they found the old night-school gradually dying out. He supposed it was first of all on account of the passing of the Elementary Education Act. Now young children were obliged to go to school ,and the three R.'s were taught, and consequently people argued that there was no necessity for the night-school. He then gave figures to show that the number of night-schools under government inspection had gone down from 1363 in 1880 to 841 in 1886. In 1880 there was an average attendance of scholars of 4606 but in 1886 the average attendance had declined to 2689. They came to ask the question, is this a good thing or is it a state of things which it would be desirable to alter? They would find that Her Majesty's inspectors throughout the country deplored the gradual fall off of the night-school, as they said there was a great deal of education which i could only be given n the night-school. He found that the average age at which children left school in a town like Wolverhampton was eleven years, and the age was decreasing, because children were passing more quickly through the standards than they used to do. At all events they might take it as a pretty well established fact that in most of their typical towns a boy left school when he was about eleven years of ape, and after that he got no more schooling of any sore, the consequence being that he forgot almost everything he had learnt at school. It had been found that boys who had passed the fifth standard when leaving the day school, after a few months only, were unable to pass the third standard at the night school, showing how very quickly the process of deterioration set in. There was another point of great importance; what did, their boys and girls do with their evenings ? He thought they;bad only to walk about the streets at night to find an answer to that. Didn't they want some place where these children could go to in the evening, where they could be instructed and interested, and where they could be kept out of mischief during those years which were certainly the most important years of a young person's life ? (Hear, hear.) He thought they ought also to do something toraise the standard of exemption at their day schools. This varied in different places, as it was fixed by the school authorities of those places. In London it was standard six, and in Warrington four. He thought they ought to consider whether that stand- ard four was the minimum standard they should expect. He urged that the point might be impressed upon the Town Council, at all events as to reconsidering the question of the standard of exemption ir their ele- mentary schools. With regard to the objects ef recrea- tive evening classes,he said people saw that the old night school was not attractive to a boy who was wearied , with his day's work. Therefore they set to work to invent seine kind of night school which would be more attractive, and yet be instructive, and so recreative evening schools came into being. The plan wasfirst tried in Nottingliam,and was I a great success. The instruction in the schools wasl partly such as to koep up what the children had learned I in the elementary schools, and partly—and this; was the ' sugar to help the other to go down—of such things as music, band performances, drawing, modelling, drill and I things of that kind for boys ; and for the girls, the higher kind of needlework, cookery, drill, and he , believed in some cases dancing and singing These schools proved immensely attractive to the children. With regard to the cost, there were at Nottingham , seven schools,which earned last session a total govern- I ment grant of £441, the school fees at 2d. per week I each amounted to £143; and books sold to pupils las. 3d. The expenditure, including £582 for teachers' salaries, amounted to £6BO 12s. leaving a balance to the bad of £9445. 10d., which had to be borne by the rates. In 1 London the cost was very much less, because they went' in for voluntary teachers, and he believed the plan I might be carried out without any adverse balance. Whether they thought anything of the kind should be done in Warrington it was for them to consider. (Hear, hear, and applause.)—ln the course of some discussion it was mentioned by Mr. Jordan that night Ischools rather after the plan mentioned by Mr. Steven- son had been carried out at Buttermarlcet-street Catholic schools. The grant earned was £25; and there was no adverse balance—Mr. F. Monks also remarked that the late Rev'. R. Filcher had conducted night classes at Cairo-street school which were very success- Madeley eventually moved that the following I gentlemen constitute a committee to consider the matter of recreative evening classes, viz —Rev. Morley Steven- son, and Messrs. R. Pierpoint, Buckton, Twiss, Jordan, Monks, Hodgins. The name of Mr. Madeley was also added.—This proposal was agreed to.—A vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Stevenson, on the motion ef Mr. W. Lone., seconded by Mr. R. Pierpoint.
SACRED CANTATA AT. WARRINGTON TRAININGe., COLLEGE.

On Thursday evening-a-Pe—rfo-r-n-M—n-ce of Men- delssohn's sacred cantata, " Lauda Sion," and a miscellaneous program me,was given by the students of Warrington Training College, assisted by mem- bers of the Parish Church choir, and others. The principal vocalists were Miss Riley and Miss Monks, and Messrs. Myatt and Robinson of Chester Cathedral. Mr. W. S. Woods conducted. The string instrumentalists were Mr. R. 11. Pearson, Mr. H. Bond, and Mr. R. Woodfield; the Rev. Morley Stevenson (principal of the College) presided at the harmonium. and Mr. W. A. Wood at, the pianoforte. The performance, so far as the stu- dents were concerned, was in the nature of a musical exercise for Sir John Stainer, who was present, but there was a select number of guests present, invited by the Principal. The first part of the programme consisted of the cantata, " Lauda Sion," and opened with the chorus, "Praise Jehovah," which was finely rendered. In the solo and chorus, "Sing of judgment," Miss Riley was the ' soloist and acquitted herself admirably. The quartett, .‘ Ye who from His ways have turned," was rendered by Miss Riley, Miss Monks, Mr. Myatt,,and Mr. Robinson, and the chorus which followed, "They that in much tribulation," was so success- fully dealt with that it was repeated at the request of Sir John Stainer. Miss Riley appeared at her best in the solo, " bord at all times." The chorus, "Save the people," and the quartett (Miss Riley, Miss Monks, Mr. Myatt and Mr. Robinson) and chorus, "Thou didst free them," brought the first part of the programme to a close. The second part was introduced by a part song, "Ring the Bells," by the senior students, who were warmly applauded for their efforts. Mr. Myatt made a very favourable impression by his expressive reindering of the song, "The Distant Shore," and, being recalled, gave "Once Again." An encore was also awarded to the instrumental quartett (piano, harmonium, violin, and violineello) by the Rev. M. Stevenson, Mr. W. S. Woods, Mr. R. 11. Pearson, and Mr. Bond. Mr. Robinson, to a 'cello accompaniment by Mr. Bond, sang with fine effect , the song," Fetters of Gold," and the audience would I fain have recalled him, but he bad to leave hastily to catch his train. The junior students next gave marked evidence of good training in the part song, "Blow Soft Winds," a performance which elicited cordial applause. The intelligent and expressive vocalisation of Miss Andrews, (ono of the senior students) in the song," An Old Gardeq," won a warm recall, when Miss Andrews gave, " The Minster , Windows." A part song, "Protect us through the coming night," by the senior students, and" God save the Queen," by the whole company, brought a pleasant gathering to a close.
