Sir,—l wonder whether the " powers that be" have decided that this street shall be paved and made decent whilst the men are in the locality. If not, why not ? In the wet weather it is particularly bad for pedestrians, as there is neither footpath nor pavement. The street is nearly built up,nn both sides, and, if not paved before the coming winter. I can only think there is some other interest to be considered before the health and comfort of the residents and general public. I enclose my card and remain,—Yours truIy,CLEANLNESS. Warrington, Sept. 26th, 1888.

CRITICS ON A " TRICYCLING TOUR." Sir,--The letter by " Reader " in your last issue, anent our " Tricycling Tour," reminded me of that old quotation about • fools rushing in." Certainly none but a person utterly lacking the qualities which go to make a man would write with such urtblustting effron- tery the baseless statements contained in his letter. I indignantly repudiate his asser ion respecting the ginative picture drawn by "A Cyclist,", and in con- firmation of my remark would remind your readers that o neither "Cyclist," "Reader," nor any other person in Warrington ever set eyes on the "Tourists." The little fact that the " Toursts " were never in Sankey-st. dis- .

poses at once of the gross calumny in the letter of, a Reader " ; and I can only repeat die statements in my last respecting our turn-out, merely adding that I can , produce an accomplished cyclist who will tes ify to the 'fit," and to the very modern character of the ma- chines we rode. In his vain attempt to make trwh of the fiction of "A Cyclist," "Reader 'has so " thorooghly " lost himself that the less I say the better it will be for his veracity.—Yours, Ac.,
TOWNSMAN.
NEWTON BUILDING SOCIETY.

Sir,—l was much interested in reading a letter signed "A Member" in your issue of the 15th inst., re Newton Building Society and its Solicitors, and quite agree with your correspondent that the solicitors of the said society are wrong in promulgating the idea that building society days are done. I believe that building societies are only in their infancy. The directors of such societies will hare to alter their lines a little; the jerry builder must be excluded; the rates of interest reduced to suit the times • and solicitors' charges arranged at a fixed sum per deed. Many societies haie already made the latter arrangements ; but for their days to be over —it is complete moonshine. There is no reason to believe that the people in this country have done "multiplying and replenishing the earth." Its population is bound to increase as much in the future proportionately as in the past, and, as a matter of course, more houses will be required than ever. Those parties who have had loans both through the medium of solicitors and building Societies are best able to judge which are cheapest and best, and, as far as I can ascertain, and I have made many inquiries, the building societies will always hold their own, and be pre- ferred by many. The calling in of private loans made through solicitors every two or three years, referred to by your correspondent, is a wretched practice, and makes the poor borrower smart, as every time the loan is called in fresh deeds have to be paid for. With regard to the Newton Building Society, there is a concensus of opinion that it is quite solvent, and its solicitors and those who are using their influence to close it, after the members, at two public meetings, passed resolutions that it should go on, have a great responsi- bility and are much to blame. Twelve months have now passed since the first meeting was called, but the wishes of the members are still ignored. I make my humble protest against the proceedings, and hope able pens than mine will take the matter up. . ANOTHER MEMBER.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

Sir.—Would you, or any of your numerous readers, kindly answer me the following questions rela ing to the Warrington Musical Society, viz The president and vice-presidents; Are hey all truly supporters of the cause of music in Warrington, either by helping it with money (more than the ordinary sub- scription for the number of seats occupied at the con- certs) or by their indivldual work or enthusiasm? If not, why are they chosen to occupy these positions? % The committee; Is it, a represen•ative one for a Sociey calling itself the "Warrington Musical Society?" Is it large enough, and why are the amateur instru- mentalists not represented upon it? Surely we cannot have too many interests at work to make a society successful. Members: Would it not be well that some better test of the abilities of intending members' of the choir be arranged, as it is quite evident that under existing cir- cumstances any one can get in? Does not this state of affairs prevent better singers joining the choir? Rehearsals ; Should not thOse talM place regularly each week during the season, and why should they give way to any other society? I think the above questions are of vital importance to the Members of the Musical Society.—l remain, dear sir, "A MEMBER." Warrington, September 28th, 1888.

Sir,—The position of the Warrington Musical Society is, it would appear, far from satisfactory. The Com- mittee " fear that unless greater interest is taken in the society its continuance for the present will be one of difficulty." Much was said at the annual meeting on Monday, as to the apathy towards the society shown by the outside public, and as to the want of inherent vitality in the society itself. But none of the -various speakers at Monday's meeting seem to me to have hit upon the real reason for.this feeling of indifference, and any adequate remedial suggestions are therefore sought in vain. If I remember rightly, there was at the annual meeting last year, an abortive attempt made on the part of one of the Committee, to discuss the propriety of nt electing Dr. Hiles as the society's conductor, and some animadversions were cast upon thn-lnanner in which recent concerts had been hrrried, afid the oratorios &c., _ . _ .

mutilated, in the interests-of those' who had a train to Manchester to catch at the close of the concert. Now, I although I am far from concurring in any personal 1 attack such as was then made, I am distinctly of 1 opinion that the cue given was the right one in so far as it raised the question of appointing a new conductor, •and I am disappointed to find that it was not followed up at Monday's meeting. Not a word is reported to have been said upon the subject of the re-election of Dr. Hues, whose office, I have always understood, is held only from year to year. If I am right, it would, I apprehend, have been quite in order to have discussed at such a moment, the advisability or otherwise of making such re-appointment, or of nominating a new conducter. But be that as it may, nothing. I take it, was as a matter of fact said upon the subject, and my own impression is that little can be done in the way of imparting new life to the society until we have for its conductor some zealous and capable musician who cares, to make himself popular and whose sympathies and, aspirations are at one with those of lovers and students of music in the town. To go at once to the root of the matter, I would ask whether the society's present conductor, master of his art though he be, possesses the minor, though highly essential qualifications, which I .have indicated- Dr. Riles' cynical observations from time to time, upon the possibility of getting together a permanent local orches- tra in connection with the society have discouraged., once and for all, any further developments trr tlliS direc- tion. And who that haslistened to the highly creditable public performances of Mr. T. J. Down's local band can do otherwise than 'agree to differ with hilt in this i matter? The feeling of the amateur instrumentalists in the town is, I have reason to believe, one of natural antipathy towards the society's present conductor,whose manner is not always of the happiest, tholigh his method be ever so scholarly. Dr. Hiles' sarcastic and often caustic style is no doubt perfectly natural to him, and amounts to nothing more than a personal peculiarity, but there is no mistaking its repellant effect upon a large portion of our musical community.. There are doubtless many vocalists who could echo this feeling, and who are, in consequence.far from being attracteclto the rehearsals of our society as at present constituted. Nor would their experience of the " qualificatien " ex‘mination by Dr. Riles about two years ago,lessen their strong disapproval at the ways of the " managem!mt " ; the direct result of that ill-advised proceeding being to disinte- grate the various elements out of which a solid and useful society must be formed. I shall be glad if the question of the society's well-bging could be thoroughly ventilated from this point of view. I am strongly of opinion that, for the money at present being expended, a conchictor could be secured whose ability,., coupled with a fair amount of tact and enthusiasm, would be equal to the task of bringing together and -utilising the material for a good society which, I feel

persuaded, exists in abundance in our numerous church] and chapel choirs, and in the local amateur orchestras presided over by Mr. Down and Mr. Gaskell. And, granted that the society could be thus healthily enlarged, a vigorous representative committee would be the immediate outcome at the improved conditions, and-the choice of works for public performance being placed in safer hands,fewer difficulties would arise from the selec- tion of pieces beyond the capabilities of the society, or necessitating an undue expenditure of its funds. The slender attendances which have marked some of the past performances is but the outward and visible signs of inward lethargy and want of heart, and for this, the present unsatisfactory state of things, I believe there is a remedy in the changes' have suggested.—Yours, &c., A MEMBER OF THE SOCIETY.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
EASTHAM TO ELLESMERE PORT.

Much blasting is now being done in the third lift at Eastham, where very hard roek is being met with. The outer embankment across the foreshore between this cutting and the rock cutting at Ellesmere Port is being rapidly pushed on. ELLESMERE PORT TO INCE.

Great progress is being made in the cutting off Stan- low Point. about midway between Ellesmere Port and Inc,e, and there are three American navvies already in the cutting. At the cutting near the offices at Ince a Priestman's grab has been got to work. The clay here is very stiff, the grab being specially suited for the work. INCE TO WESTON POINT. This section begins at the powder magazines, which are situated about two miles from the mouth of the Mer- sey. The whole of the cutting from the magazines to the Weaver is being worked. At the Weaver end a Ger- man navvy is doing good work, and a little further on the marsh are two American navvies. At the point where the canal enters the Weaver a temporary pier has been erected, up to which vessels of 300 tons can sail. WESTON. Since active operations were commenced on this section two months ago, great progress has been made, and to the visitor presents many features of interest. Mr. Weston, the agent, has now about 650 men under his control, and the difficulty of housing them is being met as quickly as possible. The village on the Marsh is approaching completion. Twenty-two huts have been erected, and Mr. Kirkham's men are now engaged in the construction of another block. Several of those built are not yet ready for occupation, but 14 are at present inhabited, and the remainder will find accommodation for a few score of navvies in the course of a day or two. The house that is to shelter the missionary, who will attend to the spiritual needs of the little colony, is fully completed; the mission room is partly built, and as soon as possible services will he conducted there. It is satisfactory to note that a capital supply of water has been obtained. Within easy distance of the huts, Mr. Timmins, engineer, of Runcorn, made a boring 220 feet deep, and had the iood fortune to come across one of the best springs in the ,County of Chester. The supply is equal to about 400 gallons 'per hour, and the water issues from the tube with such force that a fountain of considerable propor- tion is formed. In the neighbourhood the spring is regarded as quite a natural curiosity and hundreds of persons have visited the spot to see the" waters play." The cutting on the marsh is visibly lengthening and widening. There are now at work one German navvy and two Englishnarvies manfactured by Messrs. Wilson, of Liverpool, and the machines work with satis- factory results. The German machine is removing an exceptionally large amount of material. 'ln one day last week this monster filled no fewer than 660 waggons, which is equal to about 3,000 tons; and the cutting measures over a quarter of a mile in length, is 20 feet deep and over 100 feet wide. Five locomotives are kept busily employed on the section. STOCKTON HEATH AND WALTON.

Progress on the first of these sub-sections is still rapid. There are now over fifty men, and a steam navN jr, engaged between Tom Payne's and Twenty Step Bridges in removing that high ground known as George's Bank. The navvy,whichis anextra large "Rus- ton and Procter," is in the second preadth of the cutting. No further remains of the Roman camp have been dis- covered up to the present. Owing to the sandy nature of the soil, the "bucket" of the navvy is so quickly filled that the machine is able to fill two waggons alternately; so that it stands between two rows of rails,' one on each side. The navvy on the Walton side of the Old Quay Canal, near Walton Arches, is also excavating at an unusually rapid rate. At Morley Common hard rock hasbeen met with in the second ". lift,"and a large quan- tity of water lodges there. There are four of the con- vertible cranes working here. The filling up of the Old Quay Canal, where the new Jowl crosses it, is nearly completed.

THELWALL, LYMM, ETC. The two large American navvies, which are working abreast nearly opposite Cedar LOwn, are eliding through the ground at an extremely rapid rate, and are now within a few yards of somecottages which stand in the line of the canal. Considerable excitement Was caused here by the destruction of a stack of hay belonging to the contractor, which stood near the line of rails behind Cedar Lawn. The Warrington fire brigade were summoned as there was valuable property near. Nothing however but the stack was damaged. Near Morris Brook Farm is another navvy, while a little further on is a fourth which is in the second lift. The bottom of the cutting presents at present a vex./ muddy appearance some of the men working ankle deep. The embank)nents at Thelwall increase at a great rate Rlxton Ley, which formerly, to most people, was an unknown land, is now as busyra little spot as any along the canal route. South of where the canal cuts aceoss, near the old river Weir, the land is being used as a place to deposit soil from the canal cutting. Here at work is one of the German navvies, which in the short time it has been going has worked wonderfully well, On Tuesday however, there was a short stoppage owing to one of the cog wheels smashing, a part of which severely injured one of the men employed on it, he being unfortunate enough to receive a blow on the face from a fragment. Owing to the river passing ehch side of the island the water here gives a great deal of trouble, as it filters through from each side. A few weeksback it was found necessary to assist the pump in the centre of the island with one fixed on a stage near the river Weir, and this has answered so well that the old. one is being removed. On the right hand coming down from Lymm the whole of the work up to the present time has been done without the aid of steam diggers, the waggons being filled by hand labour, after which they are taken away by locomotives for the soil to be tipped. The soil being of a loose nature, con- siderable progress has been made. A POWERFUL DREDGER.

Messrs. Fleming i-,:r;a•Wrgru- -;:o;i:icaisieT,iave launched a twin-screw hopper dredger, fitted with two pairs of their patent quadruple expansion ene,ines indicating 700-horse power, and with steel gearing throughout. She is designed to cut in front 800 tons per hour at a depth of thirty feet, so as to make her own flotation. The vessel is built for Mr. Walker, contracter for the Man- chester Ship Canal, and is intended for harbour work. • SCHOOL AT THELWALL. In his monthly report to the members of the War- rington Union School Attendance Committee, Mr. T. J. Garnett, school attendance officer for the No. 3 district, said "The Ship Canal school which I mentioned in nrf last report, was opened on Monday, September -,W.h The building will accommodate about 150 children and there is a master and two mistresses. It is to ix: an elementary school, under Government inspection, and. ha l: 62 scholars now upon the register. In the Ship Canal huts at Thelwall there are 44 children bet weep 3 and 13 years of age, and I don't yet know where the remaining 18' come from, but shall be irr a position to say by your next meeting." THE RIVER WEAVER. • . The most important engineering work is, hovrever, being carried on at the mouth of the Weaver on the Weston side. Here, when the canal is completed, will be a large basin or bay, and a lock of enOrmous size will permit the vessels to pass from the Weaver Canal to the Ship Canal and vice versa. At all states of the tide, it will here be high water. Mr. Weston has commenced the construction of this lock, and the work so far pro- gresses very satisfactorily. A huge ,dam, con- structed of piles in the form of a semicircle, keeps out the aggressive waters of the Mersey, as the men dig the foundations for the lock, but water nevertheless drains into the excavation, and it is necessary to have a machine pumping day and night. The sides of the trenches are kept up by huge beams of timber. The lock will be-constructed princiPallyof concrete, and there is about a thousand tons of this material on the ground ready for- use. Three powerful steam cranes bare employed in the work. The offices at Weston Point have this week been connected with the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Co's system. Sections one, two, and three are now so connected. , FIGHT WITH A SHIP CANAL NAVVY. At the Borough Police Court, at Warrington, on Thursday morning, a powerfully built Ship Canal navvy named Joseph Toppinwas brought before Major Litton and Alderman Webster on charges of having, 01/. the day previous, (1) been, drunk and disorderly in Knuts ford-road, Latchford ; (2) of having assaulted Constable Michael Hennessey • (3) of having assaulted a civilian named Harry Peter Janson ; and (4) of having maliciously damaged a watch belonging to the police officer. Evidence was given by Constable Hennessey to the effect that at about a quarter past. nine o'clak on the previous night he was on ditty in St. James-st.,Latch- ford, when a bus driver called his attentionto the prisoner, who, he said, had entered the bus and made a distur- bance there. Witness, at the driver's request,asked prisoner to come off the bus and lie did so, and then ran along the road in front of the horse, threatening what he would do to the driver when he reached Latchford. The driver was afraid that the prison& would do him some injury, and at his request the officer rode on the 'bus with him for a short distance. When they reached the Golden Lion the prisoner and three other men were standing there. Prisoner ran away, but witness fol- lowed him to York-st. Prisoner then got over the wall of a yard and witness followed and brought him back. Prisoner refused to say where he lived, or to go home quietly, and "squared up" to the constable. The two closed, and a severe struggle ensued, which lasted
I demi

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,

nearly an hour. Prisoner, Ritnnessey said, assaulted him several times, and kicked him in a most violent manner all over the body. Prisoner also assaulted Johnson, who went to the assistance of the offi- cer. Witness added that the prisoner was the worst man that he ever had to deal with. . . .

During the struggle his (witness's) watch was damaged, and his body was all black and blue. "In the Queen's name" witness called upon another man—a sergeant in the volunteers—to assist him, but he walked away and rendered no help. Harry Peter Johnson having given corroborative evidence, Major Litton told the prisoner that the Bench must make a decided stand with the Ship Canal men. They were decent enough when sober, but beyond control when drunk. By way of a caution to his mates prisoner would be sent to prison for three months, with hard labour. To witness Johnson Major Litton expressed the thanks of the Bench for the service le had rendered in assisting the police. One man had refused to give assistance when called upon. The police would take such notice of him as the law required.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY " ARIEL." ,
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY " ARIEL." ,

That a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. That the " Golden Lion" would appear ti be just as unsavoury as the "Blue Ball " ; and the magis- trates by refusing to renew the license to the house, have received the encomiums of the greater part of the population. That the witnesses for the publican were very candid, and he would not feel flattered to learn that there was only one step from his house to the depths of perdition. That it was considered a certainty that the Quar- ter Sessions, on appeal, will confirm the decision of the Runcorn Bench.

That.the voting for the appointment of a Catholic chaplain to Dutton Workhouse, was much closer than was anticipated, and that it was gratifying to see a clergyman of the Established Church on the side of religious equality. That Mr. Speakman 6truck the right key in his speech, and the opposition, outwardly, was simply on the score of expense. That th e question is asked "Where was Mr. E. A. Wallington?" Had that gentleman been in his place. the voting would have been equal, and the onus of deciding the question would have devolved upon the amiable chairman. Perhaps Mr. Walling- ton will explain? That a motion to abolish chaplains altogether would have met with most favour, but the law did not permit. That the Runcorn ratepayers will be asked to decide a question of considerable importance on Thursday evening next. Hitherto the people of Weston have had to pay double fees to the Burial Board when any of their relatives were buried at Runcorn Cemetery, and it is sought to reduce the charges to the same ..level as, the fees paid by the Runcorn people. That the ratepayers of Runcorn tor 'inwards of 20,years have paid, and are stilt paying, for the cemetery, upon which a debt exists. , That the ratepayers. of Weston have not contri- buted a single penny. That they „had the opportunity of joining with Runcorn in the formation of the cemetery but declined. That they ought to pay extra for an advantage secured and paid for by the Runcorn people. That the Weston people have one very reasonable complaint. The ministers of religion charge double fees for burying the Weston dead although the township is in the parish of Runcorn, and under the oversight of the ministers of that town. That it would be interesting to know what extra labour the ministers are put to because the corpse has had to be carried two miles.

That the ministers ought to be satisfied with single fees, and if the matter is pcoperly put to them they probably will. That all doubt as to the formation.of a salt syndi- cate is at an end; its accomplishment is assured. That the project is full of import to Widnes, where vast quantities of salt are annually used in the manufacture of chemicals.
That the price of salt will be trebled and the effect upon the chemical trade will be far-reaching, and if not altogether disastrous, at least very preju- dicial.

That the Widnes manufacturers are too enterpris- ing to be vanquished by tiny monopoly and the 'scheme of boring for salt.mooted some months ago, is to be at once actively commenced. That this was decided upon at a meeting of the manufacturers held in the luncheon room at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co's Works on Thurs- day.
That people are saying:—May they meet with salt in abundance and confound the monopolists.
LOCAL ACTION FOR ,LIBEL BY
MR. BRADLAIAH, M.P.
The following letter has been received by the Editor of the " Warrington Observer," from Messrs. Harper and Batteock, on behalf of Mr. C. Bradlaugh, M.P. :--
HARP'II3 AND BATTCOCr,. Solicitors' . Rood Lane. . . -
London, KC., 13th §L-ptember, 1888.

Sir,—We have been instructed by our client, Mr. Charles Bradlaugh, M.P., to communicate with you with reference to an article in the "Warrington Observer," of the Ist. inst., which contains gross libels upon him, and to inform you that unless you are prepared within one week from this date to withdraw the statements con- tained in such article, and te inserr a suitable apology to be approved by Mr. Bradlaugh in your paper, proceed- ings will be taken against you for libel yeithout further notice.-r-We are, sir, your obedt. sevr HARPHR AND BATTDOCH

Mr. W. Gill, 21, Sankey-at., Warrington. [No apology having been made, we understand that, during the past week, a writ has been served on the publisher of the "Observer," through Messrs. Bunkum and Greenall, the local agents of Mr. Bradlaugh's London solicitors.]

div.head: MR. BRUNNER ON POLITICAL
div.p: MR. BRUNNER ON POLITICAL

_ QUESTIONS. A well-attended meeting to consider current political questions was held at the Town Hall, Middlewich, on Thursday night. Mr. E. 11. Moss presided, and there were also present Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., and others. Mr. Birnwricit, who was received with cheeis, dwelt on the Tory tendencyto develop the military spirit all round. Alluding to the recent naval mancenvres, he said they had recently had a most entoyable game all round the coast between various ships of her Majesty's navy, and it seemed to him that they were playing at a game which they had not practised, and were, consequently, rather rusty. But what had been the object in sending these ironclads into the various parts all :round the country? It meant this—that their eyes were to be shut to the jobbery at the A imiraltyand in the dockyards, and they were to be persturded, by the capture of Liverpool and the demand for a large ransom', to give another three millions to arm the navy, and let the jobbeiyslip.by. As a business man— having been trained to manage business all his life—he could tell them this—that, if. they only would insist on good management at the Admiralty, they would have a far better navy than they had to-day for very much less money. Let them not give way to the demand for more money until those people had set their house in order. A Royal CommisSitut was appointed not long ago to inquire into the working of the Education Act of 1870. On that commission there was a majority of Conservatives, amongst whom was the Rev Dr. Rigg, a. well-known minister of the Wesleyan body. He (Dr. Rigg) was one of the majority who had presented a report to her Majesty itt which there was a recommenda- tion that hereafter, in order to help the voluntary ' schools, money should be advanced out of the rates. But what was his surprise and delight to find that at every September meeting of the Wesleyan laxly through. out Great Britain there had been appointed two delegates—one a lay, man and the other a minister to examine into that report, anti there was not one single district committee that had not condemned that commission. (Cheers.) It was a delight to him to find that the younger men of the Wesleyan body did not mean henceforth to be led by the nose, but to act in accordance with their own con- victions. (Cheers.) A man came to his death at the chemical works at Sandbach after working 19 hours, and it was said at the Trades Union Congress that it was very likely that the Man had not his wits about him, and had become so tired that he would do almost anything to avoid further exercise. This matter had impressed itself upon his (Mr. Brunner's) mind; and he had resolved to propose, when he got back to tho }louse in November, and when they came to the report stage on the Employer's Liability Act, that just as the employer who provided works or wires, signal ropes, tackle, or chains too weak for their work, was liable therefore to the workman Or his representativeS for a sum of money, so also he should be liable for injury caused by too long hours, producing fatigue or exhaustion. (Great cheers.) ' Mr. Ettis, M.P., who was also received with applause, delivered an address on the Irish question, particularly with reference to the impending evictions. The fact that 50,000 eviction notices had been scattered amongst the Irish tenantry showed how right Mr— Dillon was when he protested against the inadequacy of the Irish

div.head: ,%ENEMBER
div.p: ,%ENEMBER

Land Act of last. year. For once, Mr. T. W. Russell, who had warned the Government, proved to be a true prophet. Under the _ circumstances, he considered it was little short of a crime for Mr. Chamberlain to go to Bradford and declare that the Irish tenants were more blessed than those of any other country in Europe. (Loud cheers.) A vote of confidence in Mr. Brunner was unanimously carried. -tee WIDNES CHAPEL TURNED INTO A DANCING SALOON. At the St. Helens County Court,on Wednesday,Mr. T. J. Peters, solicitor, Widnes, applied to Judge Collier for an injunction to restrain Matthew Grier- son, a mineral water manufactuAr at Wigan, from continuing to trespass on certain premises in Wid- nes. Mr. Peters explained that the Welsh Wesle- yan Chapel was recently disused for the purposes of worship, a new chapel having been built. The old chapel was offered for sale, and the defendant called upon several trustees offering to buy the 'place for £lOO, .£5O of which was to be paid Ido Rn. A contract was never signed, however, and I no money had been paid, but the defendant had I entered into possession, and turned it into a dancing ' saloon. The defendant told one of the trustees that he had a lot of bottles at the railway station which it was absolutely necessary should be placed elsewhere. lie was given the kg of the vestry, but was distinctly told that he must not go into the chapel, as the minister, the Rev. Hugh Owen, was away. His client subsequently heard that the chapel was being pulled to pieces,. pews being removed, the pulpit taken down, and the floor levelled, and he (Mr. Peters), on receiving instruc- tions, wrote that the defendant must leave the place or he would be turned out. The defendant did not go out, but in the meantime it was found I that the dancing meetings increased, and on Saturday nights particularly about one hundred people were invited to the dancing saloon, where they drank herb beer. They were all trespassers on the ground, without the slightest particle of right, and he applied for an injunction to restrain the defendant from entering the premises. An ' action for ejectment had been entered, and would be heard at a later period.—The judge asked if there was any opposition to the application.—Mr. Peters said notice had been served pn the defend- ant, but there was no one to oppose.—His Honor granted the injunction asked for.

GOLBORNE. Mr. James Thomas Foard, barrister-at-law, continued his revision of the voters' lists for the Newton Division on Tuesday, when he held a court at Mr. Brnwn's Schoolroom, Gelborne. The Conservatives were again represented by Mr. Wallhead and Mr. Holbrook; and Mr. P. M. Campbell attended on behalf of the Liberals Tyra COUNTY COUNCIL.-Mr. W. H. Arnott (Messrs. Mitchell, Arnott, and Co.) claimed to be on the County Council list as occupier of land and property, in addition to being on the owners' list. The proof was satisfactory, and the claim was allowed.

" DROPPIID FROMTHS Ctonne."—Peter Houlton was objected to by the Conservatives, owing to having removed during the qualifying year.—Applicant said he removed to his new house before last Christmas.—Mr. Wallhead : The rent-book produced by this man states that he only commenced paying rent in March last.— The Revising Barrister: Where did you live between Christmas and March last? I went straight from one house to the other.—The Revising Barrister: He says he removed direct from one to the other, but, as far as the proof is concerned, he might have dropped from the clouds for aught we know Howenr, he gets the benefit of .our ignorance in this casef7Thevote was allowed.

"Lois l'sNitr Novitts."—The Conservatives objected to Robert Jones. His wife produced three rent-books, but the tenancy was not shown to be continuous.—The Revising Barrister (after perusing the books) : These books are like the penny novels—they leave off abruptly. "to be continued in ournext." (Laughter).—Applicant was certain the claim was good.—At the suggestion of the barrister, applicant again searcht‘d her house; and returned with a fourth rent-book, which completed the time, and the vote was allowed.

A COLLIER'S WAGES.—William Simm was objected to by the ConiervatiVes on the ground that' he had received parochial relief: Applicant provel that this was untrue, the information being wrong..—Applicant : I must have something for coining _here and losing my work.—The Revising Barrister: What".are you ? A collier.—How Much do you get a day ?' Six s,hillings.—What, every day? No, not every day.—You mean, that would be a good day? Yes, sir.—Well, then, I allow 6s.—The Con- servative agent handed the applicant the money. In the afternoon the revising barrister held a court at the National School, Billinge, when the lists were revised for the townships of Bitlinge Chapel Edd, Billinge Higher End, and Winstanley. This closed the work of the Newton Division.

div.head: NEWTON REVISION COURT.. . .
div.p: NEWTON REVISION COURT.. . .

The annual revision of the lists of voters for the Newton portion of the Newton Parliamentary Division was commenced at the Town Hall,. New- ton, on Monday, before Mr. L. T. Foard. Reaking Barrister. The Liberals were represented by Mt. P. M. CampelL of Eariestown, registration agent,. and Mr. Wellhead (Warrington), and Mr. Holbrook (Newton registration agent) represented the Con- servatives. The townships considered were Newton, Buttonwood, Southworth-with-Croft, and Winwick. There were 12 claims and 19 objections to. the ownership list of the Newton township, one lodger claim, and 19 occupiers' tibjections. The new claims under Division 1 (Parliamentary and County voters) were 37; under Division 2 (service fran- chise) there were no claims or objections, and under division 3 (county vote only) there were 11 objec- tions and 4 now claims. On the Bortonwood lists were one occupier's objection, and one new claim; division 1, 16 objections; 7 claims: division 3, one 'objection. Southivorth-with-Croft, division 1, two new claims; division 3, two objections, two new claims. Winwick, one new claim.

A LODGER.'S QUESTIONABLE CLAIM.—John Tweddle claimed a lodger vote in respect of a furnished bedroom and sitting-room, for which he paid 14s. a week to Ann Williams, High-street.--Mr. Campbell pointed out that Mrs. Williams was already pn the list for that house as a county voter. He asked what was the rating and rental of the house.—The Assistant Overseer (Mr. E. Houghton) said the gross was £l5, and the rateable value £l2 DX—The Barrister: He only occupies two rooms and she occupies the rest of the house.—Mr. Well- head Maintained that the house was sufficiently rated.-- The Barrister did not know that it was. They could not claim in respect of furniture, but of premises which must be of the clear annual value of £lO. He wished to. know how many rooms there were and how many people lived there—The applicant said he hail only been in his own rooms.. Hehad not been through Hie house.— The Barrister: mit you can tell us if it is a four roomed house, a ten roomed home or what.—The applicant said there might be about six rooms.—The Barrister asked what he got For the 14s. per week.—Applicant said it included fire, gas, and cooking. He paid for his meals.—Mr. Campbell said it would admit many scores in that neighbourhood in that way. There had been many struckbff.=-Mr. Wellhead: Not under these cir- cumstances.—The Barrister did not think it was good enough for £lo,.leaving only £2 10s. for the rest of the house.—The applicant: If they are worth £36 a year furnished they are surely worth £lO unfurnished.—The. Barrister: That is an argument I am not prepared to enter into'—Aftersome. further conversation, the &twis- ter said they did not get the franchise for convenience they got it ?or premises, of a clear annual value, They could not take two rooms out for £lO and say that the rest were only worth £2'los.. Even granting that the two rooms wore the best in the house they could•not do. it: It wastoo clbseand the claim would not be allowed.. AN ALIEN'S NATURALP3ATION.—THE BARRISTEIU AS, Boon CRITIC.--When the list for Newton was being gone through Mr. Campbell asked the Barrister if a foreigner' resided so lbng in the country would he not become entitled to a vote.—Mr. Wellhead No he must become naturalised.—The Barrister: He must take out natural- isation papers before he can do that.—Mr. Campbell: We have seen some ruling in the country that if a man resided five years he secures a vote.—:Mr. Wellhead : That is not naturalisation.—The Barrister said hi had not sebn any such ruling as that mentioned by Mr. Campbell but he would like to do so.—Mr. Campbell said he would riot attempt to prove it but if he could come across it he would show it to the Barrister.—The Barrister: I shall be glad to see it.—At a later period Mr_ Campbell handed to the Barrister some law book. and pointed out a passage therein, remarking' that the man Schumacher, in reference to whom the question had arisen, had been ZS years in the township and voted every time up tolast year but one.—The Barrister, after reading- the-ptrtion pointed out by Mr. Campbell, said it was curious enough. He did not know where the writer got his authority. He was an Irish gentleman named Fitzgerald, and a gentleman named Guiry who. wrotait, As tar•as he knew the law an alien was are alien all hi S life until he was naturalised.—Mr. Wellhead said the section of the Act of Parliament enacted that an alien must have resided in the country at least fiveyears', before he was entitled to claim letters of naturalisation. Before any alien could obtain a certificate he must have resided in the United Kingdorn for a period' of not less than five years, or have been in the service of the Crown for that period'. He must also bring such evidence of his intention to, continue to reside in the.country.—Thb Barrister:- This is a very valuable book. It is as clearly wrong as anythim• eve:- saw in a law book in my fife. It says "-Aliens after residing in the United Kingdom or being in the services of the Crown for a term of'not less than five yearsbeceme naturalised." A more:monstrous proposition I never saw in print. You have got a good book,.anclit with serious propositions like that,.will carry you a Tong way. (Laughter.) "A HAFTT COMMUNITY."—The list for the township of. Houghton,. Middleton and Arbury was called, and the Barrister remarked that there was no objectiomnoelaims, and no deaths required names to be struck of' the regis- ter—The assistant overseer: No, sin—The. Barrister : You are a happy community. i •

ST. HELENS. Mr. T. T. Foarcl sat at the St. Helens County Court on Friday torevise thelist of county Voters in St. Helens and' surrounding districts. The Conservatives were represented by Mr. VVallhead, Mr.. W. Holbrook, (Newton), and Mr. W. Lamb, agentr in- St. Helens,: whilst the Liberals were represented by Mr. P. M. Cautribell.(Earlestown.) , Nun VreARAGE.—Mr. Frank Baster, appeared ot behalf of himself and two brothers, Henry Baxter and Ernest Baxter, and claimed in respect of an equal interest in the Old Vicarage Parr.-..-Mr. 'Baxter, in answer to Mr. Wallhead, said the gross value of the property was £5O per year.—Mr. Wallhead : Did you purchase the property P—Mr. Baxter: No, it was devised to me for life—The Revising Barrister : Are you and your brothers trustees ?—Mr. Baxter: Yes, but it , was devised for our benefit, for our own purposes.— The Revising Barrister: Have you got the will ?—Mr. Baxter: No.—The Revising Barrister: It was left to you in equal shares P—Mr. Baxter : Yes—The Revising Yiarrister : It is an unusual thing to devise property to trustees for their, (ism use.—Mr. Wallhead : His part of the old works.—The Revising.. Barrister: Then I can quite understand it..—The claim was allowed. FATHER Arni SoNA—Mr. G. J. Newsome, of Eccleston Park, appeared to support the claim of his son for a lodger vcre. He said his son paid him £1 per month 1 for :he sole use of a furnished bedroom and other rooms when he was at home.—Mr. Campbell: What is the ratable value of this house ?—Mr., Parkinson: The gross ratable value is £SO, and the set £42 10s.—The Revising Barris er : How long • has the arrangement been in force :—Mr. Newsome i The arrangement was entered intc over twelve months ago, when my son, who is a mining engineer, went to work at the Garswood Hall Collieries, near Astron. He comes home sometimes on Sa•urday and sometimes on Friday: and stays until Monday morning.—The Revising Barrster : Is there no gas included P—Mr. Newsome: He can bgve very little gas in that time.—The vote was allowed: _

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Present Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse. VVhiston, on Thursday afterhoon, when there were present Mr. J. Kenwright (chairman), Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. J. fireball, J. Ranson, C. B. Johnson, W. Mine, W. ' Middlshurst, J. Burchall, J. Leatherbarrow, J. W. Wareing, J. Musson, W. Tyrer, J. Lowe, R. A. Graves, W. Swift, J. Whalley, and S. H. Hartley (clerk.) 1 RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were -607 inmates this week, 506 last week,, and 480 in the corresponding week last year; 85 vagrants had been relieved, against 76 last year. THE .111,Law00e VACANCY. The Local Government Board wrote intimating that they would shortly issue an order for the special election of a guardian for the town- , ship of Halewood in the room of the Rev.. Thoinas-Cliam- beN, deceased. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT COUNCILS. —The Clerk re- ported the receipt of a communication from the Clerk of the Peace Containing the proposed scheme of local government under the new Act and intimating that a meeting to finally decide upon the matter would be held at Pre6ton on the 16th ult. The scheme, gave to the Union excluding St. Helens and Widnes, one member; to Prescot, including Huyton, Woolton, and Prescot Local Board district, one member ; to Widnes, one mem- ber, and to Rainhill, including Rainfcird, the Rural Sani- tary District of Prescot Union, Windle,, Eccleston, Knowsley, Whiston, Bold, Tarbock, Cronton. Ditto, Halewood, Hale, and Speke, one member.—Mr. Middle- hurst moved that the clerk attend the meeting in ques- tion, and that he be instructed to use all the authority he could to secure four members to represent the Union. —The Clerk said he thought they could-only have four by letting Widnes have two members, and he hoped they would have two.—The motion was agreed to, and the subject dropped. THE WOOLTON ASSISTANT OVERSEER.,-Mr;. E. Baxter, assistant overseer, wrote applying for an increase of salary, stating that he had held office since April 1886 and his present remuneration was sd. in-the £. Enclosed was a communication signed by the overseers stating that Mr. Baxter discharged his duties tO their satisfac- tion. The application was referred to the Finance Com- mittee. ' RESIGNATION OF THE UNION COACHMAN.—ISIMIC Wilkinson. coachman to the Union wrote resigning his position after a servitude of four years and asking for a testimonial as to his character. The resignation was accepted and it was decided to comply-with his request for a testimonial. Joseph .Alcock, of ICemble.street, Prescot, was appointed to thevacant post. WIDNES MEDICAL OFFICER.—Mr. Wareing gave notice that at the next meeting he would move, the reappoint- ment of Dr. Cooper as medical officer for the Widnes' (lower) district.

TENDER.—Two tenders for painting and lime-washing the vagrant and tramp wards were considered, and that of Mr. Tames Appleton, Market Mee, Preseot, was accepted. TRIS Poen LAW CONFERENCE —Oft the motion of Mr. Fryer, and seconded by Mr. Miallehurst, the Chairman, the Rev. Dean Finegan, and Mr. Wareing were appointed a deputation to attend the Poor Law Conference to be held at Chester on the 12th and 13th.Oetober. This was all the business. t, ,

LOCAL PRIZETAKERS AT ALTRINVITA3C.—Mr. T. H. Wheeler, of Lymm, was the winner of-the. first prize at Altrincliam Show en Thursday for Channel Island cows, and was highly commended for another entry. Mr. Bari% Warburton, was first in one offthe pg classes, and Mr. T. Nash, of Heatley, for butter: A NARROW ESCAPE. —On Wednesday afternoon a child, son of Mr. Marsh, of z+ the. Bridgewater Armsf. whilst playing on the boat-stage at Lymm, fell into' the canal. He was on a coal-boat that was fastened to the side, he being stretched between.the boat and the side, when the swell from a passing tug caused the boat to lurch, thus throu:ng him into the water. • His screams soon Attracted a youth, who managed to drag him out before the boat had a chance of coming to the side again. Had it done so he would have been In danger of being crushed between the beat and the canal side. ' At Warrington County Court on Thursday a ca was heard in which Elizabeth Gibbons, of Ileatl: near Lymm, claimed the %um of .E 6 88.-661. from Mrs. Ledward, of Oughtrington, also near Lyinto. Mr. P. Davies, who appeared for the plaintiff, explained that the case was brought against Mrs. liedward as executrix de eom tort of the late Mrs. Thomason, and that the amount that it was sought to recover was due for groceries 1 supplied to that person before her death. Mrs, Let:ward, on the death of Martha Thomason, her grandmother, received 46 insurance from the Forester's club, and £8 from the Liverpool Victoria Friendly Society. She bad not paid any debts vgth the money, although she received express ihstructiont to pay the accoung of the plaintiff for oceries. She had also taken possession of the furniture,r and some cutting frames, that had belonged to Mrs. Thomason. Defendant admitted that the money was owing, but stated that she would not pay it, because Mrs. Thomason had made her a present ofithe fidirpiture, ,and had instructed her to pay the expenses St the r funei at out of the club money. Asked howthe clubinoney had been expended, defendant said that the mourning cost £2 10s., and a like amount was spent on the funeral, at which "about forty people stt down to tea." It NAM urged by Mr. Davies that defendant was respon- iible for the debt, but she excitedly exclaimed that she ' Irou/d not pay a farthing. The judge asked Mr. Davies if he could see his way to having the claim reduced, and consent was offered to judgment being given for a, pay- able at a 10s, a month. THE NAVAL MANEEETTRES.—The Lora' of the Admiralty have appointed a Committee consisting- of Admiral Sir William Dowel, Admiral Sir Richard Vesey Hamilton, and Rear Admiral Sir Frederick Richards, to•examine all the facts in connection with the recent naval mancruyres and to report as to the lessons which, had been learned during the course of those operations. 'nor DURHAM TeAstrort—The deceased'woman, it has been found, called at the cottage of a friend situated a Wry short distance from where her dead body was sub- sequently discovered. After waiting some time at the cottage Waddle called also; and immediately the couple left together. It is supposed that they. had met there by appointment. The time 'of' their departure- was close upon nine o'clock, and this Was the last time the deceased was seen alive. How THE EMPEROR FRED/MICE' WAS TREATED. The Central News learns that Sir 'Morel! Macliensie'S forth- coming work will consist of three parts,. the first historical and narrative, being a.true version. of every- thing connected with the case-of the Emperor Frederick from the time Dr. Mackenzie was called in at the end of May, 1887. The second part of`the work will he entirety controversial. Sir Merell Mackenzie will demonstrate that if the illustrious patient had been left in his hands the patient would have lived' twenty' months" longer, and that, in point of fact, the life of the Emperor was cut short by the was of skill of some of the German doctors. The third tart supports Sir Morel's views by statistics of cases.

OONFERENOS OF LIRERAL UNIONISM—A conference of Liberal Unionists of the Midland Counties was held at Nottingham on Wednesday; Mr. Powell Williams, M.P., preskling. Lord Selborne sent a letter of apology, hi' 'Which he insisted in the importance of steady adherence to Liberal Unionists principles, the future welfare of both Great Britian and Ireland being at stake. Resolutions were submitted expressing approval of the 1 policy of the Government in Ireland, and affirming tile desirability of imprnved organization to familiarise the electors to Uaionist principles. Mr. Chamberlain in the evening addressed a crowded meeting of Unionists at Nottingham. Replying to a resolution of welcome, be said that the policy of the Liberal Unionists was the 1 policy of the whole Liberal party down to 1886. It was I the policy of Mr. Gladstone himself until the unhappy ' moment when he accepted the policy of Mr. Parnell and i Ids paymasters the Amerean

BRITISH WORKMAN'S ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. Established 1866. Incorporated under the Companies Act, 1862. CHIEF OFFICIO, BROAD-ST. CORNER, BIRMINGHAM. EXTRACTS PROM THE DIRECTORS' REPORT for the year ending ApTil 30th, 1888. Notwithstanding the liberal terms and conditions of the Company's Policies, and the heavy amount paid in claims, and for extension expenses (resulting in the largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), the Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to carry forward a balance exceeding £15,000. Mr. James Sketehley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. J. C. Fowke. who for upwards of twenty years had been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to fill up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consented to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Fowke is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his own life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. The total Income of the Company for the year was £178,310 18s Bd, being an increase of £21,928 119 9d. The total amount of payments was £163,018 14s Id, leaving a balance upon the year's accounts of £15,292 4s 7d, making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 19s Od. The amount paid in Claims during the year was £77,479, including £4,411 6s Surrender Claims. The total sum paid np to the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 is I.od. The number of Assurants upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 18s 10d, showing a net increase of 39,070 Assurants, and £27,820 lie 9d in Premium Income. HENRY PORT, Managing Director. D. A. BECKETT, Secretary. DISTRICT OFFICE: MARKET GATE CHAMBERS, WAIIRINOTONI S. GREEN, SITFEMNTENDENT.
